## Terms — 13.8. Pattern Matching {#manual-terms-138-pattern-matching}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Pattern-Matching/

*Pattern matching* is a way to recognize and destructure values using a syntax of *patterns* that are a subset of the terms.
A pattern that recognizes and destructures a value is similar to the syntax that would be used to construct the value.
One or more *match discriminants* are simultaneously compared to a series of *match alternatives*.
Discriminants may be named.
Each alternative contains one or more comma-separated sequences of patterns; all pattern sequences must contain the same number of patterns as there are discriminants.
When a pattern sequence matches all of the discriminants, the term following the corresponding [`=>`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match) is evaluated in an environment extended with values for each [pattern variable]](#manual---tech-term-Pattern-variables) as well as an equality hypothesis for each named discriminant.
This term is called the *right-hand side* of the match alternative.

syntaxPattern Matching

```lean
term ::= ...
    | match
          ((generalizing := (trueVal | falseVal)))?
          ((motive := term))?
          matchDiscr,*
        with
      (| (term,*)|* => term)*
```

syntaxMatch Discriminants

```lean
matchDiscr ::=
    term
```

```lean
matchDiscr ::= ...
    | ident : term
```

Pattern matching expressions may alternatively use [quasiquotations](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Macros/#--tech-term-Quasiquotation) as patterns, matching the corresponding `[Lean.Syntax](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Defining-New-Syntax/#Lean___Syntax___missing)` values and treating the contents of [antiquotations](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Macros/#--tech-term-antiquotations) as ordinary patterns.
Quotation patterns are compiled differently than other patterns, so if one pattern in a [`match`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match) is syntax, then all of them must be.
Quotation patterns are described in [the section on quotations](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Macros/#quote-patterns).

Patterns are a subset of the terms.
They consist of the following:

Catch-All Patterns
:   The hole syntax `_` is a pattern that matches any value and binds no pattern variables.
    Catch-all patterns are not entirely equivalent to unused pattern variables.
    They can be used in positions where the pattern's typing would otherwise require a more specific [inaccessible pattern]](#manual---tech-term-Inaccessible-patterns), while variables cannot be used in these positions.

Identifiers
:   If an identifier is not bound in the current scope and is not applied to arguments, then it represents a pattern variable.
    *Pattern variables* match any value, and the values thus matched are bound to the pattern variable in the local environment in which the [right-hand side]](#manual---tech-term-right-hand-side) is evaluated.
    If the identifier is bound, it is a pattern if it is bound to the [constructor]](#manual---tech-term-constructors) of an [inductive type]](#manual---tech-term-Inductive-types) or if its definition has the `match_pattern` attribute.

Applications
:   Function applications are patterns if the function being applied is an identifier that is bound to a constructor or that has the `match_pattern` attribute and if all arguments are also patterns.
    If the identifier is a constructor, the pattern matches values built with that constructor if the argument patterns match the constructor's arguments.
    If it is a function with the `match_pattern` attribute, then the function application is unfolded and the resulting term's [normal form]](#manual---tech-term-normal-form) is used as the pattern.
    Default arguments are inserted as usual, and their normal forms are used as patterns.
    [Ellipses]](#manual---tech-term-ellipsis), however, result in all further arguments being treated as universal patterns, even those with associated default values or tactics.

Literals
:   [Character literals](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Characters/#char-syntax) and [string literals](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#string-syntax) are patterns that match the corresponding character or string.
    [Raw string literals](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#raw-string-literals) are allowed as patterns, but [interpolated strings](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#string-interpolation) are not.
    [Natural number literals](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#nat-syntax) in patterns are interpreted by synthesizing the corresponding `[OfNat]](#manual-OfNat___mk)` instance and reducing the resulting term to [normal form]](#manual---tech-term-normal-form), which must be a pattern.
    Similarly, [scientific literals]](#manual---tech-term-scientific-literals) are interpreted via the corresponding `[OfScientific]](#manual-OfScientific___mk)` instance.

Structure Instances
:   [Structure instances]](#manual---tech-term-structure-instance) may be used as patterns.
    They are interpreted as the corresponding structure constructor.

Quoted names
:   Quoted names, such as ``x` and ```[none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`, match the corresponding `Lean.Name` value.

Macros
:   Macros in patterns are expanded.
    They are patterns if the resulting expansions are patterns.

Inaccessible patterns
:   Inaccessible patterns are patterns that are forced to have a particular value by later typing constraints.
    Any term may be used as an inaccessible term.
    Inaccessible terms are parenthesized, with a preceding period (`.`).

syntaxInaccessible Patterns

```lean
term ::= ...
    | .(term)
```

**Example: Inaccessible Patterns**

A number's *parity* is whether it's even or odd:

```lean
inductive Parity : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Type where
| even (h : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Parity]](#manual-Parity-_LPAR_in-Inaccessible-Patterns_RPAR_) (h + h)
| odd (h : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Parity]](#manual-Parity-_LPAR_in-Inaccessible-Patterns_RPAR_) ((h + h) + 1)
def Nat.parity (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Parity]](#manual-Parity-_LPAR_in-Inaccessible-Patterns_RPAR_) n :=
[match]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match) n [with]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| 0 => [.even]](#manual-Parity___even-_LPAR_in-Inaccessible-Patterns_RPAR_) 0
| n' + 1 =>
[match]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match) n'.[parity]](#manual-Nat___parity-_LPAR_in-Inaccessible-Patterns_RPAR_) [with]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [.even]](#manual-Parity___even-_LPAR_in-Inaccessible-Patterns_RPAR_) h => [.odd]](#manual-Parity___odd-_LPAR_in-Inaccessible-Patterns_RPAR_) h
| [.odd]](#manual-Parity___odd-_LPAR_in-Inaccessible-Patterns_RPAR_) h =>
have eq : (h + 1) + (h + 1) = (h + h + 1 + 1) :=
byn:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ h [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 1 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) [(]](#manual-HAdd___mk)h [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 1[)]](#manual-HAdd___mk) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) h [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) h [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 1 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 1 [omega](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#omega)All goals completed! 🐙
eq ▸ [.even]](#manual-Parity___even-_LPAR_in-Inaccessible-Patterns_RPAR_) (h + 1)
```

Because a value of type `[Parity]](#manual-Parity-_LPAR_in-Inaccessible-Patterns_RPAR_)` contains half of a number (rounded down) as part of its representation of evenness or oddness, division by two can be implemented (in an unconventional manner) by finding a parity and then extracting the number.

```lean
def half (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[match]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match) n, n.[parity]](#manual-Nat___parity-_LPAR_in-Inaccessible-Patterns_RPAR_) [with]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| .(h + h), [.even]](#manual-Parity___even-_LPAR_in-Inaccessible-Patterns_RPAR_) h => h
| .(h + h + 1), [.odd]](#manual-Parity___odd-_LPAR_in-Inaccessible-Patterns_RPAR_) h => h
```

Because the index structure of `[Parity.even]](#manual-Parity___even-_LPAR_in-Inaccessible-Patterns_RPAR_)` and `[Parity.odd]](#manual-Parity___odd-_LPAR_in-Inaccessible-Patterns_RPAR_)` force the number to have a certain form that is not otherwise a valid pattern, patterns that match on it must use inaccessible patterns for the number being divided.

Patterns may additionally be named.
Named patterns associate a name with a pattern; in subsequent patterns and on the right-hand side of the match alternative, the name refers to the part of the value that was matched by the given pattern.
Named patterns are written with an `@` between the name and the pattern.
Just like discriminants, named patterns may also be provided with names for equality assumptions.

syntaxNamed Patterns

```lean
term ::= ...
    | ident@term
```

```lean
term ::= ...
    | ident@ident:term
```

### 13.8.1. Types {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Terms--Pattern-Matching--Types}

Each discriminant must be well typed.
Because patterns are a subset of terms, their types can also be checked.
Each pattern that matches a given discriminant must have the same type as the corresponding discriminant.

The [right-hand side]](#manual---tech-term-right-hand-side) of each match alternative should have the same type as the overall [`match`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match) term.
To support dependent types, matching a discriminant against a pattern refines the types that are expected within the scope of the pattern.
In both subsequent patterns in the same match alternative and the right-hand side's type, occurrences of the discriminant are replaced by the pattern that it was matched against.

**Example: Type Refinement**

This [indexed family]](#manual---tech-term-indexed-families) describes mostly-balanced trees, with the depth encoded in the type.

```lean
inductive BalancedTree (α : Type u) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Type u where
| empty : [BalancedTree]](#manual-BalancedTree-_LPAR_in-Type-Refinement_RPAR_) α 0
| branch
(left : [BalancedTree]](#manual-BalancedTree-_LPAR_in-Type-Refinement_RPAR_) α n)
(val : α)
(right : [BalancedTree]](#manual-BalancedTree-_LPAR_in-Type-Refinement_RPAR_) α n) :
[BalancedTree]](#manual-BalancedTree-_LPAR_in-Type-Refinement_RPAR_) α (n + 1)
| lbranch
(left : [BalancedTree]](#manual-BalancedTree-_LPAR_in-Type-Refinement_RPAR_) α (n + 1))
(val : α)
(right : [BalancedTree]](#manual-BalancedTree-_LPAR_in-Type-Refinement_RPAR_) α n) :
[BalancedTree]](#manual-BalancedTree-_LPAR_in-Type-Refinement_RPAR_) α (n + 2)
| rbranch
(left : [BalancedTree]](#manual-BalancedTree-_LPAR_in-Type-Refinement_RPAR_) α n)
(val : α)
(right : [BalancedTree]](#manual-BalancedTree-_LPAR_in-Type-Refinement_RPAR_) α (n + 1)) :
[BalancedTree]](#manual-BalancedTree-_LPAR_in-Type-Refinement_RPAR_) α (n + 2)
```

To begin the implementation of a function to construct a perfectly balanced tree with some initial element and a given depth, a [hole](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Holes/#--tech-term-hole) can be used for the definition.

```lean
def BalancedTree.filledWith
(x : α) (depth : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) :
[BalancedTree]](#manual-BalancedTree-_LPAR_in-Type-Refinement_RPAR_) α depth :=
_
```

The error message demonstrates that the tree should have the indicated depth.

```lean
don't know how to synthesize placeholder
context:
α:Type ux:αdepth:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ [BalancedTree]](#manual-BalancedTree-_LPAR_in-Type-Refinement_RPAR_) α depth
```

Matching on the expected depth and inserting holes results in an error message for each hole.
These messages demonstrate that the expected type has been refined, with `depth` replaced by the matched values.

```lean
def BalancedTree.filledWith
(x : α) (depth : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) :
[BalancedTree]](#manual-BalancedTree-_LPAR_in-Type-Refinement_RPAR_) α depth :=
[match]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match) depth [with]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| 0 => _
| n + 1 => _
```

The first hole yields the following message:

```lean
don't know how to synthesize placeholder
context:
α:Type ux:αdepth:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ [BalancedTree]](#manual-BalancedTree-_LPAR_in-Type-Refinement_RPAR_) α 0
```

The second hole yields the following message:

```lean
don't know how to synthesize placeholder
context:
α:Type ux:αdepth n:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ [BalancedTree]](#manual-BalancedTree-_LPAR_in-Type-Refinement_RPAR_) α [(]](#manual-HAdd___mk)n [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 1[)]](#manual-HAdd___mk)
```

Matching on the depth of a tree and the tree itself leads to a refinement of the tree's type according to the depth's pattern.
This means that certain combinations are not well-typed, such as `0` and `[branch]](#manual-BalancedTree___branch-_LPAR_in-Type-Refinement_RPAR_)`, because refining the second discriminant's type yields `[BalancedTree]](#manual-BalancedTree-_LPAR_in-Type-Refinement_RPAR_) α 0` which does not match the constructor's type.

```lean
def BalancedTree.isPerfectlyBalanced
(n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (t : [BalancedTree]](#manual-BalancedTree-_LPAR_in-Type-Refinement_RPAR_) α n) : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) :=
[match]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match) n, t [with]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| 0, [.empty]](#manual-BalancedTree___empty-_LPAR_in-Type-Refinement_RPAR_) => [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| 0, [.branch]](#manual-BalancedTree___branch-_LPAR_in-Type-Refinement_RPAR_) left val right =>
isPerfectlyBalanced left &&
isPerfectlyBalanced right
| _, _ => false
```

```lean
Type mismatch
  left.[branch]](#manual-BalancedTree___branch-_LPAR_in-Type-Refinement_RPAR_) val right
has type
  [BalancedTree]](#manual-BalancedTree-_LPAR_in-Type-Refinement_RPAR_) ?m.13 [(]](#manual-HAdd___mk)?m.12 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 1[)]](#manual-HAdd___mk)
but is expected to have type
  [BalancedTree]](#manual-BalancedTree-_LPAR_in-Type-Refinement_RPAR_) α 0
```

#### 13.8.1.1. Pattern Equality Proofs {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Terms--Pattern-Matching--Types--Pattern-Equality-Proofs}

When a discriminant is named, [`match`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match) generates a proof that the pattern and discriminant are equal, binding it to the provided name in the [right-hand side]](#manual---tech-term-right-hand-side).
This is useful to bridge the gap between dependent pattern matching on indexed families and APIs that expect explicit propositional arguments, and it can help tactics that make use of assumptions to succeed.

**Example: Pattern Equality Proofs**

The function `[last?]](#manual-last___-_LPAR_in-Pattern-Equality-Proofs_RPAR_)`, which either throws an exception or returns the last element of its argument, uses the standard library function `[List.getLast](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___getLast)`.
This function expects a proof that the list in question is nonempty.
Naming the match on `xs` ensures that there's an assumption in scope that states that `xs` is equal to `_ :: _`, which `[simp_all](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp_all)` uses to discharge the goal.

```lean
def last? (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : [Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) α :=
[match]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match) h : xs [with]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [] =>
[.error](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) "Can't take first element of empty list"
| _ :: _ =>
[.ok](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) <| xs.[getLast](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___getLast) (show xs ≠ [] byAll goals completed! 🐙 [intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#intro) h'α:Type ?u.3xs:[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) αhead✝:αtail✝:[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) αh:xs [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) head✝ [::](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) tail✝h':xs [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)⊢ [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False); [simp_all](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp_all)All goals completed! 🐙)
```

Without the name, `[simp_all](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp_all)` is unable to find the contradiction.

```lean
def last?' (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : [Except](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) α :=
[match]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match) xs [with]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [] =>
[.error](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) "Can't take first element of empty list"
| _ :: _ =>
[.ok](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#Except___error) <| xs.[getLast](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___getLast) (show xs ≠ [] byα:Type ?u.3xs:[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) αhead✝:αtail✝:[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) αh':xs [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)⊢ [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False) [intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#intro) h'α:Type ?u.3xs:[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) αhead✝:αtail✝:[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) αh':xs [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)⊢ [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False); [simp_all](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp_all)α:Type ?u.3xs:[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) αhead✝:αtail✝:[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) αh':xs [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)⊢ [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False))
```

```lean
simp_all made no progress
```

#### 13.8.1.2. Explicit Motives {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Terms--Pattern-Matching--Types--Explicit-Motives}

Pattern matching is not a built-in primitive of Lean.
Instead, it is translated to applications of [recursors]](#manual---tech-term-recursor) via [auxiliary matching functions]](#manual---tech-term-auxiliary-matching-functions).
Both require a [*motive*]](#manual---tech-term-motive) that explains the relationship between the discriminant and the resulting type.
Generally, the [`match`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match) elaborator is capable of synthesizing an appropriate motive, and the refinement of types that occurs during pattern matching is a result of the motive that was selected.
In some specialized circumstances, a different motive may be needed and may be provided explicitly using the `(motive := …)` syntax of [`match`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match).
This motive should be a function type that expects at least as many parameters as there are discriminants.
The type that results from applying a function with this type to the discriminants in order is the type of the entire [`match`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match) term, and the type that results from applying a function with this type to all patterns in each alternative is the type of that alternative's [right-hand side]](#manual---tech-term-right-hand-side).

**Example: Matching with an Explicit Motive**

An explicit motive can be used to provide type information that is otherwise unavailable from the surrounding context.
Attempting to match on a number and a proof that it is in fact `5` is an error, because there's no reason to connect the number to the proof:

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval)
[match]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match) 5, [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next) [with]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| 5, [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next) => "ok"
```

```lean
Invalid match expression: This pattern contains metavariables:
  [Eq.refl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) ?m.14
```

An explicit motive explains the relationship between the discriminants:

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval)
[match]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match) (motive := (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) → n = 5 → [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) 5, [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next) [with]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| 5, [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next) => "ok"
```

```lean
"ok"
```

#### 13.8.1.3. Discriminant Refinement {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Terms--Pattern-Matching--Types--Discriminant-Refinement}

When matching on an indexed family, the indices must also be discriminants.
Otherwise, the pattern would not be well typed: it is a type error if an index is just a variable but the type of a constructor requires a more specific value.
However, a process called discriminant refinement automatically adds indices as additional discriminants.

**Example: Discriminant Refinement**

In the definition of `[f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-Discriminant-Refinement_RPAR_)`, the equality proof is the only discriminant.
However, equality is an indexed family, and the match is only valid when `n` is an additional discriminant.

```lean
def f (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (p : n = 3) : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) :=
[match]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match) p [with]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next) => "ok"
```

Using `#print` demonstrates that the additional discriminant was added automatically.

```lean
#print [f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-Discriminant-Refinement_RPAR_)
```

```lean
def f : (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) → n [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 3 → [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) :=
fun n p =>
  match 3, p with
  | .(n), ⋯ => "ok"
```

#### 13.8.1.4. Generalization {#manual-match-generalization}

The pattern match elaborator automatically determines the motive by finding occurrences of the discriminants in the expected type, generalizing them in the types of subsequent discriminants so that the appropriate pattern can be substituted.
Additionally, occurrences of the discriminants in the types of variables in the context are generalized and substituted by default.
This latter behavior can be turned off by passing the `(generalizing := false)` flag to [`match`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match).

**Example: Matching, With and Without Generalization**

In this definition of `boolCases`, the assumption `b` is generalized in the type of `h` and then replaced with the actual pattern.
This means that `ifTrue` and `ifFalse` have the types `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) = [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) → α` and `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) = [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) → α` in their respective cases, but `h`'s type mentions the original discriminant.

```lean
def boolCases (b : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false))
(ifTrue : b = [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) → α)
(ifFalse : b = [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) → α) :
α :=
[match]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match) h : b [with]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) => ifTrue h
| [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) => ifFalse h
```

The error for the first case is typical of both:

```lean
Application type mismatch: The argument
  h
has type
  b [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
but is expected to have type
  [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
in the application
  ifTrue h
```

Turning off generalization allows type checking to succeed, because `b` remains in the types of `ifTrue` and `ifFalse`.

```lean
def boolCases (b : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false))
(ifTrue : b = [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) → α)
(ifFalse : b = [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) → α) :
α :=
[match]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match) (generalizing := false) h : b [with]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) => ifTrue h
| [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) => ifFalse h
```

In the generalized version, `[rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)` could have been used as the proof arguments as an alternative.

### 13.8.2. Custom Pattern Functions {#manual-match_pattern-functions}

In patterns, defined constants with the `match_pattern` attribute are unfolded and normalized rather than rejected.
This allows a more convenient syntax to be used for many patterns.
In the standard library, `[Nat.add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___add)`, `[HAdd.hAdd]](#manual-HAdd___mk)`, `[Add.add]](#manual-Add___mk)`, and `[Neg.neg]](#manual-Neg___mk)` all have this attribute, which allows patterns like `n + 1` instead of `[Nat.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) n`.
Similarly, `[Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit)` and `[Unit.unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit___unit)` are definitions that set the respective [universe parameters]](#manual---tech-term-universe-parameters) of `[PUnit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#PUnit___unit)` and `[PUnit.unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#PUnit___unit)` to 0; the `match_pattern` attribute on `[Unit.unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit___unit)` allows it to be used in patterns, where it expands to `[PUnit.unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#PUnit___unit).{0}`.

attributeAttribute for Match Patterns

The `match_pattern` attribute indicates that a definition should be unfolded, rather than rejected, in a pattern.

```lean
attr ::= ...
    | match_pattern
```

**Example: Match Patterns Follow Reduction**

The following function can't be compiled:

```lean
def nonzero (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) :=
[match]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match) n [with]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| 0 => [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| 1 + k => true
```

The error message on the pattern `1 + _` is:

```lean
Invalid pattern(s): `k` is an explicit pattern variable, but it only occurs in positions that are inaccessible to pattern matching:
  .([Nat.add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___add) 1 k)
```

This is because `[Nat.add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___add)` is defined by recursion on its second parameter, equivalently to:

```lean
def add : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| a, [Nat.zero](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) => a
| a, [Nat.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) b => [Nat.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) ([Nat.add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___add) a b)
```

No [ι-reduction]](#manual---tech-term-___-reduction) is possible, because the value being matched is a variable, not a constructor.
`1 + k` gets stuck as `[Nat.add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___add) 1 k`, which is not a valid pattern.

In the case of `k + 1`, that is, `[Nat.add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___add) k ([.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [.zero](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))`, the second pattern matches, so it reduces to `[Nat.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) ([Nat.add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___add) k [.zero](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))`.
The second pattern now matches, yielding `[Nat.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) k`, which is a valid pattern.

### 13.8.3. Pattern Matching Functions {#manual-pattern-fun}

syntaxPattern-Matching Functions

Functions may be specified via pattern matching by writing a sequence of patterns after `fun`, each preceded by a vertical bar (`|`).

```lean
term ::= ...
    | fun
        (| term,* => term)*
```

This desugars to a function that immediately pattern-matches on its arguments.

**Example: Pattern-Matching Functions**

`[isZero]](#manual-isZero-_LPAR_in-Pattern-Matching-Functions_RPAR_)` is defined using a pattern-matching function abstraction, while `[isZero']](#manual-isZero___-_LPAR_in-Pattern-Matching-Functions_RPAR_)` is defined using a pattern match expression:

```lean
def isZero : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) :=
fun
| 0 => [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| _ => [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
def isZero' : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) :=
fun n =>
[match]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match) n [with]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| 0 => [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| _ => [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

Because the former is syntactic sugar for the latter, they are definitionally equal:

```lean
example : [isZero]](#manual-isZero-_LPAR_in-Pattern-Matching-Functions_RPAR_) = [isZero']](#manual-isZero___-_LPAR_in-Pattern-Matching-Functions_RPAR_) := [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)
```

The desugaring is visible in the output of `#print`:

```lean
#print [isZero]](#manual-isZero-_LPAR_in-Pattern-Matching-Functions_RPAR_)
```

outputs

```lean
def isZero : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) :=
fun x =>
  match x with
  | 0 => [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
  | x => [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

while

```lean
#print [isZero']](#manual-isZero___-_LPAR_in-Pattern-Matching-Functions_RPAR_)
```

outputs

```lean
def isZero' : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) :=
fun n =>
  match n with
  | 0 => [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
  | x => [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

### 13.8.4. Other Pattern Matching Operators {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Terms--Pattern-Matching--Other-Pattern-Matching-Operators}

In addition to [`match`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match) and [`if let`]](#manual-termIfLet), there are a few other operators that perform pattern matching.

syntaxThe `matches` Operator

The [`matches`]](#manual-Lean____FLQQ_term_Matches_____FLQQ_) operator returns `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` if the term on the left matches the pattern on the right.

```lean
term ::= ...
    | term matches term
```

When branching on the result of [`matches`]](#manual-Lean____FLQQ_term_Matches_____FLQQ_), it's usually better to use [`if let`]](#manual-termIfLet), which can bind pattern variables in addition to checking whether a pattern matches.

If there are no constructor patterns that could match a discriminant or sequence of discriminants, then the code in question is unreachable, as there must be a false assumption in the local context.
The [`nomatch`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___nomatch) expression is a match with zero cases that can have any type whatsoever, so long as there are no possible cases that could match the discriminants.

syntaxCaseless Pattern Matches

```lean
term ::= ...
    | nomatch term,*
```

**Example: Inconsistent Indices**

There are no constructor patterns that can match both proofs in this example:

```lean
example (p1 : x = "Hello") (p2 : x = "world") : [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False) :=
[nomatch]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___nomatch) p1, p2
```

This is because they separately refine the value of `x` to unequal strings.
Thus, the [`nomatch`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___nomatch) operator allows the example's body to prove `[False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)` (or any other proposition or type).

When the expected type is a function type, [`nofun`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___nofun) is shorthand for a function that takes as many parameters as the type indicates in which the body is [`nomatch`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___nomatch) applied to all of the parameters.

syntaxCaseless Functions

```lean
term ::= ...
    | nofun
```

**Example: Impossible Functions**

Instead of introducing arguments for both equality proofs and then using both in a [`nomatch`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___nomatch), it is possible to use [`nofun`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___nofun).

```lean
example : x = "Hello" → x = "world" → [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False) := [nofun]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___nofun)
```

---



## Terms — 13.9. Holes {#manual-terms-139-holes}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Holes/

A *hole* or *placeholder term* is a term that indicates the absence of instructions to the elaborator.
In terms, holes can be automatically filled when the surrounding context would only allow one type-correct term to be written where the hole is.
Otherwise, a hole is an error.
In patterns, holes represent universal patterns that can match anything.

syntaxHoles

Holes are written with underscores.

```lean
term ::= ...
    | _
```

**Example: Filling Holes with Unification**

The function `[the]](#manual-the-_LPAR_in-Filling-Holes-with-Unification_RPAR_)` can be used similarly to `show` or a [type ascription](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Type-Ascription/#--tech-term-Type-ascriptions).

```lean
def the (α : Sort u) (x : α) : α := x
```

If the second parameter's type can be inferred, then the first parameter can be a hole.
Both of these commands are equivalent:

```lean
[#check]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___check) [the]](#manual-the-_LPAR_in-Filling-Holes-with-Unification_RPAR_) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) "Hello!"
[#check]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___check) [the]](#manual-the-_LPAR_in-Filling-Holes-with-Unification_RPAR_) _ "Hello"
```

When writing proofs, it can be convenient to explicitly introduce unknown values.
This is done via *synthetic holes*, which are never solved by unification and may occur in multiple positions.
They are primarily useful in tactic proofs, and are described in [the section on metavariables in proofs](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Reading-Proof-States/#metavariables-in-proofs).

syntaxSynthetic Holes

```lean
term ::= ...
    | ?ident
```

```lean
term ::= ...
    | ?_
```

## Terms — 13.10. Type Ascription {#manual-terms-1310-type-ascription}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Type-Ascription/

*Type ascriptions* explicitly annotate terms with their types.
They are a way to provide Lean with the expected type for a term.
This type must be definitionally equal to the type that is expected based on the term's context.
Type ascriptions are useful for more than just documenting a program:

- There may not be sufficient information in the program text to derive a type for a term. Ascriptions are one way to provide the type.
- An inferred type may not be the one that was desired for a term.
- The expected type of a term is used to drive the insertion of [coercions]](#manual---tech-term-coercion), and ascriptions are one way to control where coercions are inserted.

syntaxPostfix Type Ascriptions

Type ascriptions must be surrounded by parentheses.
They indicate that the first term's type is the second term.

```lean
term ::= ...
    | ([anonymous]term : term)
```

In cases where the term that requires a type ascription is long, such as a tactic proof or a [`do`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do) block, the postfix type ascription with its mandatory parentheses can be difficult to read.
Additionally, for both proofs and [`do`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do) blocks, the term's type is essential to its interpretation.
In these cases, the prefix versions can be easier to read.

syntaxPrefix Type Ascriptions

```lean
term ::= ...
    | show term from term
```

When the term in the body of `show` is a tactic proof, the keyword `from` may be omitted.

```lean
term ::= ...
    | show term by tacticSeq
```

**Example: Ascribing Types to do Blocks**

This example lacks sufficient type information to synthesize the `[Pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk)` instance.

```lean
example := [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
return 5
```

```lean
typeclass instance problem is stuck
  [Pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) ?m.8

Note: Lean will not try to resolve this typeclass instance problem because the type argument to `[Pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk)` is a metavariable. This argument must be fully determined before Lean will try to resolve the typeclass.

Hint: Adding type annotations and supplying implicit arguments to functions can give Lean more information for typeclass resolution. For example, if you have a variable `x` that you intend to be a `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, but Lean reports it as having an unresolved type like `?m`, replacing `x` with `(x : Nat)` can get typeclass resolution un-stuck.
```

A prefix type ascription with `show`, together with a [hole]](#manual---tech-term-hole), can be used to indicate the monad.
The [default]](#manual---tech-term-default-instances) `[OfNat]](#manual-OfNat___mk) _ 5` instance provides enough type information to fill the hole with `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`.

```lean
example := show [StateM](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#StateM) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) _ from [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
return 5
```

There is an important difference between postfix type ascriptions and `show`.
Ordinary postfix type ascriptions change the type that is expected for the term, which can change the way that the term elaborates.
After elaboration, however, Lean infers the type of the resulting term and uses that inferred type for further elaboration tasks.
On the other hand, `show` elaborates to a term whose inferred type is the ascribed type.
The difference can be observed when using [generalized field notation]](#manual---tech-term-generalized-field-notation), where the ascribed type is only guaranteed to be used to resolve fields when using `show`.

**Example: Postfix Ascription vs show**

This definition establishes an alternative name for `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)`:

```lean
def Colors := [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)
```

A postfix type ascription provides the type information that's needed to determine the implicit argument `[String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)` to `[List.nil](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)`, but the resulting type is still `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)`:

```lean
[#check]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___check) ([] : [Colors]](#manual-Colors-_LPAR_in-Postfix-Ascription-vs--show_RPAR_))
```

```lean
[[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)
```

When using `show`, on the other hand, the elaborated term is constructed in such a way that the inferred type is `[Colors]](#manual-Colors-_LPAR_in-Postfix-Ascription-vs--show_RPAR_)`:

```lean
[#check]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___check) (show [Colors]](#manual-Colors-_LPAR_in-Postfix-Ascription-vs--show_RPAR_) from [])
```

```lean
have this := [[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil);
this : [Colors]](#manual-Colors-_LPAR_in-Postfix-Ascription-vs--show_RPAR_)
```

This function is designed to be invoked using [generalized field notation]](#manual---tech-term-generalized-field-notation):

```lean
def Colors.hasYellow (cs : [Colors]](#manual-Colors-_LPAR_in-Postfix-Ascription-vs--show_RPAR_)) : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) :=
cs.[any](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___any) (·.[toLower](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___toLower) == "yellow")
```

Due to the differences in their inferred types, it can be used with `show`, but not with the postfix type ascription:

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) ([] : [Colors]](#manual-Colors-_LPAR_in-Postfix-Ascription-vs--show_RPAR_)).hasYellow
```

```lean

of type `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)`
```

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) (show [Colors]](#manual-Colors-_LPAR_in-Postfix-Ascription-vs--show_RPAR_) from []).[hasYellow]](#manual-Colors___hasYellow-_LPAR_in-Postfix-Ascription-vs--show_RPAR_)
```

## Tactic Proofs {#manual-tactic-proofs}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/

The tactic language is a special-purpose programming language for constructing proofs.
In Lean, [propositions]](#manual---tech-term-Propositions) are represented by types, and proofs are terms that inhabit these types.
The [section on propositions]](#manual-propositions) describes propositions in more detail.
While terms are designed to make it convenient to indicate a specific inhabitant of a type, tactics are designed to make it convenient to demonstrate that a type is inhabited.
This distinction exists because it's important that definitions pick out the precise objects of interest and that programs return the intended results, but proof irrelevance means that there's no *technical* reason to prefer one proof term over another.
For example, given two assumptions of a given type, a program must be carefully written to use the correct one, while a proof may use either without consequence.

Tactics are imperative programs that modify a *proof state*.
A proof state consists of an ordered sequence of *goals*, which are contexts of local assumptions together with types to be inhabited; a tactic may either *succeed* with a possibly-empty sequence of further goals (called *subgoals*) or *fail* if it cannot make progress.
If a tactic succeeds with no subgoals, then the proof is complete.
If it succeeds with one or more subgoals, then its goal or goals will be proved when those subgoals have been proved.
The first goal in the proof state is called the *main goal*.
While most tactics affect only the main goal, operators such as `[<;>](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/The-Tactic-Language/#_LT__SEMI__GT_)` and `[all_goals](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/The-Tactic-Language/#all_goals)` can be used to apply a tactic to many goals, and operators such as bullets, `[next](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/The-Tactic-Language/#next)` or `[case](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/The-Tactic-Language/#case)` can narrow the focus of subsequent tactics to only a single goal in the proof state.

Behind the scenes, tactics construct proof terms.
Proof terms are independently checkable evidence of a theorem's truth, written in Lean's type theory.
Each proof is checked in the [kernel]](#manual---tech-term-kernel), and can be verified with independently-implemented external checkers, so the worst outcome from a bug in a tactic is a confusing error message, rather than an incorrect proof.
Each goal in a tactic proof corresponds to an incomplete portion of a proof term.

## Tactic Proofs — 14.1. Running Tactics {#manual-tactic-proofs-141-running-tactics}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Running-Tactics/

syntaxTactic Proofs with `by`

Tactics are included in terms using `by`, which is followed by a sequence of tactics in which each has the same indentation:

```lean
term ::= ...
    | by
      tacticSeq
```

Alternatively, explicit braces and semicolons may be used:

```lean
term ::= ...
    | by { tactic* }
```

Tactics are invoked using the `by` term.
When the elaborator encounters `by`, it invokes the tactic interpreter to construct the resulting term.
Tactic proofs may be embedded via `by` in any context in which a term can occur.

---



## Tactic Proofs — 14.2. Reading Proof States {#manual-tactic-proofs-142-reading-proof-states}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Reading-Proof-States/

The goals in a proof state are displayed in order, with the main goal on top.
Goals may be either named or anonymous.
Named goals are indicated with `case` at the top (called a *case label*), while anonymous goals have no such indicator.
Tactics assign goal names, typically on the basis of constructor names, parameter names, structure field names, or the nature of the reasoning step implemented by the tactic.

**Example: Named goals**

This proof state contains four goals, all of which are named.
This is part of a proof that the `[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` instance is lawful (that is, to provide the `[LawfulMonad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Laws/#LawfulMonad___mk) [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` instance), and the case names (highlighted below) come from the names of the fields of `[LawfulMonad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Laws/#LawfulMonad___mk)`.

**Example: Anonymous Goals**

This proof state contains a single anonymous goal.

n:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)k:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ n [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) k [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) k [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) n

The `[case](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/The-Tactic-Language/#case)` and `[case'](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/The-Tactic-Language/#case___)` tactics can be used to select a new main goal using the desired goal's name.
When names are assigned in the context of a goal which itself has a name, the new goals' names are appended to the main goal's name with a dot (`'.', Unicode FULL STOP (0x2e)`) between them.

**Example: Hierarchical Goal Names**

Each goal consists of a sequence of assumptions and a desired conclusion.
Each assumption has a name and a type; the conclusion is a type.
Assumptions are either arbitrary elements of some type or statements that are presumed true.

**Example: Assumption Names and Conclusion**

This goal has four assumptions:

consα:Type ?u.3x:αxs:[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) αih:xs [++]](#manual-HAppend___mk) [[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) xs⊢ x [::](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) xs [++]](#manual-HAppend___mk) [[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) x [::](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) xs

They are:

- `α`, an arbitrary type
- `x`, an arbitrary `α`
- `xs`, an arbitrary `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α`
- `ih`, an induction hypothesis that asserts that appending the empty list to `xs` is equal to `xs`.

The conclusion is the statement that prepending `x` to both sides of the equality in the induction hypothesis results in equal lists.

Some assumptions are *inaccessible*,   which means that they cannot be referred to explicitly by name.
Inaccessible assumptions occur when an assumption is created without a specified name or when the assumption's name is shadowed by a later assumption.
Inaccessible assumptions should be regarded as anonymous; they are presented as if they had names because they may be referred to in later assumptions or in the conclusion, and displaying a name allows these references to be distinguished from one another.
In particular, inaccessible assumptions are presented with daggers (`†`) after their names.

**Example: Accessible Assumption Names**

In this proof state, all assumptions are accessible.

bind\_pure\_compα:Type ?u.3β:Type ?u.3f:α → βx:[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) α⊢ (do
let a ← x
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (f a)) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl)
f [<$>](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk) x

**Example: Inaccessible Assumption Names**

In this proof state, only the first and third assumptions are accessible.
The second and fourth are inaccessible, and their names include a dagger to indicate that they cannot be referenced.

bind\_pure\_compα:Type ?u.3β✝:Type ?u.3f:α → β✝x✝:[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) α⊢ (do
let a ← x✝
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) (f a)) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl)
f [<$>](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Functor___mk) x✝

Inaccessible assumptions can still be used.
Tactics such as `[assumption](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#assumption)` or `[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)` can scan the entire list of assumptions, finding one that is useful, and `[contradiction](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#contradiction)` can eliminate the current goal by finding an impossible assumption without naming it.
Other tactics, such as `[rename_i](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/The-Tactic-Language/#rename_i)` and `[next](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/The-Tactic-Language/#next)`, can be used to name inaccessible assumptions, making them accessible.
Additionally, assumptions can be referred to by their type, by writing the type in single guillemets.

syntaxAssumptions by Type

Single guillemets around a term represent a reference to some term in scope with that type.

```lean
term ::= ...
    | ‹term›
```

This can be used to refer to local lemmas by their theorem statement rather than by name, or to refer to assumptions regardless of whether they have explicit names.

**Example: Assumptions by Type**

In the following proof, `[cases](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#cases)` is repeatedly used to analyze a number.
At the beginning of the proof, the number is named `x`, but `[cases](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#cases)` generates an inaccessible name for subsequent numbers.
Rather than providing names, the proof takes advantage of the fact that there is a single assumption of type `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` at any given time and uses `‹Nat›` to refer to it.
After the iteration, there is an assumption that `n + 3 < 3`, which `[contradiction](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#contradiction)` can use to remove the goal from consideration.

```lean

[intros](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#intros)x:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)a✝:x [<]](#manual-LT___mk) 3⊢ x ∈ [[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)0[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 1[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 2[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
[iterate](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/The-Tactic-Language/#iterate) 3
[cases](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#cases) ‹Nat›succ.succ.zeroa✝:0 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 1 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 1 [<]](#manual-LT___mk) 3⊢ 0 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 1 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 1 ∈ [[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)0[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 1[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 2[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)succ.succ.succn✝:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)a✝:n✝ [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 1 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 1 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 1 [<]](#manual-LT___mk) 3⊢ n✝ [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 1 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 1 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 1 ∈ [[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)0[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 1[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 2[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
```

**Example: Assumptions by Type, Outside Proofs**

Single-guillemet syntax also works outside of proofs:

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval)
let x := 1
let y := 2
‹Nat›
```

```lean
2
```

This is generally not a good idea for non-propositions, however—when it matters *which* element of a type is selected, it's better to select it explicitly.

### 14.2.1. Hiding Proofs and Large Terms {#manual-hiding-terms-in-proof-states}

Terms in proof states can be quite big, and there may be many assumptions.
Because of definitional proof irrelevance, proof terms typically give little useful information.
By default, they are not shown in goals in proof states unless they are *atomic*, meaning that they contain no subterms.
Hiding proofs is controlled by two options: `[pp.proofs]](#manual-pp___proofs)` turns the feature on and off, while `[pp.proofs.threshold]](#manual-pp___proofs___threshold)` determines a size threshold for proof hiding.

**Example: Hiding Proof Terms**

In this proof state, the proof that `0 < n` is hidden.

n:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)i:[Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) ngt:↑i > 5⊢ [⟨](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk)0[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) ⋯[⟩](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) [<]](#manual-LT___mk) i

option

```lean
pp.proofs
```

Default value: `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`

(pretty printer) display proofs when true, and replace proofs appearing within expressions by `⋯` when false

option

```lean
pp.proofs.threshold
```

Default value: `0`

(pretty printer) when `[pp.proofs]](#manual-pp___proofs)` is false, controls the complexity of proofs at which they begin being replaced with `⋯`

Additionally, non-proof terms may be hidden when they are too large.
In particular, Lean will hide terms that are below a configurable depth threshold, and it will hide the remainder of a term once a certain amount in total has been printed.
Showing deep terms can be enabled or disabled with the option `[pp.deepTerms]](#manual-pp___deepTerms)`, and the depth threshold can be configured with the option `[pp.deepTerms.threshold]](#manual-pp___deepTerms___threshold)`.
The maximum number of pretty printer steps can be configured with the option `[pp.maxSteps]](#manual-pp___maxSteps)`.
Printing very large terms can lead to slowdowns or even stack overflows in tooling; please be conservative when adjusting these options' values.

option

```lean
pp.deepTerms
```

Default value: `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`

(pretty printer) display deeply nested terms, replacing them with `⋯` if set to false

option

```lean
pp.deepTerms.threshold
```

Default value: `50`

(pretty printer) when `[pp.deepTerms]](#manual-pp___deepTerms)` is false, the depth at which terms start being replaced with `⋯`

option

```lean
pp.maxSteps
```

Default value: `5000`

(pretty printer) maximum number of expressions to visit, after which terms will pretty print as `⋯`

### 14.2.2. Metavariables {#manual-metavariables-in-proofs}

Terms that begin with a question mark are *metavariables* that correspond to an unknown value.
They may stand for either [universe]](#manual---tech-term-universes) levels or for terms.
Some metavariables arise as part of Lean's elaboration process, when not enough information is yet available to determine a value.
These metavariables' names have a numeric component at the end, such as `?m.392` or `?u.498`.
Other metavariables come into existence as a result of tactics or [synthetic holes]](#manual---tech-term-synthetic-holes).
These metavariables' names do not have a numeric component.
Metavariables that result from tactics frequently appear as goals whose [case labels]](#manual---tech-term-case-label) match the name of the metavariable.

**Example: Universe Level Metavariables**

In this proof state, the universe level of `α` is unknown:

α:Type ?u.4x:αxs:[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) αelem:x ∈ xs⊢ xs.[length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length) > 0

**Example: Type Metavariables**

In this proof state, the type of list elements is unknown.
The metavariable is repeated because the unknown type must be the same in both positions.

x:?m.8xs:[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) ?m.8elem:x ∈ xs⊢ xs.[length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length) > 0

**Example: Metavariables in Proofs**

In this proof state,

i:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)j:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)k:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h1:i [<]](#manual-LT___mk) jh2:j [<]](#manual-LT___mk) k⊢ i [<]](#manual-LT___mk) k

applying the tactic `[apply](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#apply) Nat.lt_transh₁i:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)j:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)k:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h1:i [<]](#manual-LT___mk) jh2:j [<]](#manual-LT___mk) k⊢ i [<]](#manual-LT___mk) ?mai:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)j:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)k:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h1:i [<]](#manual-LT___mk) jh2:j [<]](#manual-LT___mk) k⊢ ?m [<]](#manual-LT___mk) kmi:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)j:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)k:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h1:i [<]](#manual-LT___mk) jh2:j [<]](#manual-LT___mk) k⊢ [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` results in the following proof state, in which the middle value of the transitivity step `?m` is unknown:

h₁i:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)j:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)k:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h1:i [<]](#manual-LT___mk) jh2:j [<]](#manual-LT___mk) k⊢ i [<]](#manual-LT___mk) ?mai:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)j:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)k:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h1:i [<]](#manual-LT___mk) jh2:j [<]](#manual-LT___mk) k⊢ ?m [<]](#manual-LT___mk) kmi:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)j:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)k:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h1:i [<]](#manual-LT___mk) jh2:j [<]](#manual-LT___mk) k⊢ [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)

**Example: Explicitly-Created Metavariables**

Explicit named holes are represented by metavariables, and additionally give rise to proof goals.
In this proof state,

i:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)j:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)k:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h1:i [<]](#manual-LT___mk) jh2:j [<]](#manual-LT___mk) k⊢ i [<]](#manual-LT___mk) k

The display of metavariable numbers can be disabled using the `[pp.mvars]](#manual-pp___mvars)`.
This can be useful when using features such as [`#guard_msgs`]](#manual-Lean___guardMsgsCmd) that match Lean's output against a desired string, which is very useful when writing tests for custom tactics.

option

```lean
pp.mvars
```

Default value: `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`

(pretty printer) display names of metavariables when true, and otherwise display them as '?*' (for expression metavariables) and as '*' (for universe level metavariables)

## Tactic Proofs — 14.3. The Tactic Language {#manual-tactic-proofs-143-the-tactic-language}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/The-Tactic-Language/

A tactic script consists of a sequence of tactics, separated either by semicolons or newlines.
When separated by newlines, tactics must be indented to the same level.
Explicit curly braces and semicolons may be used instead of indentation.
Tactic sequences may be grouped by parentheses.
This allows a sequence of tactics to be used in a position where a single tactic would otherwise be grammatically expected.

Generally, execution proceeds from top to bottom, with each tactic running in the proof state left behind by the prior tactic.
The tactic language contains a number of control structures that can modify this flow.

Each tactic is a syntax extension in the `tactic` category.
This means that tactics are free to define their own concrete syntax and parsing rules.
However, with a few exceptions, the majority of tactics can be identified by a leading keyword; the exceptions are typically frequently-used built-in control structures such as `[<;>]](#manual-_LT__SEMI__GT_)`.

### 14.3.1. Control Structures {#manual-tactic-language-control}

Strictly speaking, there is no fundamental distinction between control structures and other tactics.
Any tactic is free to take others as arguments and arrange for their execution in any context that it sees fit.
Even if a distinction is arbitrary, however, it can still be useful.
The tactics in this section are those that resemble traditional control structures from programming, or those that *only* recombine other tactics rather than making progress themselves.

#### 14.3.1.1. Success and Failure {#manual-tactic-language-success-failure}

When run in a proof state, every tactic either succeeds or fails.
Tactic failure is akin to exceptions: failures typically “bubble up” until handled.
Unlike exceptions, there is no operator to distinguish between reasons for failure; `[first]](#manual-first)` simply takes the first branch that succeeds.

tactic

```lean
[fail]](#manual-fail)
```

`fail msg` is a tactic that always fails, and produces an error using the given message.

tactic

```lean
[fail_if_success]](#manual-fail_if_success)
```

`fail_if_success t` fails if the tactic `t` succeeds.

tactic

```lean
[try]](#manual-try)
```

`try tac` runs `tac` and succeeds even if `tac` failed.

tactic

```lean
[first]](#manual-first)
```

`first | tac | ...` runs each `tac` until one succeeds, or else fails.

#### 14.3.1.2. Branching {#manual-tactic-language-branching}

Tactic proofs may use pattern matching and conditionals.
However, their meaning is not quite the same as it is in terms.
While terms are expected to be executed once the values of their variables are known, proofs are executed with their variables left abstract and should consider *all* cases simultaneously.
Thus, when `if` and `match` are used in tactics, their meaning is reasoning by cases rather than selection of a concrete branch.
All of their branches are executed, and the condition or pattern match is used to refine the main goal with more information in each branch, rather than to select a single branch.

tactic

```lean
[if]](#manual-if)
```

In tactic mode, `[if]](#manual-termIfThenElse) t [then]](#manual-termIfThenElse) tac1 [else]](#manual-termIfThenElse) tac2` is alternative syntax for:

```lean
by_cases t
· tac1
· tac2
```

It performs case distinction on `h† : t` or `h† : ¬t`, where `h†` is an anonymous hypothesis, and
`tac1` and `tac2` are the subproofs. (It doesn't actually use nondependent `[if]](#manual-if)`, since this wouldn't
add anything to the context and hence would be useless for proving theorems. To actually insert an
`ite` application use `[refine](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#refine) [if]](#manual-termIfThenElse) t [then]](#manual-termIfThenElse) ?_ [else]](#manual-termIfThenElse) ?_`.)

The assumptions in each subgoal can be named. `[if]](#manual-termDepIfThenElse) h : t [then]](#manual-termDepIfThenElse) tac1 [else]](#manual-termDepIfThenElse) tac2` can be used as
alternative syntax for:

```
by_cases h : t
· tac1
· tac2
```

It performs case distinction on `h : t` or `h : ¬t`.

You can use `?_` or `_` for either subproof to delay the goal to after the tactic, but
if a tactic sequence is provided for `tac1` or `tac2` then it will require the goal to be closed
by the end of the block.

**Example: Reasoning by cases with if**

In each branch of the [`if`]](#manual-if), an assumption is added that reflects whether `n = 0`.

```lean
example (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [if]](#manual-termIfThenElse) n = 0 [then]](#manual-termIfThenElse) n < 1 [else]](#manual-termIfThenElse) n > 0 := byn:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ if n [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0 then n [<]](#manual-LT___mk) 1 else n > 0
[if]](#manual-if) n = 0 [then]](#manual-if)n:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h✝:n [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0⊢ if n [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0 then n [<]](#manual-LT___mk) 1 else n > 0
[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp) [*]All goals completed! 🐙
[else]](#manual-if)n:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h✝:[¬](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)n [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0⊢ if n [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0 then n [<]](#manual-LT___mk) 1 else n > 0
[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp) [only](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp) [↓reduceIte, gt_iff_lt, *]n:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h✝:[¬](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)n [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0⊢ 0 [<]](#manual-LT___mk) n
[omega](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#omega)All goals completed! 🐙
```

tactic

```lean
[match]](#manual-match)
```

`[match]](#manual-match)` performs case analysis on one or more expressions.
See [Induction and Recursion](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/induction_and_recursion.html).
The syntax for the `[match]](#manual-match)` tactic is the same as term-mode `[match]](#manual-match)`, except that
the match arms are tactics instead of expressions.

```lean
example (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : n = n := byn:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ n [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) n
[match]](#manual-match) n [with]](#manual-match)
| 0 =>n:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ 0 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0 [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#rfl)All goals completed! 🐙
| i+1 =>n:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)i:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ i [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 1 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) i [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 1 [simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)All goals completed! 🐙
```
