When pattern matching, instances of the [discriminant]](#manual---tech-term-match-discriminants) in the goal are replaced with the patterns that match them in each branch.
Each branch must then prove the refined goal.
Compared to the `cases` tactic, using `match` can allow a greater degree of flexibility in the cases analysis being performed, but the requirement that each branch solve its goal completely makes it more difficult to incorporate into larger automation scripts.

**Example: Reasoning by cases with match**

In each branch of the [`match`]](#manual-match), the discriminant `n` has been replaced by either `0` or `k + 1`.

```lean
example (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [if]](#manual-termIfThenElse) n = 0 [then]](#manual-termIfThenElse) n < 1 [else]](#manual-termIfThenElse) n > 0 := byn:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ if n [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0 then n [<]](#manual-LT___mk) 1 else n > 0
[match]](#manual-match) n [with]](#manual-match)
| 0 =>n:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ if 0 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0 then 0 [<]](#manual-LT___mk) 1 else 0 > 0
[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)All goals completed! 🐙
| k + 1 =>n:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)k:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ if k [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 1 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0 then k [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 1 [<]](#manual-LT___mk) 1 else k [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 1 > 0
[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)All goals completed! 🐙
```

#### 14.3.1.3. Goal Selection {#manual-tactic-language-goal-selection}

Most tactics affect the [main goal]](#manual---tech-term-main-goal).
Goal selection tactics provide a way to treat a different goal as the main one, rearranging the sequence of goals in the proof state.

tactic

```lean
[case]](#manual-case)
```

- `case tag => tac` focuses on the goal with case name `tag` and solves it using `tac`,
  or else fails.
- `case tag x₁ ... xₙ => tac` additionally renames the `n` most recent hypotheses
  with inaccessible names to the given names.
- `case tag₁ | tag₂ => tac` is equivalent to `(case tag₁ => tac); (case tag₂ => tac)`.

tactic

```lean
[case']](#manual-case___)
```

`[case']](#manual-case___)` is similar to the `case tag => tac` tactic, but does not ensure the goal
has been solved after applying `tac`, nor admits the goal if `tac` failed.
Recall that `[case]](#manual-case)` closes the goal using `[sorry](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#sorry)` when `tac` fails, and
the tactic execution is not interrupted.

tactic

```lean
[rotate_left]](#manual-rotate_left)
```

`rotate_left n` rotates goals to the left by `n`. That is, `[rotate_left]](#manual-rotate_left) 1`
takes the main goal and puts it to the back of the subgoal list.
If `n` is omitted, it defaults to `1`.

tactic

```lean
[rotate_right]](#manual-rotate_right)
```

Rotate the goals to the right by `n`. That is, take the goal at the back
and push it to the front `n` times. If `n` is omitted, it defaults to `1`.

##### 14.3.1.3.1. Sequencing {#manual-tactic-language-sequencing}

In addition to running tactics one after the other, each being used to solve the main goal, the tactic language supports sequencing tactics according to the way in which goals are produced.
The `[<;>]](#manual-_LT__SEMI__GT_)` tactic combinator allows a tactic to be applied to *every* [subgoal]](#manual---tech-term-subgoals) produced by some other tactic.
If no new goals are produced, then the second tactic is not run.

tactic

```lean
[<;>]](#manual-_LT__SEMI__GT_)
```

`tac <;> tac'` runs `tac` on the main goal and `tac'` on each produced goal,
concatenating all goals produced by `tac'`.

If the tactic fails on any of the [subgoals]](#manual---tech-term-subgoals), then the whole `[<;>]](#manual-_LT__SEMI__GT_)` tactic fails.

**Example: Subgoal Sequencing**

In this proof state:

x:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h:x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 1 [∨](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 2⊢ x [<]](#manual-LT___mk) 3

the tactic `[cases](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#cases) hinlx:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h✝:x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 1⊢ x [<]](#manual-LT___mk) 3inrx:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h✝:x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 2⊢ x [<]](#manual-LT___mk) 3` yields the following two goals:

inlx:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h✝:x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 1⊢ x [<]](#manual-LT___mk) 3inrx:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h✝:x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 2⊢ x [<]](#manual-LT___mk) 3

Running `[cases](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#cases) hinlx:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h✝:x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 1⊢ x [<]](#manual-LT___mk) 3inrx:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h✝:x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 2⊢ x [<]](#manual-LT___mk) 3 ; [simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp) [*]inrx:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h✝:x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 2⊢ x [<]](#manual-LT___mk) 3` causes `[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)` to solve the first goal, leaving the second behind:

inrx:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h✝:x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 2⊢ x [<]](#manual-LT___mk) 3

Replacing the `;` with `[<;>]](#manual-_LT__SEMI__GT_)` and running `[cases](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#cases) hinlx:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h✝:x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 1⊢ x [<]](#manual-LT___mk) 3inrx:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h✝:x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 2⊢ x [<]](#manual-LT___mk) 3 <;>inlx:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h✝:x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 1⊢ x [<]](#manual-LT___mk) 3inrx:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h✝:x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 2⊢ x [<]](#manual-LT___mk) 3 [simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp) [*]All goals completed! 🐙` solves **both** of the new goals with `[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)`:

All goals completed! 🐙

##### 14.3.1.3.2. Working on Multiple Goals {#manual-tactic-language-multiple-goals}

The tactics `[all_goals]](#manual-all_goals)` and `[any_goals]](#manual-any_goals)` allow a tactic to be applied to every goal in the proof state.
The difference between them is that if the tactic fails for in any of the goals, `[all_goals]](#manual-all_goals)` itself fails, while `[any_goals]](#manual-any_goals)` fails only if the tactic fails in all of the goals.

tactic

```lean
[all_goals]](#manual-all_goals)
```

`all_goals tac` runs `tac` on each goal, concatenating the resulting goals.
If the tactic fails on any goal, the entire `all_goals` tactic fails.

See also `any_goals tac`.

tactic

```lean
[any_goals]](#manual-any_goals)
```

`any_goals tac` applies the tactic `tac` to every goal,
concatenating the resulting goals for successful tactic applications.
If the tactic fails on all of the goals, the entire `any_goals` tactic fails.

This tactic is like `all_goals try tac` except that it fails if none of the applications of `tac` succeeds.

#### 14.3.1.4. Focusing {#manual-tactic-language-focusing}

Focusing tactics remove some subset of the proof goals (typically leaving only the main goal) from the consideration of some further tactics.
In addition to the tactics described here, the `[case]](#manual-case)` and `[case']](#manual-case___)` tactics focus on the selected goal.

tactic

```lean
[·]](#manual-___)
```

`· tac` focuses on the main goal and tries to solve it using `tac`, or else fails.

It is generally considered good Lean style to use bullets whenever a tactic line results in more than one new subgoal.
This makes it easier to read and maintain proofs, because the connections between steps of reasoning are more clear and any change in the number of subgoals while editing the proof will have a localized effect.

tactic

```lean
[next]](#manual-next)
```

`next => tac` focuses on the next goal and solves it using `tac`, or else fails.
`next x₁ ... xₙ => tac` additionally renames the `n` most recent hypotheses with
inaccessible names to the given names.

tactic

```lean
[focus]](#manual-focus)
```

`focus tac` focuses on the main goal, suppressing all other goals, and runs `tac` on it.
Usually `· tac`, which enforces that the goal is closed by `tac`, should be preferred.

#### 14.3.1.5. Repetition and Iteration {#manual-tactic-language-iteration}

tactic

```lean
[iterate]](#manual-iterate)
```

`iterate n tac` runs `tac` exactly `n` times.
`iterate tac` runs `tac` repeatedly until failure.

`[iterate]](#manual-iterate)`'s argument is a tactic sequence,
so multiple tactics can be run using `iterate n (tac₁; tac₂; ⋯)` or

```lean
iterate n
tac₁
tac₂
⋯
```

tactic

```lean
[repeat]](#manual-repeat)
```

`repeat tac` repeatedly applies `tac` so long as it succeeds.
The tactic `tac` may be a tactic sequence, and if `tac` fails at any point in its execution,
`[repeat]](#manual-repeat)` will revert any partial changes that `tac` made to the tactic state.

The tactic `tac` should eventually fail, otherwise `repeat tac` will run indefinitely.

See also:

- `try tac` is like `repeat tac` but will apply `tac` at most once.
- `repeat' tac` recursively applies `tac` to each goal.
- `first | tac1 | tac2` implements the backtracking used by `[repeat]](#manual-repeat)`

tactic

```lean
[repeat']](#manual-repeat___)
```

`repeat' tac` recursively applies `tac` on all of the goals so long as it succeeds.
That is to say, if `tac` produces multiple subgoals, then `repeat' tac` is applied to each of them.

See also:

- `repeat tac` simply repeatedly applies `tac`.
- `repeat1' tac` is `repeat' tac` but requires that `tac` succeed for some goal at least once.

tactic

```lean
[repeat1']](#manual-repeat1___)
```

`repeat1' tac` recursively applies to `tac` on all of the goals so long as it succeeds,
but `repeat1' tac` fails if `tac` succeeds on none of the initial goals.

See also:

- `repeat tac` simply applies `tac` repeatedly.
- `repeat' tac` is like `repeat1' tac` but it does not require that `tac` succeed at least once.

### 14.3.2. Names and Hygiene {#manual-tactic-language-hygiene}

Behind the scenes, tactics generate proof terms.
These proof terms exist in a local context, because assumptions in proof states correspond to local binders in terms.
Uses of assumptions correspond to variable references.
It is very important that the naming of assumptions be predictable; otherwise, small changes to the internal implementation of a tactic could either lead to variable capture or to a broken reference if they cause different names to be selected.

Lean's tactic language is *hygienic*. 
This means that the tactic language respects lexical scope: names that occur in a tactic refer to the enclosing binding in the source code, rather than being determined by the generated code, and the tactic framework is responsible for maintaining this property.
Variable references in tactic scripts refer either to names that were in scope at the beginning of the script or to bindings that were explicitly introduced as part of the tactics, rather than to the names chosen for use in the proof term behind the scenes.

A consequence of hygienic tactics is that the only way to refer to an assumption is to explicitly name it.
Tactics cannot assign assumption names themselves, but must rather accept names from users; users are correspondingly obligated to provide names for assumptions that they wish to refer to.
When an assumption does not have a user-provided name, it is shown in the proof state with a dagger (`'†', DAGGER 0x2020`).
The dagger indicates that the name is *inaccessible* and cannot be explicitly referred to.

Hygiene can be disabled by setting the option `[tactic.hygienic]](#manual-tactic___hygienic)` to `false`.
This is not recommended, as many tactics rely on the hygiene system to prevent capture and thus do not incur the overhead of careful manual name selection.

option

```lean
tactic.hygienic
```

Default value: `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`

make sure tactics are hygienic

**Example: Tactic hygiene: inaccessible assumptions**

When proving that `∀ (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)), 0 + n = n`, the initial proof state is:

⊢ ∀ (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)), 0 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) n [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) n

The tactic `[intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#intro)n✝:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ 0 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) n✝ [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) n✝` results in a proof state with an inaccessible assumption:

n✝:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ 0 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) n✝ [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) n✝

**Example: Tactic hygiene: accessible assumptions**

When proving that `∀ (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)), 0 + n = n`, the initial proof state is:

⊢ ∀ (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)), 0 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) n [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) n

The tactic `[intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#intro) nn:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ 0 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) n [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) n`, with the explicit name `n`, results in a proof state with an accessibly-named assumption:

n:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ 0 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) n [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) n

#### 14.3.2.1. Accessing Assumptions {#manual-tactic-language-assumptions}

Many tactics provide a means of specifying names for the assumptions that they introduce.
For example, `[intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#intro)` and `[intros](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#intros)` take assumption names as arguments, and `[induction](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#induction)`'s [`with`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#induction)-form allows simultaneous case selection, assumption naming, and focusing.
When an assumption does not have a name, one can be assigned using `[next]](#manual-next)`, `[case]](#manual-case)`, or `[rename_i]](#manual-rename_i)`.

tactic

```lean
[rename_i]](#manual-rename_i)
```

`rename_i x_1 ... x_n` renames the last `n` inaccessible names using the given names.

### 14.3.3. Assumption Management {#manual-tactic-language-assumption-management}

Larger proofs can benefit from management of proof states, removing irrelevant assumptions and making their names easier to understand.
Along with these operators, `[rename_i]](#manual-rename_i)` allows inaccessible assumptions to be renamed, and `[intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#intro)`, `[intros](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#intros)` and `[rintro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#rintro)` convert goals that are implications or universal quantification into goals with additional assumptions.

tactic

```lean
[rename]](#manual-rename)
```

`[rename]](#manual-rename) t => x` renames the most recent hypothesis whose type matches `t`
(which may contain placeholders) to `x`, or fails if no such hypothesis could be found.

tactic

```lean
[revert]](#manual-revert)
```

`revert x...` is the inverse of `intro x...`: it moves the given hypotheses
into the main goal's target type.

tactic

```lean
[clear]](#manual-clear)
```

`clear x...` removes the given hypotheses, or fails if there are remaining
references to a hypothesis.

### 14.3.4. Local Definitions and Proofs {#manual-tactic-language-local-defs}

`[have]](#manual-have)` and `[let]](#manual-let)` both create local assumptions.
Generally speaking, `[have]](#manual-have)` should be used when proving an intermediate lemma; `[let]](#manual-let)` should be reserved for local definitions.

tactic

```lean
[have]](#manual-have)
```

The `[have]](#manual-have)` tactic is for adding opaque definitions and hypotheses to the local context of the main goal.
The definitions forget their associated value and cannot be unfolded, unlike definitions added by the `[let]](#manual-let)` tactic.

- `[have]](#manual-have) h : t := e` adds the hypothesis `h : t` if `e` is a term of type `t`.
- `[have]](#manual-have) h := e` uses the type of `e` for `t`.
- `[have]](#manual-have) : t := e` and `[have]](#manual-have) := e` use `this` for the name of the hypothesis.
- `[have]](#manual-have) pat := e` for a pattern `pat` is equivalent to `[match]](#manual-match) e [with]](#manual-match) | pat => _`,
  where `_` stands for the tactics that follow this one.
  It is convenient for types that have only one applicable constructor.
  For example, given `h : p ∧ q ∧ r`, `[have]](#manual-have) ⟨h₁, h₂, h₃⟩ := h` produces the
  hypotheses `h₁ : p`, `h₂ : q`, and `h₃ : r`.
- The syntax `[have]](#manual-have) (eq := h) pat := e` is equivalent to `[match]](#manual-match) h : e [with]](#manual-match) | pat => _`,
  which adds the equation `h : e = pat` to the local context.

The tactic supports all the same syntax variants and options as the `[have]](#manual-have)` term.

**Properties and relations**

- It is not possible to unfold a variable introduced using `[have]](#manual-have)`, since the definition's value is forgotten.
  The `[let]](#manual-let)` tactic introduces definitions that can be unfolded.
- The `[have]](#manual-have) h : t := e` is like doing `let h : t := e; clear_value h`.
- The `[have]](#manual-have)` tactic is preferred for propositions, and `[let]](#manual-let)` is preferred for non-propositions.
- Sometimes `[have]](#manual-have)` is used for non-propositions to ensure that the variable is never unfolded,
  which may be important for performance reasons.
  Consider using the equivalent `let +nondep` to indicate the intent.

tactic

```lean
[have']](#manual-have___)
```

Similar to `[have]](#manual-have)`, but using `[refine'](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#refine___)`

tactic

```lean
[let]](#manual-let)
```

The `[let]](#manual-let)` tactic is for adding definitions to the local context of the main goal.
The definition can be unfolded, unlike definitions introduced by `[have]](#manual-have)`.

- `[let]](#manual-let) x : t := e` adds the definition `x : t := e` if `e` is a term of type `t`.
- `[let]](#manual-let) x := e` uses the type of `e` for `t`.
- `[let]](#manual-let) : t := e` and `[let]](#manual-let) := e` use `this` for the name of the hypothesis.
- `[let]](#manual-let) pat := e` for a pattern `pat` is equivalent to `[match]](#manual-match) e [with]](#manual-match) | pat => _`,
  where `_` stands for the tactics that follow this one.
  It is convenient for types that let only one applicable constructor.
  For example, given `p : α × β × γ`, `[let]](#manual-let) ⟨x, y, z⟩ := p` produces the
  local variables `x : α`, `y : β`, and `z : γ`.
- The syntax `[let]](#manual-let) (eq := h) pat := e` is equivalent to `[match]](#manual-match) h : e [with]](#manual-match) | pat => _`,
  which adds the equation `h : e = pat` to the local context.

The tactic supports all the same syntax variants and options as the `[let]](#manual-let)` term.

**Properties and relations**

- Unlike `[have]](#manual-have)`, it is possible to unfold definitions introduced using `[let]](#manual-let)`, using tactics
  such as `[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)`, `[dsimp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#dsimp)`, `[unfold](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#unfold)`, and `[subst](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#subst)`.
- The `[clear_value](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#clear_value)` tactic turns a `[let]](#manual-let)` definition into a `[have]](#manual-have)` definition after the fact.
  The tactic might fail if the local context depends on the value of the variable.
- The `[let]](#manual-let)` tactic is preferred for data (non-propositions).
- Sometimes `[have]](#manual-have)` is used for non-propositions to ensure that the variable is never unfolded,
  which may be important for performance reasons.

tactic

```lean
[let rec]](#manual-let-rec)
```

`[let]](#manual-let-rec) [rec]](#manual-let-rec) f : t := e` adds a recursive definition `f` to the current goal.
The syntax is the same as term-mode `[let rec]](#manual-let-rec)`.

The tactic supports all the same syntax variants and options as the `[let]](#manual-let)` term.

tactic

```lean
[letI]](#manual-letI)
```

`[letI]](#manual-letI)` behaves like `[let]](#manual-let)`, but inlines the value instead of producing a `[let]](#manual-let)` term.

tactic

```lean
[let']](#manual-let___)
```

Similar to `[let]](#manual-let)`, but using `[refine'](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#refine___)`

### 14.3.5. Configuration {#manual-tactic-config}

Many tactics are configurable.
By convention, tactics share a configuration syntax, described using `optConfig`.
The specific options available to each tactic are described in the tactic's documentation.

syntaxTactic Configuration

A tactic configuration consists of zero or more configuration items:

```lean
[optConfig]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___optConfig-next) ::=
    configItem*
```

syntaxTactic Configuration Items

Each configuration item has a name that corresponds to an underlying tactic option.
Boolean options may be enabled or disabled using prefix `+` and `-`:

```lean
configItem ::=
    +ident
```

```lean
configItem ::= ...
    | -ident
```

Options may be assigned specific values using a syntax similar to that for named function arguments:

```lean
configItem ::= ...
    | (ident := term)
```

Finally, the name `config` is reserved; it is used to pass an entire set of options as a data structure.
The specific type expected depends on the tactic.

```lean
configItem ::= ...
    | (config := term)
```

### 14.3.6. Namespace and Option Management {#manual-tactic-language-namespaces-options}

Namespaces and options can be adjusted in tactic scripts using the same syntax as in terms.

tactic

```lean
[set_option]](#manual-set_option)
```

`set_option opt val in tacs` (the tactic) acts like `set_option opt val` at the command level,
but it sets the option only within the tactics `tacs`.

tactic

```lean
[open]](#manual-open)
```

`open Foo in tacs` (the tactic) acts like `open Foo` at command level,
but it opens a namespace only within the tactics `tacs`.

#### 14.3.6.1. Controlling Unfolding {#manual-tactic-language-unfolding}

By default, only definitions marked reducible are unfolded, except when checking definitional equality.
These operators allow this default to be adjusted for some part of a tactic script.

tactic

```lean
with_reducible_and_instances
```

`with_reducible_and_instances tacs` executes `tacs` using the `.instances` transparency setting.
In this setting only definitions tagged as `[reducible]` or type class instances are unfolded.

tactic

```lean
with_reducible
```

`with_reducible tacs` executes `tacs` using the reducible transparency setting.
In this setting only definitions tagged as `[reducible]` are unfolded.

tactic

```lean
with_unfolding_all
```

`with_unfolding_all tacs` executes `tacs` using the `.all` transparency setting.
In this setting all definitions that are not opaque are unfolded.

---



## Tactic Proofs — 14.4. Options {#manual-tactic-proofs-144-options}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Options/

These options affect the meaning of tactics.

option

```lean
tactic.customEliminators
```

Default value: `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`

enable using custom eliminators in the 'induction' and 'cases' tactics defined using the '@[induction\_eliminator]' and '@[cases\_eliminator]' attributes

option

```lean
tactic.skipAssignedInstances
```

Default value: `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`

in the `[rw](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#rw)` and `[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)` tactics, if an instance implicit argument is assigned, do not try to synthesize instance.

option

```lean
tactic.simp.trace
```

Default value: `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`

When tracing is enabled, calls to `[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)` or `[dsimp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#dsimp)` will print an equivalent `[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp) [only](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)` call.

---



## Tactic Proofs — 14.5. Tactic Reference {#manual-tactic-proofs-145-tactic-reference}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/

### 14.5.1. Classical Logic {#manual-tactic-ref-classical}

tactic

```lean
[classical]](#manual-classical)
```

`classical tacs` runs `tacs` in a scope where `Classical.propDecidable` is a low priority
local instance.

Note that `[classical]](#manual-classical)` is a scoping tactic: it adds the instance only within the
scope of the tactic.

### 14.5.2. Assumptions {#manual-tactic-ref-assumptions}

tactic

```lean
[assumption]](#manual-assumption)
```

`[assumption]](#manual-assumption)` tries to solve the main goal using a hypothesis of compatible type, or else fails.
Note also the `‹t›` term notation, which is a shorthand for `show t by [assumption]](#manual-assumption)`.

tactic

```lean
[apply_assumption]](#manual-apply_assumption)
```

`[apply_assumption]](#manual-apply_assumption)` looks for an assumption of the form `... → ∀ _, ... → head`
where `head` matches the current goal.

You can specify additional rules to apply using `apply_assumption [...]`.
By default `[apply_assumption]](#manual-apply_assumption)` will also try `[rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)`, `trivial`, `[congrFun](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#congrFun)`, and `[congrArg](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#congrArg)`.
If you don't want these, or don't want to use all hypotheses, use `apply_assumption only [...]`.
You can use `[apply_assumption]](#manual-apply_assumption) [-h]` to omit a local hypothesis.
You can use `apply_assumption using [a₁, ...]` to use all lemmas which have been labelled
with the attributes `aᵢ` (these attributes must be created using `register_label_attr`).

`[apply_assumption]](#manual-apply_assumption)` will use consequences of local hypotheses obtained via `[symm]](#manual-symm)`.

If `[apply_assumption]](#manual-apply_assumption)` fails, it will call `[exfalso]](#manual-exfalso)` and try again.
Thus if there is an assumption of the form `P → ¬ Q`, the new tactic state
will have two goals, `P` and `Q`.

You can pass a further configuration via the syntax `apply_rules (config := {...}) lemmas`.
The options supported are the same as for `[solve_by_elim]](#manual-solve_by_elim)` (and include all the options for `[apply]](#manual-apply)`).

### 14.5.3. Quantifiers {#manual-tactic-ref-quantifiers}

tactic

```lean
[exists]](#manual-exists)
```

`exists e₁, e₂, ...` is shorthand for `refine ⟨e₁, e₂, ...⟩; try trivial`.
It is useful for existential goals.

tactic

```lean
[intro]](#manual-intro)
```

Introduces one or more hypotheses, optionally naming and/or pattern-matching them.
For each hypothesis to be introduced, the remaining main goal's target type must
be a `[let]](#manual-let)` or function type.

- `intro` by itself introduces one anonymous hypothesis, which can be accessed
  by e.g. `[assumption]](#manual-assumption)`. It is equivalent to `[intro]](#manual-intro) _`.
- `[intro]](#manual-intro) x y` introduces two hypotheses and names them. Individual hypotheses
  can be anonymized via `_`, given a type ascription, or matched against a pattern:

  ```lean
  intro (a, b)
  -- ..., a : α, b : β ⊢ ...
  ```
- `[intro]](#manual-intro) rfl` is short for `intro h; subst h`, if `h` is an equality where the left-hand or right-hand side
  is a variable.
- Alternatively, `intro` can be combined with pattern matching much like `fun`:

  ```
  intro
  | n + 1, 0 => tac
  | ...
  ```

tactic

```lean
[intros]](#manual-intros)
```

`[intros]](#manual-intros)` repeatedly applies `[intro]](#manual-intro)` to introduce zero or more hypotheses
until the goal is no longer a *binding expression*
(i.e., a universal quantifier, function type, implication, or `[have]](#manual-have)`/`[let]](#manual-let)`),
without performing any definitional reductions (no unfolding, beta, eta, etc.).
The introduced hypotheses receive inaccessible (hygienic) names.

`[intros]](#manual-intros) x y z` is equivalent to `[intro]](#manual-intro) x y z` and exists only for historical reasons.
The `[intro]](#manual-intro)` tactic should be preferred in this case.

**Properties and relations**

- `[intros]](#manual-intros)` succeeds even when it introduces no hypotheses.
- `[repeat]](#manual-repeat) [intro]](#manual-intro)` is like `[intros]](#manual-intros)`, but it performs definitional reductions
  to expose binders, and as such it may introduce more hypotheses than `[intros]](#manual-intros)`.
- `[intros]](#manual-intros)` is equivalent to `intro _ _ … _`,
  with the fewest trailing `_` placeholders needed so that the goal is no longer a binding expression.
  The trailing introductions do not perform any definitional reductions.

**Examples**

Implications:

```lean
example (p q : Prop) : p → q → p := byp:Propq:Prop⊢ p → q → p
[intros]](#manual-intros)p:Propq:Propa✝¹:pa✝:q⊢ p
/- Tactic state
a✝¹ : p
a✝ : q
⊢ p -/
[assumption]](#manual-assumption)All goals completed! 🐙
```

Let-bindings:

```lean
example : let n := 1; let k := 2; n + k = 3 := by⊢ let n := 1;
let k := 2;
n [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) k [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 3
[intros]](#manual-intros)n✝:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := 1k✝:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := 2⊢ n✝ [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) k✝ [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 3
/- n✝ : Nat := 1
k✝ : Nat := 2
⊢ n✝ + k✝ = 3 -/
[rfl]](#manual-rfl)All goals completed! 🐙
```

Does not unfold definitions:

```lean
def AllEven (f : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) := ∀ n, f n % 2 = 0
example : ∀ (f : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)), AllEven f → AllEven (fun k => f (k + 1)) := by⊢ ∀ (f : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)), AllEven f → AllEven fun k => f [(]](#manual-HAdd___mk)k [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 1[)]](#manual-HAdd___mk)
[intros]](#manual-intros)f✝:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)a✝:AllEven f✝⊢ AllEven fun k => f✝ [(]](#manual-HAdd___mk)k [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 1[)]](#manual-HAdd___mk)
/- Tactic state
f✝ : Nat → Nat
a✝ : AllEven f✝
⊢ AllEven fun k => f✝ (k + 1) -/
[sorry]](#manual-sorry)All goals completed! 🐙
```

tactic

```lean
[rintro]](#manual-rintro)
```

The `[rintro]](#manual-rintro)` tactic is a combination of the `[intros]](#manual-intros)` tactic with `[rcases]](#manual-rcases)` to
allow for destructuring patterns while introducing variables. See `[rcases]](#manual-rcases)` for
a description of supported patterns. For example, `[rintro]](#manual-rintro) (a | ⟨b, c⟩) ⟨d, e⟩`
will introduce two variables, and then do case splits on both of them producing
two subgoals, one with variables `a d e` and the other with `b c d e`.

`[rintro]](#manual-rintro)`, unlike `[rcases]](#manual-rcases)`, also supports the form `(x y : ty)` for introducing
and type-ascripting multiple variables at once, similar to binders.

### 14.5.4. Relations {#manual-tactic-ref-relations}

tactic

```lean
[rfl]](#manual-rfl)
```

This tactic applies to a goal whose target has the form `x ~ x`,
where `~` is equality, heterogeneous equality or any relation that
has a reflexivity lemma tagged with the attribute @[refl].

tactic

```lean
[rfl']](#manual-rfl___)
```

`[rfl']](#manual-rfl___)` is similar to `[rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)`, but disables smart unfolding and unfolds all kinds of definitions,
theorems included (relevant for declarations defined by well-founded recursion).

tactic

```lean
[apply_rfl]](#manual-apply_rfl)
```

The same as `[rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)`, but without trying `[eq_refl]](#manual-eq_refl)` at the end.

attributeReflexive Relations

The `refl` attribute marks a lemma as a proof of reflexivity for some relation.
These lemmas are used by the `[rfl]](#manual-rfl)`, `[rfl']](#manual-rfl___)`, and `[apply_rfl]](#manual-apply_rfl)` tactics.

```lean
attr ::= ...
    | refl
```

tactic

```lean
[symm]](#manual-symm)
```

- `[symm]](#manual-symm)` applies to a goal whose target has the form `t ~ u` where `~` is a symmetric relation,
  that is, a relation which has a symmetry lemma tagged with the attribute [symm].
  It replaces the target with `u ~ t`.
- `[symm]](#manual-symm) at h` will rewrite a hypothesis `h : t ~ u` to `h : u ~ t`.

tactic

```lean
[symm_saturate]](#manual-symm_saturate)
```

For every hypothesis `h : a ~ b` where a `@[symm]` lemma is available,
add a hypothesis `h_symm : b ~ a`.

attributeSymmetric Relations

The `symm` attribute marks a lemma as a proof that a relation is symmetric.
These lemmas are used by the `[symm]](#manual-symm)` and `[symm_saturate]](#manual-symm_saturate)` tactics.

```lean
attr ::= ...
    | symm
```

tactic

```lean
[calc]](#manual-calc)
```

Step-wise reasoning over transitive relations.

```
calc
  a = b := pab
  b = c := pbc
  ...
  y = z := pyz
```

proves `a = z` from the given step-wise proofs. `=` can be replaced with any
relation implementing the typeclass `[Trans]](#manual-Trans___mk)`. Instead of repeating the right-
hand sides, subsequent left-hand sides can be replaced with `_`.

```
calc
  a = b := pab
  _ = c := pbc
  ...
  _ = z := pyz
```

It is also possible to write the *first* relation as `<lhs>\n _ = <rhs> := <proof>`. This is useful for aligning relation symbols, especially on longer
identifiers:

```
calc abc
  _ = bce := pabce
  _ = cef := pbcef
  ...
  _ = xyz := pwxyz
```

`[calc]](#manual-calc)` works as a term, as a tactic or as a `conv` tactic.

See [Theorem Proving in Lean 4](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/quantifiers_and_equality.html#calculational-proofs) for more information.

type class

```lean
[Trans.{u, v, w, u_1, u_2, u_3}]](#manual-Trans___mk) {α : Sort u_1} {β : Sort u_2}
  {γ : Sort u_3} (r : α → β → Sort u) (s : β → γ → Sort v)
  (t : [outParam]](#manual-outParam) (α → γ → Sort w)) :
  Sort (max (max (max (max (max (max 1 u) u_1) u_2) u_3) v) w)



[Trans.{u, v, w, u_1, u_2, u_3}]](#manual-Trans___mk)
  {α : Sort u_1} {β : Sort u_2}
  {γ : Sort u_3} (r : α → β → Sort u)
  (s : β → γ → Sort v)
  (t : [outParam]](#manual-outParam) (α → γ → Sort w)) :
  Sort
    (max
        (max
            (max
                (max (max (max 1 u) u_1)
                    u_2)
                u_3)
            v)
        w)
```

Transitive chaining of proofs, used e.g. by `[calc]](#manual-calc)`.

It takes two relations `r` and `s` as "input", and produces an "output"
relation `t`, with the property that `r a b` and `s b c` implies `t a c`.
The `[calc]](#manual-calc)` tactic uses this so that when it sees a chain with `a ≤ b` and `b < c`
it knows that this should be a proof of `a < c` because there is an instance
`Trans (·≤·) (·<·) (·<·)`.

Instance Constructor

```lean
[Trans.mk]](#manual-Trans___mk).{u, v, w, u_1, u_2, u_3}
```

Methods

```lean
trans : {a : α} → {b : β} → {c : γ} → r a b → s b c → t a c
```

Compose two proofs by transitivity, generalized over the relations involved.

#### 14.5.4.1. Equality {#manual-tactic-ref-equality}

tactic

```lean
[subst]](#manual-subst)
```

`subst x...` substitutes each hypothesis `x` with a definition found in the local context,
then eliminates the hypothesis.

- If `x` is a local definition, then its definition is used.
- Otherwise, if there is a hypothesis of the form `x = e` or `e = x`,
  then `e` is used for the definition of `x`.

If `h : a = b`, then `[subst]](#manual-subst) h` may be used if either `a` or `b` unfolds to a local hypothesis.
This is similar to the `[cases]](#manual-cases) h` tactic.

See also: `[subst_vars]](#manual-subst_vars)` for substituting all local hypotheses that have a defining equation.

tactic

```lean
[subst_eqs]](#manual-subst_eqs)
```

`subst_eq` repeatedly substitutes according to the equality proof hypotheses in the context,
replacing the left side of the equality with the right, until no more progress can be made.

tactic

```lean
[subst_vars]](#manual-subst_vars)
```

Applies `[subst]](#manual-subst)` to all hypotheses of the form `h : x = t` or `h : t = x`.

tactic

```lean
[congr]](#manual-congr)
```

Apply congruence (recursively) to goals of the form `⊢ f as = f bs` and `⊢ f as ≍ f bs`.
The optional parameter is the depth of the recursive applications.
This is useful when `[congr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#congr-next)` is too aggressive in breaking down the goal.
For example, given `⊢ f (g (x + y)) = f (g (y + x))`,
`[congr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#congr-next)` produces the goals `⊢ x = y` and `⊢ y = x`,
while `[congr]](#manual-congr) 2` produces the intended `⊢ x + y = y + x`.

tactic

```lean
[eq_refl]](#manual-eq_refl)
```

`[eq_refl]](#manual-eq_refl)` is equivalent to `[exact]](#manual-exact) rfl`, but has a few optimizations.

tactic

```lean
[ac_rfl]](#manual-ac_rfl)
```

`[ac_rfl]](#manual-ac_rfl)` proves equalities up to application of an associative and commutative operator.

```lean
instance : Std.Associative (α := [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (.+.) := ⟨Nat.add_assoc⟩
instance : Std.Commutative (α := [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (.+.) := ⟨Nat.add_comm⟩
example (a b c d : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : a + b + c + d = d + (b + c) + a := bya:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)b:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)c:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)d:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ a [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) b [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) c [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) d [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) d [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) [(]](#manual-HAdd___mk)b [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) c[)]](#manual-HAdd___mk) [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) a [ac_rfl]](#manual-ac_rfl)All goals completed! 🐙
```

### 14.5.5. Associativity and Commutativity {#manual-tactic-ref-associativity-commutativity}

tactic

```lean
[ac_nf]](#manual-ac_nf)
```

`[ac_nf]](#manual-ac_nf)` normalizes equalities up to application of an associative and commutative operator.

- `[ac_nf]](#manual-ac_nf)` normalizes all hypotheses and the goal target of the goal.
- `[ac_nf]](#manual-ac_nf) at l` normalizes at location(s) `l`, where `l` is either `*` or a
  list of hypotheses in the local context. In the latter case, a turnstile `⊢` or `|-`
  can also be used, to signify the target of the goal.

```lean
instance : Std.Associative (α := [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (.+.) := ⟨Nat.add_assoc⟩
instance : Std.Commutative (α := [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (.+.) := ⟨Nat.add_comm⟩
example (a b c d : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : a + b + c + d = d + (b + c) + a := bya:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)b:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)c:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)d:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ a [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) b [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) c [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) d [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) d [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) [(]](#manual-HAdd___mk)b [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) c[)]](#manual-HAdd___mk) [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) a
[ac_nf]](#manual-ac_nf)All goals completed! 🐙
-- goal: a + (b + (c + d)) = a + (b + (c + d))
```

tactic

```lean
[ac_nf0]](#manual-ac_nf0)
```

Implementation of `[ac_nf]](#manual-ac_nf)` (the full `[ac_nf]](#manual-ac_nf)` calls `trivial` afterwards).

### 14.5.6. Lemmas {#manual-tactic-ref-lemmas}

tactic

```lean
[exact]](#manual-exact)
```

`[exact]](#manual-exact) e` closes the main goal if its target type matches that of `e`.

tactic

```lean
[apply]](#manual-apply)
```

`[apply]](#manual-apply) e` tries to match the current goal against the conclusion of `e`'s type.
If it succeeds, then the tactic returns as many subgoals as the number of premises that
have not been fixed by type inference or type class resolution.
Non-dependent premises are added before dependent ones.

The `[apply]](#manual-apply)` tactic uses higher-order pattern matching, type class resolution,
and first-order unification with dependent types.

tactic

```lean
[refine]](#manual-refine)
```

`[refine]](#manual-refine) e` behaves like `[exact]](#manual-exact) e`, except that named (`?x`) or unnamed (`?_`)
holes in `e` that are not solved by unification with the main goal's target type
are converted into new goals, using the hole's name, if any, as the goal case name.

tactic

```lean
[refine']](#manual-refine___)
```

`[refine']](#manual-refine___) e` behaves like `[refine]](#manual-refine) e`, except that unsolved placeholders (`_`)
and implicit parameters are also converted into new goals.

tactic

```lean
[solve_by_elim]](#manual-solve_by_elim)
```

`[solve_by_elim]](#manual-solve_by_elim)` calls `[apply]](#manual-apply)` on the main goal to find an assumption whose head matches
and then repeatedly calls `[apply]](#manual-apply)` on the generated subgoals until no subgoals remain,
performing at most `maxDepth` (defaults to 6) recursive steps.

`[solve_by_elim]](#manual-solve_by_elim)` discharges the current goal or fails.

`[solve_by_elim]](#manual-solve_by_elim)` performs backtracking if subgoals can not be solved.

By default, the assumptions passed to `[apply]](#manual-apply)` are the local context, `[rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)`, `trivial`,
`[congrFun](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#congrFun)` and `[congrArg](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#congrArg)`.

The assumptions can be modified with similar syntax as for `[simp]](#manual-simp)`:

- `solve_by_elim [h₁, h₂, ..., hᵣ]` also applies the given expressions.
- `solve_by_elim only [h₁, h₂, ..., hᵣ]` does not include the local context,
  `[rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)`, `trivial`, `[congrFun](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#congrFun)`, or `[congrArg](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#congrArg)` unless they are explicitly included.
- `solve_by_elim [-h₁, ... -hₙ]` removes the given local hypotheses.
- `solve_by_elim using [a₁, ...]` uses all lemmas which have been labelled
  with the attributes `aᵢ` (these attributes must be created using `register_label_attr`).

`[solve_by_elim]](#manual-solve_by_elim)*` tries to solve all goals together, using backtracking if a solution for one goal
makes other goals impossible.
(Adding or removing local hypotheses may not be well-behaved when starting with multiple goals.)

Optional arguments passed via a configuration argument as `solve_by_elim (config := { ... })`

- `maxDepth`: number of attempts at discharging generated subgoals
- `[symm]](#manual-symm)`: adds all hypotheses derived by `[symm]](#manual-symm)` (defaults to `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`).
- `[exfalso]](#manual-exfalso)`: allow calling `[exfalso]](#manual-exfalso)` and trying again if `[solve_by_elim]](#manual-solve_by_elim)` fails
  (defaults to `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`).
- `transparency`: change the transparency mode when calling `[apply]](#manual-apply)`. Defaults to `.default`,
  but it is often useful to change to `.reducible`,
  so semireducible definitions will not be unfolded when trying to apply a lemma.

See also the doc-comment for `Lean.Meta.Tactic.Backtrack.BacktrackConfig` for the options
`proc`, `suspend`, and `discharge` which allow further customization of `[solve_by_elim]](#manual-solve_by_elim)`.
Both `[apply_assumption]](#manual-apply_assumption)` and `[apply_rules]](#manual-apply_rules)` are implemented via these hooks.

tactic

```lean
[apply_rules]](#manual-apply_rules)
```

`apply_rules [l₁, l₂, ...]` tries to solve the main goal by iteratively
applying the list of lemmas `[l₁, l₂, ...]` or by applying a local hypothesis.
If `[apply]](#manual-apply)` generates new goals, `[apply_rules]](#manual-apply_rules)` iteratively tries to solve those goals.
You can use `[apply_rules]](#manual-apply_rules) [-h]` to omit a local hypothesis.

`[apply_rules]](#manual-apply_rules)` will also use `[rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)`, `trivial`, `[congrFun](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#congrFun)` and `[congrArg](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#congrArg)`.
These can be disabled, as can local hypotheses, by using `apply_rules only [...]`.

You can use `apply_rules using [a₁, ...]` to use all lemmas which have been labelled
with the attributes `aᵢ` (these attributes must be created using `register_label_attr`).

You can pass a further configuration via the syntax `apply_rules (config := {...})`.
The options supported are the same as for `[solve_by_elim]](#manual-solve_by_elim)` (and include all the options for `[apply]](#manual-apply)`).

`[apply_rules]](#manual-apply_rules)` will try calling `[symm]](#manual-symm)` on hypotheses and `[exfalso]](#manual-exfalso)` on the goal as needed.
This can be disabled with `[apply_rules]](#manual-apply_rules) (config := {symm := false, exfalso := false})`.

You can bound the iteration depth using the syntax `[apply_rules]](#manual-apply_rules) (config := {maxDepth := n})`.

Unlike `[solve_by_elim]](#manual-solve_by_elim)`, `[apply_rules]](#manual-apply_rules)` does not perform backtracking, and greedily applies
a lemma from the list until it gets stuck.

tactic

```lean
[as_aux_lemma]](#manual-as_aux_lemma)
```

`as_aux_lemma => tac` does the same as `tac`, except that it wraps the resulting expression
into an auxiliary lemma. In some cases, this significantly reduces the size of expressions
because the proof term is not duplicated.

### 14.5.7. Falsehood {#manual-tactic-ref-false}

tactic

```lean
[exfalso]](#manual-exfalso)
```

`[exfalso]](#manual-exfalso)` converts a goal `⊢ tgt` into `⊢ False` by applying `[False.elim](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False___elim)`.

tactic

```lean
[contradiction]](#manual-contradiction)
```

`[contradiction]](#manual-contradiction)` closes the main goal if its hypotheses are "trivially contradictory".

- Inductive type/family with no applicable constructors

  ```lean
  example (h : [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)) : p := byp:Sort ?u.3h:[False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)⊢ p [contradiction]](#manual-contradiction)All goals completed! 🐙
  ```
- Injectivity of constructors

  ```lean
  example (h : [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) = [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) : p := byp:Sort ?u.6h:[none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)⊢ p [contradiction]](#manual-contradiction)All goals completed! 🐙 --
  ```
- Decidable false proposition

  ```lean
  example (h : 2 + 2 = 3) : p := byp:Sort ?u.13h:2 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 2 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 3⊢ p [contradiction]](#manual-contradiction)All goals completed! 🐙
  ```
- Contradictory hypotheses

  ```lean
  example (h : p) (h' : ¬ p) : q := byp:Propq:Sort ?u.5h:ph':[¬](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)p⊢ q [contradiction]](#manual-contradiction)All goals completed! 🐙
  ```
- Other simple contradictions such as

  ```lean
  example (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (h : x ≠ x) : p := byp:Sort ?u.5x:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h:x ≠ x⊢ p [contradiction]](#manual-contradiction)All goals completed! 🐙
  ```

tactic

```lean
[false_or_by_contra]](#manual-false_or_by_contra)
```

Changes the goal to `[False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)`, retaining as much information as possible:

- If the goal is `[False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)`, do nothing.
- If the goal is an implication or a function type, introduce the argument and restart.
  (In particular, if the goal is `x ≠ y`, introduce `x = y`.)
- Otherwise, for a propositional goal `P`, replace it with `¬ ¬ P`
  (attempting to find a `[Decidable]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse)` instance, but otherwise falling back to working classically)
  and introduce `¬ P`.
- For a non-propositional goal use `[False.elim](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False___elim)`.

### 14.5.8. Goal Management {#manual-tactic-ref-goals}

tactic

```lean
[suffices]](#manual-suffices)
```

Given a main goal `ctx ⊢ t`, `[suffices]](#manual-suffices) h : t' from e` replaces the main goal with `ctx ⊢ t'`,
`e` must have type `t` in the context `ctx, h : t'`.

The variant `suffices h : t' by tac` is a shorthand for `suffices h : t' from by tac`.
If `h :` is omitted, the name `this` is used.

tactic

```lean
[change]](#manual-change)
```

- `[change]](#manual-change) tgt'` will change the goal from `tgt` to `tgt'`,
  assuming these are definitionally equal.
- `[change]](#manual-change) t' at h` will change hypothesis `h : t` to have type `t'`, assuming
  assuming `t` and `t'` are definitionally equal.
- `change a with b` will change occurrences of `a` to `b` in the goal,
  assuming `a` and `b` are definitionally equal.
- `change a with b at h` similarly changes `a` to `b` in the type of hypothesis `h`.

tactic

```lean
[generalize]](#manual-generalize)
```

- `generalize ([h :] e = x),+` replaces all occurrences `e`s in the main goal
  with a fresh hypothesis `x`s. If `h` is given, `h : e = x` is introduced as well.
- `[generalize]](#manual-generalize) e = x at h₁ ... hₙ` also generalizes occurrences of `e`
  inside `h₁`, ..., `hₙ`.
- `[generalize]](#manual-generalize) e = x at *` will generalize occurrences of `e` everywhere.

tactic

```lean
[specialize]](#manual-specialize)
```

`[specialize]](#manual-specialize) h a₁ ... aₙ` is equivalent to `[replace]](#manual-replace) h := h a₁ ... aₙ`.
It specializes the local hypothesis `h` by instantiating
universal quantifications and implications using the concrete terms `a₁` ... `aₙ`.
The tactic adds a new hypothesis with the same name and tries to remove
the original `h` if possible.

Example: given `h : ∀ (n : Nat), p n → q n` and `h' : p 2`,
then `[specialize]](#manual-specialize) h 2 h'` replaces `h` with `h : q 2`.

The tactic also supports instantiating particular universal quantifiers
using named argument syntax. Example: given `h : ∀ (m n : Nat), p m n`,
then `[specialize]](#manual-specialize) h (n := 2)` replaces `h` with `h : ∀ (m : Nat), p m 2`.

tactic

```lean
[obtain]](#manual-obtain)
```

The `[obtain]](#manual-obtain)` tactic is a combination of `[have]](#manual-have)` and `[rcases]](#manual-rcases)`. See `[rcases]](#manual-rcases)` for
a description of supported patterns.

```
obtain ⟨patt⟩ : type := proof
```

is equivalent to

```
have h : type := proof
rcases h with ⟨patt⟩
```

If `⟨patt⟩` is omitted, `[rcases]](#manual-rcases)` will try to infer the pattern.

If `type` is omitted, `:= proof` is required.

tactic

```lean
[show]](#manual-show)
```

`[show]](#manual-show) t` finds the first goal whose target unifies with `t`. It makes that the main goal,
performs the unification, and replaces the target with the unified version of `t`.

tactic

```lean
[show_term]](#manual-show_term)
```

`show_term tac` runs `tac`, then prints the generated term in the form
"exact X Y Z" or "refine X ?\_ Z" (prefixed by `[expose_names]](#manual-expose_names)` if necessary)
if there are remaining subgoals.

(For some tactics, the printed term will not be human readable.)

### 14.5.9. Cast Management {#manual-tactic-ref-casts}

The tactics in this section make it easier avoid getting stuck on *casts*, which are functions that coerce data from one type to another, such as converting a natural number to the corresponding integer.
They are described in more detail by Lewis and Madelaine (2020)Robert Y. Lewis and Paul-Nicolas Madelaine, 2020. [“Simplifying Casts and Coercions”](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.10594). arXiv:2001.10594.

tactic

```lean
[norm_cast]](#manual-norm_cast)
```

The `[norm_cast]](#manual-norm_cast)` family of tactics is used to normalize certain coercions (*casts*) in expressions.

- `[norm_cast]](#manual-norm_cast)` normalizes casts in the target.
- `[norm_cast]](#manual-norm_cast) at h` normalizes casts in hypothesis `h`.

The tactic is basically a version of `[simp]](#manual-simp)` with a specific set of lemmas to move casts
upwards in the expression.
Therefore even in situations where non-terminal `[simp]](#manual-simp)` calls are discouraged (because of fragility),
`[norm_cast]](#manual-norm_cast)` is considered to be safe.
It also has special handling of numerals.

For instance, given an assumption

```
a b : ℤ
h : ↑a + ↑b < (10 : ℚ)
```

writing `[norm_cast]](#manual-norm_cast) at h` will turn `h` into

```
h : a + b < 10
```

There are also variants of basic tactics that use `[norm_cast]](#manual-norm_cast)` to normalize expressions during
their operation, to make them more flexible about the expressions they accept
(we say that it is a tactic *modulo* the effects of `[norm_cast]](#manual-norm_cast)`):

- `[exact_mod_cast]](#manual-exact_mod_cast)` for `[exact]](#manual-exact)` and `[apply_mod_cast]](#manual-apply_mod_cast)` for `[apply]](#manual-apply)`.
  Writing `[exact_mod_cast]](#manual-exact_mod_cast) h` and `[apply_mod_cast]](#manual-apply_mod_cast) h` will normalize casts
  in the goal and `h` before using `[exact]](#manual-exact) h` or `[apply]](#manual-apply) h`.
- `[rw_mod_cast]](#manual-rw_mod_cast)` for `[rw]](#manual-rw)`. It applies `[norm_cast]](#manual-norm_cast)` between rewrites.
- `[assumption_mod_cast]](#manual-assumption_mod_cast)` for `[assumption]](#manual-assumption)`.
  This is effectively `norm_cast at *; assumption`, but more efficient.
  It normalizes casts in the goal and, for every hypothesis `h` in the context,
  it will try to normalize casts in `h` and use `[exact]](#manual-exact) h`.

See also `[push_cast]](#manual-push_cast)`, which moves casts inwards rather than lifting them outwards.

tactic

```lean
[push_cast]](#manual-push_cast)
```

`[push_cast]](#manual-push_cast)` rewrites the goal to move certain coercions (*casts*) inward, toward the leaf nodes.
This uses `[norm_cast]](#manual-norm_cast)` lemmas in the forward direction.
For example, `↑(a + b)` will be written to `↑a + ↑b`.

- `[push_cast]](#manual-push_cast)` moves casts inward in the goal.
- `[push_cast]](#manual-push_cast) at h` moves casts inward in the hypothesis `h`.
  It can be used with extra simp lemmas with, for example, `[push_cast]](#manual-push_cast) [Int.add_zero]`.

Example:

```lean
example (a b : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
(h1 : ((a + b : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)) = 10)
(h2 : ((a + b + 0 : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)) = 10) :
((a + b : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)) = 10 := bya:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)b:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h1:↑[(]](#manual-HAdd___mk)a [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) b[)]](#manual-HAdd___mk) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 10h2:↑[(]](#manual-HAdd___mk)a [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) b [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 0[)]](#manual-HAdd___mk) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 10⊢ ↑[(]](#manual-HAdd___mk)a [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) b[)]](#manual-HAdd___mk) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 10
/-
h1 : ↑(a + b) = 10
h2 : ↑(a + b + 0) = 10
⊢ ↑(a + b) = 10
-/
[push_cast]](#manual-push_cast)a:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)b:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h1:↑[(]](#manual-HAdd___mk)a [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) b[)]](#manual-HAdd___mk) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 10h2:↑[(]](#manual-HAdd___mk)a [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) b [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 0[)]](#manual-HAdd___mk) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 10⊢ ↑a [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) ↑b [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 10
/- Now
⊢ ↑a + ↑b = 10
-/
[push_cast]](#manual-push_cast) at h1a:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)b:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h1:↑a [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) ↑b [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 10h2:↑[(]](#manual-HAdd___mk)a [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) b [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 0[)]](#manual-HAdd___mk) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 10⊢ ↑a [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) ↑b [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 10
[push_cast]](#manual-push_cast) [Int.add_zero] at h2a:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)b:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h1:↑a [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) ↑b [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 10h2:↑a [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) ↑b [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 10⊢ ↑a [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) ↑b [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 10
/- Now
h1 h2 : ↑a + ↑b = 10
-/
[exact]](#manual-exact) h1All goals completed! 🐙
```

See also `[norm_cast]](#manual-norm_cast)`.

tactic

```lean
[exact_mod_cast]](#manual-exact_mod_cast)
```

Normalize casts in the goal and the given expression, then close the goal with `[exact]](#manual-exact)`.

tactic

```lean
[apply_mod_cast]](#manual-apply_mod_cast)
```

Normalize casts in the goal and the given expression, then `[apply]](#manual-apply)` the expression to the goal.

tactic

```lean
[rw_mod_cast]](#manual-rw_mod_cast)
```

Rewrites with the given rules, normalizing casts prior to each step.

tactic

```lean
[assumption_mod_cast]](#manual-assumption_mod_cast)
```

`[assumption_mod_cast]](#manual-assumption_mod_cast)` is a variant of `[assumption]](#manual-assumption)` that solves the goal
using a hypothesis. Unlike `[assumption]](#manual-assumption)`, it first pre-processes the goal and
each hypothesis to move casts as far outwards as possible, so it can be used
in more situations.

Concretely, it runs `[norm_cast]](#manual-norm_cast)` on the goal. For each local hypothesis `h`, it also
normalizes `h` with `[norm_cast]](#manual-norm_cast)` and tries to use that to close the goal.

### 14.5.10. Managing `let` Expressions {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Tactic-Proofs--Tactic-Reference--Managing--let--Expressions}

tactic

```lean
[extract_lets]](#manual-extract_lets)
```

Extracts `[let]](#manual-let)` and `[have]](#manual-have)` expressions from within the target or a local hypothesis,
introducing new local definitions.

- `[extract_lets]](#manual-extract_lets)` extracts all the lets from the target.
- `[extract_lets]](#manual-extract_lets) x y z` extracts all the lets from the target and uses `x`, `y`, and `z` for the first names.
  Using `_` for a name leaves it unnamed.
- `[extract_lets]](#manual-extract_lets) x y z at h` operates on the local hypothesis `h` instead of the target.

For example, given a local hypotheses if the form `h : let x := v; b x`, then `[extract_lets]](#manual-extract_lets) z at h`
introduces a new local definition `z := v` and changes `h` to be `h : b z`.

tactic

```lean
[lift_lets]](#manual-lift_lets)
```

Lifts `[let]](#manual-let)` and `[have]](#manual-have)` expressions within a term as far out as possible.
It is like `[extract_lets]](#manual-extract_lets) +lift`, but the top-level lets at the end of the procedure
are not extracted as local hypotheses.

- `[lift_lets]](#manual-lift_lets)` lifts let expressions in the target.
- `[lift_lets]](#manual-lift_lets) at h` lifts let expressions at the given local hypothesis.

For example,

```
example : (let x := 1; x) = 1 := by
  lift_lets
  -- ⊢ let x := 1; x = 1
  ...
```

tactic

```lean
[let_to_have]](#manual-let_to_have)
```

Transforms `[let]](#manual-let)` expressions into `[have]](#manual-have)` expressions when possible.

- `[let_to_have]](#manual-let_to_have)` transforms `[let]](#manual-let)`s in the target.
- `[let_to_have]](#manual-let_to_have) at h` transforms `[let]](#manual-let)`s in the given local hypothesis.

tactic

```lean
[clear_value]](#manual-clear_value)
```

- `clear_value x...` clears the values of the given local definitions.
  A local definition `x : α := v` becomes a hypothesis `x : α`.
- `[clear_value]](#manual-clear_value) (h : x = _)` adds a hypothesis `h : x = v` before clearing the value of `x`.
  This is short for `have h : x = v := rfl; clear_value x`.
  Any value definitionally equal to `v` can be used in place of `_`.
- `[clear_value]](#manual-clear_value) *` clears values of all hypotheses that can be cleared.
  Fails if none can be cleared.

These syntaxes can be combined. For example, `[clear_value]](#manual-clear_value) x y *` ensures that `x` and `y` are cleared
while trying to clear all other local definitions,
and `clear_value (hx : x = _) y * with hx` does the same while first adding the `hx : x = v` hypothesis.

### 14.5.11. Extensionality {#manual-tactic-ref-ext}

tactic

```lean
[ext]](#manual-ext)
```

Applies extensionality lemmas that are registered with the `@[ext]` attribute.

- `ext pat*` applies extensionality theorems as much as possible,
  using the patterns `pat*` to introduce the variables in extensionality theorems using `[rintro]](#manual-rintro)`.
  For example, the patterns are used to name the variables introduced by lemmas such as `[funext]](#manual-funext)`.
- Without patterns,`[ext]](#manual-ext)` applies extensionality lemmas as much
  as possible but introduces anonymous hypotheses whenever needed.
- `ext pat* : n` applies ext theorems only up to depth `n`.

The `ext1 pat*` tactic is like `ext pat*` except that it only applies a single extensionality theorem.

Unused patterns will generate warning.
Patterns that don't match the variables will typically result in the introduction of anonymous hypotheses.

tactic

```lean
[ext1]](#manual-ext1)
```

`ext1 pat*` is like `ext pat*` except that it only applies a single extensionality theorem rather
than recursively applying as many extensionality theorems as possible.

The `pat*` patterns are processed using the `[rintro]](#manual-rintro)` tactic.
If no patterns are supplied, then variables are introduced anonymously using the `[intros]](#manual-intros)` tactic.

tactic

```lean
[apply_ext_theorem]](#manual-apply_ext_theorem)
```

Apply a single extensionality theorem to the current goal.

tactic

```lean
[funext]](#manual-funext-next)
```

Apply function extensionality and introduce new hypotheses.
The tactic `[funext]](#manual-funext-next)` will keep applying the `[funext]](#manual-funext)` lemma until the goal target is not reducible to

```
  |-  ((fun x => ...) = (fun x => ...))
```

The variant `[funext]](#manual-funext-next) h₁ ... hₙ` applies `[funext]](#manual-funext)` `n` times, and uses the given identifiers to name the new hypotheses.
Patterns can be used like in the `[intro]](#manual-intro)` tactic. Example, given a goal

```
  |-  ((fun x : Nat × Bool => ...) = (fun x => ...))
```

`[funext]](#manual-funext-next) (a, b)` applies `[funext]](#manual-funext)` once and performs pattern matching on the newly introduced pair.

### 14.5.12. SMT-Inspired Automation {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Tactic-Proofs--Tactic-Reference--SMT-Inspired-Automation}

tactic

```lean
[grind]](#manual-grind)
```

`[grind]](#manual-grind)` is a tactic inspired by modern SMT solvers. **Picture a virtual whiteboard**:
every time grind discovers a new equality, inequality, or logical fact,
it writes it on the board, groups together terms known to be equal,
and lets each reasoning engine read from and contribute to the shared workspace.
These engines work together to handle equality reasoning, apply known theorems,
propagate new facts, perform case analysis, and run specialized solvers
for domains like linear arithmetic and commutative rings.

See [the reference manual's chapter on `[grind]](#manual-grind)`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0-rc1/find/?domain=Verso.Genre.Manual.section&name=grind-tactic) for more information.

`[grind]](#manual-grind)` is *not* designed for goals whose search space explodes combinatorially,
think large pigeonhole instances, graph‑coloring reductions, high‑order N‑queens boards,
or a 200‑variable Sudoku encoded as Boolean constraints. Such encodings require
thousands (or millions) of case‑splits that overwhelm `[grind]](#manual-grind)`’s branching search.

For **bit‑level or combinatorial problems**, consider using **`[bv_decide]](#manual-bv_decide)`**.
`[bv_decide]](#manual-bv_decide)` calls a state‑of‑the‑art SAT solver (CaDiCaL) and then returns a
*compact, machine‑checkable certificate*.

**Equality reasoning**

`[grind]](#manual-grind)` uses **congruence closure** to track equalities between terms.
When two terms are known to be equal, congruence closure automatically deduces
equalities between more complex expressions built from them.
For example, if `a = b`, then congruence closure will also conclude that `f a` = `f b`
for any function `f`. This forms the foundation for efficient equality reasoning in `[grind]](#manual-grind)`.
Here is an example:

```lean
example (f : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (h : a = b) : f (f b) = f (f a) := bya:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)b:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)f:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h:a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) b⊢ f (f b) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) f (f a)
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

**Applying theorems using E-matching**

To apply existing theorems, `[grind]](#manual-grind)` uses a technique called **E-matching**,
which finds matches for known theorem patterns while taking equalities into account.
Combined with congruence closure, E-matching helps `[grind]](#manual-grind)` discover
non-obvious consequences of theorems and equalities automatically.

Consider the following functions and theorems:

```lean
def [f](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/releases/v4.27.0/#f) (a : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
a + 1
def g (a : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
a - 1
@[grind =]
theorem gf (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : g ([f](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/releases/v4.27.0/#f) x) = x := byx:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ g ([f](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/releases/v4.27.0/#f) x) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) x
[simp]](#manual-simp) [[f](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/releases/v4.27.0/#f), g]All goals completed! 🐙
```

The theorem `gf` asserts that `g (f x) = x` for all natural numbers `x`.
The attribute `[grind =]` instructs `[grind]](#manual-grind)` to use the left-hand side of the equation,
`g (f x)`, as a pattern for E-matching.
Suppose we now have a goal involving:

```
example {a b} (h : f b = a) : g a = b := by
  grind
```

Although `g a` is not an instance of the pattern `g (f x)`,
it becomes one modulo the equation `f b = a`. By substituting `a`
with `f b` in `g a`, we obtain the term `g (f b)`,
which matches the pattern `g (f x)` with the assignment `x := b`.
Thus, the theorem `gf` is instantiated with `x := b`,
and the new equality `g (f b) = b` is asserted.
`[grind]](#manual-grind)` then uses congruence closure to derive the implied equality
`g a = g (f b)` and completes the proof.

The pattern used to instantiate theorems affects the effectiveness of `[grind]](#manual-grind)`.
For example, the pattern `g (f x)` is too restrictive in the following case:
the theorem `gf` will not be instantiated because the goal does not even
contain the function symbol `g`.

```
example (h₁ : f b = a) (h₂ : f c = a) : b = c := by
  grind
```

You can use the command `grind_pattern` to manually select a pattern for a given theorem.
In the following example, we instruct `[grind]](#manual-grind)` to use `f x` as the pattern,
allowing it to solve the goal automatically:

```
grind_pattern gf => f x

example {a b c} (h₁ : f b = a) (h₂ : f c = a) : b = c := by
  grind
```

You can enable the option `[trace.grind.ematch.instance](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/E___matching/#trace___grind___ematch___instance)` to make `[grind]](#manual-grind)` print a
trace message for each theorem instance it generates.

You can also specify a **multi-pattern** to control when `[grind]](#manual-grind)` should apply a theorem.
A multi-pattern requires that all specified patterns are matched in the current context
before the theorem is applied. This is useful for theorems such as transitivity rules,
where multiple premises must be simultaneously present for the rule to apply.
The following example demonstrates this feature using a transitivity axiom for a binary relation `R`:

```lean
opaque [R](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Bigger-Examples/#R) : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) → [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) → Prop
[axiom]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___axiom-next) Rtrans {x y z : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)} : [R](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Bigger-Examples/#R) x y → [R](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Bigger-Examples/#R) y z → [R](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Bigger-Examples/#R) x z
grind_pattern Rtrans => [R](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Bigger-Examples/#R) x y, [R](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Bigger-Examples/#R) y z
```
