```lean
example {a b c d} : [R](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Bigger-Examples/#R) a b → [R](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Bigger-Examples/#R) b c → [R](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Bigger-Examples/#R) c d → [R](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Bigger-Examples/#R) a d := bya:[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)b:[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)c:[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)d:[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)⊢ [R](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Bigger-Examples/#R) a b → [R](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Bigger-Examples/#R) b c → [R](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Bigger-Examples/#R) c d → [R](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Bigger-Examples/#R) a d
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

By specifying the multi-pattern `R x y, R y z`, we instruct `[grind]](#manual-grind)` to
instantiate `Rtrans` only when both `R x y` and `R y z` are available in the context.
In the example, `[grind]](#manual-grind)` applies `Rtrans` to derive `R a c` from `R a b` and `R b c`,
and can then repeat the same reasoning to deduce `R a d` from `R a c` and `R c d`.

Instead of using `grind_pattern` to explicitly specify a pattern,
you can use the `@[grind]` attribute or one of its variants, which will use a heuristic to
generate a (multi-)pattern. The complete list is available in the reference manual. The main ones are:

- `@[grind →]` will select a multi-pattern from the hypotheses of the theorem (i.e. it will use the theorem for forwards reasoning).
  In more detail, it will traverse the hypotheses of the theorem from left-to-right, and each time it encounters a minimal indexable
  (i.e. has a constant as its head) subexpression which "covers" (i.e. fixes the value of) an argument which was not
  previously covered, it will add that subexpression as a pattern, until all arguments have been covered.
- `@[grind ←]` will select a multi-pattern from the conclusion of theorem (i.e. it will use the theorem for backwards reasoning).
  This may fail if not all the arguments to the theorem appear in the conclusion.
- `@[grind]` will traverse the conclusion and then the hypotheses left-to-right, adding patterns as they increase the coverage,
  stopping when all arguments are covered.
- `@[grind =]` checks that the conclusion of the theorem is an equality, and then uses the left-hand-side of the equality as a pattern.
  This may fail if not all of the arguments appear in the left-hand-side.

Here is the previous example again but using the attribute `[grind →]`

```lean
opaque [R](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Bigger-Examples/#R) : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) → [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) → Prop
@[grind →] [axiom]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___axiom-next) Rtrans {x y z : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)} : [R](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Bigger-Examples/#R) x y → [R](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Bigger-Examples/#R) y z → [R](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Bigger-Examples/#R) x z
```

To control theorem instantiation and avoid generating an unbounded number of instances,
`[grind]](#manual-grind)` uses a generation counter. Terms in the original goal are assigned generation zero.
When `[grind]](#manual-grind)` applies a theorem using terms of generation `≤ n`, any new terms it creates
are assigned generation `n + 1`. This limits how far the tactic explores when applying
theorems and helps prevent an excessive number of instantiations.

**Key options:**

- `grind (ematch := <num>)` controls the number of E-matching rounds.
- `grind [<name>, ...]` instructs `[grind]](#manual-grind)` to use the declaration `name` during E-matching.
- `grind only [<name>, ...]` is like `grind [<name>, ...]` but does not use theorems tagged with `@[grind]`.
- `grind (gen := <num>)` sets the maximum generation.

**Linear integer arithmetic (`[lia]](#manual-lia)`)**

`[grind]](#manual-grind)` can solve goals that reduce to **linear integer arithmetic (LIA)** using an
integrated decision procedure called **`[lia]](#manual-lia)`**. It understands

- equalities   `p = 0`
- inequalities  `p ≤ 0`
- disequalities `p ≠ 0`
- divisibility  `d ∣ p`

The solver incrementally assigns integer values to variables; when a partial
assignment violates a constraint it adds a new, implied constraint and retries.
This *model-based* search is **complete for LIA**.

**Key options:**

- `[grind]](#manual-grind) -lia` disable the solver (useful for debugging)
- `[grind]](#manual-grind) +qlia` accept rational models (shrinks the search space but is incomplete for ℤ)
- `[grind]](#manual-grind) (liaSteps := n)` cap the number of steps performed by the model search (the solver becomes incomplete when the threshold is reached)

**Examples:**

```lean

2 * x + 3 * y = 0 → 1 ≤ x → y < 1 := byx:[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)y:[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)⊢ 2 [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) x [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 3 [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) y [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0 → 1 [≤]](#manual-LE___mk) x → y [<]](#manual-LT___mk) 1
```

**Algebraic solver (`ring`)**

`[grind]](#manual-grind)` ships with an algebraic solver nick-named **`ring`** for goals that can
be phrased as polynomial equations (or disequations) over commutative rings,
semirings, or fields.

*Works out of the box*
All core numeric types and relevant Mathlib types already provide the required
type-class instances, so the solver is ready to use in most developments.

What it can decide:

- equalities of the form `p = q`
- disequalities `p ≠ q`
- basic reasoning under field inverses (`a / b := a * b⁻¹`)
- goals that mix ring facts with other `[grind]](#manual-grind)` engines

**Key options:**

- `[grind]](#manual-grind) -ring` turn the solver off (useful when debugging)
- `[grind]](#manual-grind) (ringSteps := n)` cap the number of steps performed by this procedure.

**Other options**

- `grind (splits := <num>)` caps the *depth* of the search tree. Once a branch performs `num` splits
  `[grind]](#manual-grind)` stops splitting further in that branch.
- `[grind]](#manual-grind) -splitIte` disables case splitting on if-then-else expressions.
- `[grind]](#manual-grind) -splitMatch` disables case splitting on `[match]](#manual-match)` expressions.
- `[grind]](#manual-grind) +splitImp` instructs `[grind]](#manual-grind)` to split on any hypothesis `A → B` whose antecedent `A` is **propositional**.
- `[grind]](#manual-grind) -linarith` disables the linear arithmetic solver for (ordered) modules and rings.

tactic

```lean
[grind?]](#manual-grind___)
```

`[grind?]](#manual-grind___)` takes the same arguments as `[grind]](#manual-grind)`, but reports an equivalent call to `[grind]](#manual-grind) [only]](#manual-grind)`
that would be sufficient to close the goal. This is useful for reducing the size of the `[grind]](#manual-grind)`
theorems in a local invocation.

tactic

```lean
[lia]](#manual-lia)
```

`[lia]](#manual-lia)` solves linear integer arithmetic goals.

It is a implemented as a thin wrapper around the `[grind]](#manual-grind)` tactic, enabling only the `[lia]](#manual-lia)` solver.
Please use `[grind]](#manual-grind)` instead if you need additional capabilities.

tactic

```lean
[grobner]](#manual-grobner)
```

`[grobner]](#manual-grobner)` solves goals that can be phrased as polynomial equations (with further polynomial equations as hypotheses)
over commutative (semi)rings, using the Grobner basis algorithm.

It is a implemented as a thin wrapper around the `[grind]](#manual-grind)` tactic, enabling only the `[grobner]](#manual-grobner)` solver.
Please use `[grind]](#manual-grind)` instead if you need additional capabilities.

### 14.5.13. Simplification {#manual-simp-tactics}

The simplifier is described in greater detail in [its dedicated chapter](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The-Simplifier/#the-simplifier).

tactic

```lean
[simp]](#manual-simp)
```

The `[simp]](#manual-simp)` tactic uses lemmas and hypotheses to simplify the main goal target or
non-dependent hypotheses. It has many variants:

- `[simp]](#manual-simp)` simplifies the main goal target using lemmas tagged with the attribute `[simp]`.
- `simp [h₁, h₂, ..., hₙ]` simplifies the main goal target using the lemmas tagged
  with the attribute `[simp]` and the given `hᵢ`'s, where the `hᵢ`'s are expressions.-
- If an `hᵢ` is a defined constant `f`, then `f` is unfolded. If `f` has equational lemmas associated
  with it (and is not a projection or a `reducible` definition), these are used to rewrite with `f`.
- `[simp]](#manual-simp) [*]` simplifies the main goal target using the lemmas tagged with the
  attribute `[simp]` and all hypotheses.
- `simp only [h₁, h₂, ..., hₙ]` is like `simp [h₁, h₂, ..., hₙ]` but does not use `[simp]` lemmas.
- `simp [-id₁, ..., -idₙ]` simplifies the main goal target using the lemmas tagged
  with the attribute `[simp]`, but removes the ones named `idᵢ`.
- `[simp]](#manual-simp) at h₁ h₂ ... hₙ` simplifies the hypotheses `h₁ : T₁` ... `hₙ : Tₙ`. If
  the target or another hypothesis depends on `hᵢ`, a new simplified hypothesis
  `hᵢ` is introduced, but the old one remains in the local context.
- `[simp]](#manual-simp) at *` simplifies all the hypotheses and the target.
- `[simp]](#manual-simp) [*] at *` simplifies target and all (propositional) hypotheses using the
  other hypotheses.

tactic

```lean
[simp!]](#manual-simp___)
```

`[simp!]](#manual-simp___)` is shorthand for `[simp]](#manual-simp)` with `autoUnfold := true`.
This will unfold applications of functions defined by pattern matching, when one of the patterns applies.
This can be used to partially evaluate many definitions.

tactic

```lean
[simp?]](#manual-simp___-next)
```

`[simp?]](#manual-simp___-next)` takes the same arguments as `[simp]](#manual-simp)`, but reports an equivalent call to `[simp]](#manual-simp) [only]](#manual-simp)`
that would be sufficient to close the goal. This is useful for reducing the size of the simp
set in a local invocation to speed up processing.

```lean
example (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : ([if]](#manual-termIfThenElse) [True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro) [then]](#manual-termIfThenElse) x + 2 [else]](#manual-termIfThenElse) 3) = x + 2 := byx:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ (if [True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro) then x [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 2 else 3) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) x [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 2
[simp?]](#manual-simp___-next)All goals completed! 🐙 -- prints "Try this: simp only [ite_true]"
```

This command can also be used in `[simp_all]](#manual-simp_all)` and `[dsimp]](#manual-dsimp)`.

tactic

```lean
[simp?!]](#manual-simp______)
```

```lean
[simpa]](#manual-simpa)
```

This is a "finishing" tactic modification of `[simp]](#manual-simp)`. It has two forms.

- `[simpa]](#manual-simpa) [rules, ⋯] using e` will simplify the goal and the type of
  `e` using `rules`, then try to close the goal using `e`.

  Simplifying the type of `e` makes it more likely to match the goal
  (which has also been simplified). This construction also tends to be
  more robust under changes to the simp lemma set.

  The final match between the simplified `e` and the simplified goal uses
  **reducible** transparency, so it does not unfold semireducible definitions.
  Write `simpa [rules, ⋯] using! e` to perform the match at the ambient
  (default/semireducible) transparency instead.
- `[simpa]](#manual-simpa) [rules, ⋯]` will simplify the goal and the type of a
  hypothesis `this` if present in the context, then try to close the goal using
  the `[assumption]](#manual-assumption)` tactic.

As with `[simp]](#manual-simp)`, the `!` modifier after `[simpa]](#manual-simpa)` enables auto-unfolding of
definitions in the simp set.

### 14.5.14. Rewriting {#manual-tactic-ref-rw}

tactic

```lean
[rw]](#manual-rw)
```

`[rw]](#manual-rw)` is like `[rewrite]](#manual-rewrite)`, but also tries to close the goal by "cheap" (reducible) `[rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)` afterwards.

tactic

```lean
[rewrite]](#manual-rewrite)
```

`[rewrite]](#manual-rewrite) [e]` applies identity `e` as a rewrite rule to the target of the main goal.
If `e` is preceded by left arrow (`←` or `<-`), the rewrite is applied in the reverse direction.
If `e` is a defined constant, then the equational theorems associated with `e` are used.
This provides a convenient way to unfold `e`.

- `rewrite [e₁, ..., eₙ]` applies the given rules sequentially.
- `[rewrite]](#manual-rewrite) [e] at l` rewrites `e` at location(s) `l`, where `l` is either `*` or a
  list of hypotheses in the local context. In the latter case, a turnstile `⊢` or `|-`
  can also be used, to signify the target of the goal.

Using `[rw]](#manual-rw) (occs := .pos L) [e]`,
where `L : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, you can control which "occurrences" are rewritten.
(This option applies to each rule, so usually this will only be used with a single rule.)
Occurrences count from `1`.
At each allowed occurrence, arguments of the rewrite rule `e` may be instantiated,
restricting which later rewrites can be found.
(Disallowed occurrences do not result in instantiation.)
`(occs := .neg L)` allows skipping specified occurrences.

tactic

```lean
[erw]](#manual-erw)
```

`[erw]](#manual-erw) [rules]` is a shorthand for `[rw]](#manual-rw) (transparency := .default) [rules]`.
This does rewriting up to unfolding of regular definitions (by comparison to regular `[rw]](#manual-rw)`
which only unfolds `@[reducible]` definitions).

tactic

```lean
[rwa]](#manual-rwa)
```

`[rwa]](#manual-rwa)` is short-hand for `rw; assumption`.

inductive type

```lean
[Lean.Meta.TransparencyMode]](#manual-Lean___Meta___TransparencyMode___all) : Type



[Lean.Meta.TransparencyMode]](#manual-Lean___Meta___TransparencyMode___all) : Type
```

Controls which constants `isDefEq` (definitional equality) and `whnf` (weak head normal form)
are allowed to unfold.

**Background: "try-hard" vs "speculative" modes**

During **type checking of user input**, we assume the input is most likely correct, and we want
Lean to try hard before reporting a failure. Here, it is fine to unfold `[semireducible]` definitions
(the `.default` setting).

During **proof automation** (`[simp]](#manual-simp)`, `[rw]](#manual-rw)`, type class resolution), we perform many speculative
`isDefEq` calls — most of which *fail*. In this setting, we do *not* want to try hard: unfolding
too many definitions is a performance footgun. This is why `.reducible` exists.

**The transparency hierarchy**

The levels form a linear order: `none < reducible < instances < implicit < default < all`.
Each level unfolds everything the previous level does, plus more:

- **`reducible`**: Only unfolds `[reducible]` definitions. Used for speculative `isDefEq` checks
  (e.g., discrimination tree lookups in `[simp]](#manual-simp)`, type class resolution). Think of `[reducible]` as
  `[inline]` for type checking and indexing.
- **`instances`**: Also unfolds `[instance_reducible]` definitions (auto-applied to type class
  instances by the `[instance]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Attr___instance)` command). Primarily but not exclusively used during type class synthesis
  when unifying an instance's type with the expected type. Constants that play a role in an instance's
  discrimination pattern must not be instance-reducible; they must at least be implicit-reducible.
  For example, if `id : α → α` was instance-reducible, under some circumstances an instance of type
  `C (id x)` can be applied when an instance of type `C x` is requested. If this is undesirable,
  `id` (in this example) should be at most implicit-reducible.
  Most users should follow a simple rule: Make declarations that are meant to return instances but
  were not declared using the `[instance]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Attr___instance)` command instance-reducible.
  Most users will never need to manually annotate anything else with `[instance_reducible]` and they
  should not unless they understand what they do. There are some more subtle corners of the
  elaborator where instance-reducible constants have a special role, such as in the lazy WHNF
  mechanism and the generation of `[sizeOf]](#manual-SizeOf___mk)` equational lemmas. `[instance_reducible]` also affects
  the compiler's specialization and inlining behavior.
- **`implicit`**: Also unfolds `[implicit_reducible]` definitions. Implicit arguments and instance
  arguments are always checked at implicit transparency, even if the ambient transparency is `reducible`
  or `instances`. It is usually cheaper to compare terms at implicit transparency than it is to
  compare them at default transparency (see below) because it is more restrictive at unfolding.
  Tactics such as `[simp]](#manual-simp)` unify lemmas with subterms at `reducible` transparency. For example, when
  `[simp]](#manual-simp)` applies a lemma to a subterm, it puts metavariables in the place of its parameters and then
  unifies the lemma's conclusion with the subterm at `reducible` transparency, bumping the
  transparency to `implicit` for implicit and instance arguments. When `[simp]](#manual-simp)` does not apply a lemma
  that it should, it can be because `[simp]](#manual-simp)` would need to unfold a semireducible declaration during
  the unification process. In that case, marking that declaration `[implicit_reducible]` can be a
  solution.

  `[implicit_reducible]` is the right annotation in several situations, such as the following ones.

  - Because instance arguments are always compared at (at least) implicit transparency,
    marking constants as `[implicit_reducible]` can prevent instance diamonds.
  - Operations used in type parameters (such as in the `n` of `[Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) n`) should, as a basic rule,
    be implicit-reducible, at least as soon as `backward.isDefEq.respectTransparency.types` is
    enabled, because types during metavariable assignments are then compared at implicit
    transparency.
  - The left-hand side and right-hand side of a `[rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)` lemma should be definitionally equal at
    implicit transparency. Marking constants as `[implicit_reducible]` allows for more `[rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)` lemmas.

  The downside is that every implicit-reducible constant makes the definitional equality checker
  do more unfolding, which can get expensive.
- **`[default]](#manual-Inhabited___mk)`**: Also unfolds `[semireducible]` definitions (anything not `[irreducible]`).
  Used for type checking user input where we want to try hard.
- **`all`**: Also unfolds `[irreducible]` definitions. Rarely used.

**Implicit arguments and transparency**

When proof automation (e.g., `[simp]](#manual-simp)`, `[rw]](#manual-rw)`) applies a lemma, explicit arguments are checked at the
caller's transparency (typically `.reducible`). But implicit arguments are often "invisible" to the
user — if a lemma fails to apply because of an implicit argument mismatch, the user is confused.
Historically, Lean bumped transparency to `.default` for implicit arguments, but this eventually
became a performance bottleneck in Mathlib. The option `backward.isDefEq.respectTransparency true`
(default: `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`) disables this bump. Instead, implicit arguments (`{..}`) and instance-implicit
arguments (`[..]`) are checked at `.implicit` (so implicit-reducible definitions additionally unfold
and instance diamonds resolve), or at the
caller's transparency when `backward.isDefEq.implicitBump` is `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`.

See also: `ReducibilityStatus`, `backward.isDefEq.respectTransparency`,
`backward.whnf.reducibleClassField`.

Constructors

```lean
[Lean.Meta.TransparencyMode.all]](#manual-Lean___Meta___TransparencyMode___all) : [Lean.Meta.TransparencyMode]](#manual-Lean___Meta___TransparencyMode___all)
```

Unfolds all constants, even those tagged as `@[irreducible]`.

```lean
[Lean.Meta.TransparencyMode.default]](#manual-Lean___Meta___TransparencyMode___all) :
  [Lean.Meta.TransparencyMode]](#manual-Lean___Meta___TransparencyMode___all)
```

Unfolds all constants except those tagged as `@[irreducible]`. Used for type checking
user-written terms where we expect the input to be correct and want to try hard.

```lean
[Lean.Meta.TransparencyMode.reducible]](#manual-Lean___Meta___TransparencyMode___all) :
  [Lean.Meta.TransparencyMode]](#manual-Lean___Meta___TransparencyMode___all)
```

Unfolds only constants tagged with the `@[reducible]` attribute. Used for speculative
`isDefEq` in proof automation (`simp`, `[rw]](#manual-rw)`, type class resolution) where most checks fail
and we must not try too hard.

```lean
[Lean.Meta.TransparencyMode.instances]](#manual-Lean___Meta___TransparencyMode___all) :
  [Lean.Meta.TransparencyMode]](#manual-Lean___Meta___TransparencyMode___all)
```

Unfolds reducible constants and constants tagged with `@[instance_reducible]` (e.g. type
class instances). Does *not* unfold `[implicit_reducible]`.

```lean
[Lean.Meta.TransparencyMode.none]](#manual-Lean___Meta___TransparencyMode___all) : [Lean.Meta.TransparencyMode]](#manual-Lean___Meta___TransparencyMode___all)
```

Do not unfold anything.

```lean
[Lean.Meta.TransparencyMode.implicit]](#manual-Lean___Meta___TransparencyMode___all) :
  [Lean.Meta.TransparencyMode]](#manual-Lean___Meta___TransparencyMode___all)
```

Unfolds reducible, `[instance_reducible]`, and `[implicit_reducible]` constants.
Used for checking definitional equality of implicit and instance-implicit arguments.

def

```lean
[Lean.Meta.Rewrite.NewGoals]](#manual-Lean___Meta___Rewrite___NewGoals) : Type



[Lean.Meta.Rewrite.NewGoals]](#manual-Lean___Meta___Rewrite___NewGoals) : Type
```

Controls which new mvars are turned in to goals by the `[apply]](#manual-apply)` tactic.

- `nonDependentFirst` mvars that don't depend on other goals appear first in the goal list.
- `nonDependentOnly` only mvars that don't depend on other goals are added to goal list.
- `all` all unassigned mvars are added to the goal list.

tactic

```lean
[unfold]](#manual-unfold)
```

- `[unfold]](#manual-unfold) id` unfolds all occurrences of definition `id` in the target.
- `unfold id1 id2 ...` is equivalent to `unfold id1; unfold id2; ...`.
- `[unfold]](#manual-unfold) id at h` unfolds at the hypothesis `h`.

Definitions can be either global or local definitions.

For non-recursive global definitions, this tactic is identical to `[delta]](#manual-delta)`.
For recursive global definitions, it uses the "unfolding lemma" `id.eq_def`,
which is generated for each recursive definition, to unfold according to the recursive definition given by the user.
Only one level of unfolding is performed, in contrast to `[simp]](#manual-simp) [only]](#manual-simp) [id]`, which unfolds definition `id` recursively.

Implemented by `Lean.Elab.Tactic.evalUnfold`.

tactic

```lean
[replace]](#manual-replace)
```

`[replace]](#manual-replace) h := e` is like `[have]](#manual-have) h := e`, but it removes a previous hypothesis
of the same name as this one if possible. For example, if the state is:

```
f : α → β
h : α
⊢ goal
```

Then after `[replace]](#manual-replace) h := f h` the state will be:

```
f : α → β
h : β
⊢ goal
```

whereas `[have]](#manual-have) h := f h` would result in:

```
f : α → β
h† : α
h : β
⊢ goal
```

The tactic `[specialize]](#manual-specialize) h a₁ ... aₙ` is a way to write `[replace]](#manual-replace) h := h a₁ ... aₙ`,
automatically inferring which hypothesis should be replaced.

The `[replace]](#manual-replace)` tactic can be used to simulate Rocq's `apply at` tactic.

tactic

```lean
[delta]](#manual-delta)
```

`delta id1 id2 ...` delta-expands the definitions `id1`, `id2`, ....
This is a low-level tactic, it will expose how recursive definitions have been
compiled by Lean.

### 14.5.15. Inductive Types {#manual-tactic-ref-inductive}

#### 14.5.15.1. Introduction {#manual-tactic-ref-inductive-intro}

tactic

```lean
[constructor]](#manual-constructor)
```

If the main goal's target type is an inductive type, `[constructor]](#manual-constructor)` solves it with
the first matching constructor, or else fails.

tactic

```lean
[injection]](#manual-injection)
```

The `[injection]](#manual-injection)` tactic is based on the fact that constructors of inductive data
types are injections.
That means that if `c` is a constructor of an inductive datatype, and if `(c t₁)`
and `(c t₂)` are two terms that are equal then `t₁` and `t₂` are equal too.
If `q` is a proof of a statement of conclusion `t₁ = t₂`, then injection applies
injectivity to derive the equality of all arguments of `t₁` and `t₂` placed in
the same positions. For example, from `(a::b) = (c::d)` we derive `a=c` and `b=d`.
To use this tactic `t₁` and `t₂` should be constructor applications of the same constructor.
Given `h : a::b = c::d`, the tactic `[injection]](#manual-injection) h` adds two new hypothesis with types
`a = c` and `b = d` to the main goal.
The tactic `[injection]](#manual-injection) h [with]](#manual-injection) h₁ h₂` uses the names `h₁` and `h₂` to name the new hypotheses.

tactic

```lean
[injections]](#manual-injections)
```

`[injections]](#manual-injections)` applies `[injection]](#manual-injection)` to all hypotheses recursively
(since `[injection]](#manual-injection)` can produce new hypotheses). Useful for destructing nested
constructor equalities like `(a::b::c) = (d::e::f)`.

tactic

```lean
[left]](#manual-left)
```

Applies the first constructor when
the goal is an inductive type with exactly two constructors, or fails otherwise.

```lean
example : [True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro) ∨ [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False) := by⊢ [True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro) [∨](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)
[left]](#manual-left)⊢ [True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro)
[trivial]](#manual-trivial)All goals completed! 🐙
```

tactic

```lean
[right]](#manual-right)
```

Applies the second constructor when
the goal is an inductive type with exactly two constructors, or fails otherwise.

```lean
example {p q : Prop} (h : q) : p ∨ q := byp:Propq:Proph:q⊢ p [∨](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) q
[right]](#manual-right)p:Propq:Proph:q⊢ q
[exact]](#manual-exact) hAll goals completed! 🐙
```

#### 14.5.15.2. Elimination {#manual-tactic-ref-inductive-elim}

Elimination tactics use [recursors]](#manual-recursors) and the automatically-derived [`casesOn` helper]](#manual-recursor-elaboration-helpers) to implement induction and case splitting.
The [subgoals]](#manual---tech-term-subgoals) that result from these tactics are determined by the types of the minor premises of the eliminators, and using different eliminators with the `using` option results in different subgoals.

**Example: Choosing Eliminators**

When attempting to prove that `∀(i : [Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) (n + 1)), 0 + i = i`, after introducing the hypotheses the tactic `[induction]](#manual-induction) imkn:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)val✝:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)isLt✝:val✝ [<]](#manual-LT___mk) n [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 1⊢ 0 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) [⟨](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk)val✝[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) isLt✝[⟩](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [⟨](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk)val✝[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) isLt✝[⟩](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk)` results in:

mkn:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)val✝:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)isLt✝:val✝ [<]](#manual-LT___mk) n [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 1⊢ 0 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) [⟨](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk)val✝[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) isLt✝[⟩](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [⟨](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk)val✝[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) isLt✝[⟩](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk)

This is because `[Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk)` is a [structure]](#manual---tech-term-Structures) with a single non-recursive constructor.
Its recursor has a single minor premise for this constructor:

```lean
Fin.rec.{u} {n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)} {motive : [Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) n → Sort u}
(mk : (val : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) →
(isLt : val < n) →
motive ⟨val, isLt⟩)
(t : [Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) n) : motive t
```

Using the tactic `[induction]](#manual-induction) i [using]](#manual-induction) [Fin.induction](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___induction)zeron:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ 0 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 0 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0succn:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)i✝:[Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) na✝:0 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) i✝.[castSucc](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___castSucc) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) i✝.[castSucc](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___castSucc)⊢ 0 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) i✝.[succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___succ) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) i✝.[succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___succ)` instead results in:

zeron:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ 0 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 0 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0succn:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)i✝:[Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) na✝:0 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) i✝.[castSucc](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___castSucc) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) i✝.[castSucc](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___castSucc)⊢ 0 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) i✝.[succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___succ) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) i✝.[succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___succ)

`[Fin.induction](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___induction)` is an alternative eliminator that implements induction on the underlying `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`:

```lean
[Fin.induction](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___induction).{u} {n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)}
{motive : [Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) (n + 1) → Sort u}
(zero : motive 0)
(succ : (i : [Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) n) →
motive i.[castSucc](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___castSucc) →
motive i.[succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___succ))
(i : [Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) (n + 1)) : motive i
```

Custom eliminators can be registered using the `induction_eliminator` and `cases_eliminator` attributes.
The eliminator is registered for its explicit targets (i.e. those that are explicit, rather than implicit, parameters to the eliminator function) and will be applied when `[induction]](#manual-induction)` or `[cases]](#manual-cases)` is used on targets of those types.
When present, custom eliminators take precedence over recursors.
Setting `[tactic.customEliminators]](#manual-tactic___customEliminators)` to `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` disables the use of custom eliminators.

attributeCustom Eliminators

The `induction_eliminator` attribute registers an eliminator for use by the `[induction]](#manual-induction)` tactic.

```lean
attr ::= ...
    | induction_eliminator
```

The `cases_eliminator` attribute registers an eliminator for use by the `[cases]](#manual-cases)` tactic.

```lean
attr ::= ...
    | cases_eliminator
```

tactic

```lean
[cases]](#manual-cases)
```

Assuming `x` is a variable in the local context with an inductive type,
`[cases]](#manual-cases) x` splits the main goal, producing one goal for each constructor of the
inductive type, in which the target is replaced by a general instance of that constructor.
If the type of an element in the local context depends on `x`,
that element is reverted and reintroduced afterward,
so that the case split affects that hypothesis as well.
`[cases]](#manual-cases)` detects unreachable cases and closes them automatically.

For example, given `n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` and a goal with a hypothesis `h : P n` and target `Q n`,
`[cases]](#manual-cases) n` produces one goal with hypothesis `h : P 0` and target `Q 0`,
and one goal with hypothesis `h : P (Nat.succ a)` and target `Q (Nat.succ a)`.
Here the name `a` is chosen automatically and is not accessible.
You can use `with` to provide the variables names for each constructor.

- `[cases]](#manual-cases) e`, where `e` is an expression instead of a variable, generalizes `e` in the goal,
  and then cases on the resulting variable.
- Given `as : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α`, `cases as with | nil => tac₁ | cons a as' => tac₂`,
  uses tactic `tac₁` for the `nil` case, and `tac₂` for the `cons` case,
  and `a` and `as'` are used as names for the new variables introduced.
- `[cases]](#manual-cases) h : e`, where `e` is a variable or an expression,
  performs cases on `e` as above, but also adds a hypothesis `h : e = ...` to each goal,
  where `...` is the constructor instance for that particular case.

tactic

```lean
[rcases]](#manual-rcases)
```

`[rcases]](#manual-rcases)` is a tactic that will perform `[cases]](#manual-cases)` recursively, according to a pattern. It is used to
destructure hypotheses or expressions composed of inductive types like `h1 : a ∧ b ∧ c ∨ d` or
`h2 : ∃ x y, trans_rel R x y`. Usual usage might be `[rcases]](#manual-rcases) h1 [with]](#manual-rcases) ⟨ha, hb, hc⟩ | hd` or
`[rcases]](#manual-rcases) h2 [with]](#manual-rcases) ⟨x, y, _ | ⟨z, hxz, hzy⟩⟩` for these examples.

Each element of an `[rcases]](#manual-rcases)` pattern is matched against a particular local hypothesis (most of which
are generated during the execution of `[rcases]](#manual-rcases)` and represent individual elements destructured from
the input expression). An `[rcases]](#manual-rcases)` pattern has the following grammar:

- A name like `x`, which names the active hypothesis as `x`.
- A blank `_`, which does nothing (letting the automatic naming system used by `[cases]](#manual-cases)` name the
  hypothesis).
- A hyphen `-`, which clears the active hypothesis and any dependents.
- The keyword `[rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)`, which expects the hypothesis to be `h : a = b`, and calls `[subst]](#manual-subst)` on the
  hypothesis (which has the effect of replacing `b` with `a` everywhere or vice versa).
- A type ascription `p : ty`, which sets the type of the hypothesis to `ty` and then matches it
  against `p`. (Of course, `ty` must unify with the actual type of `h` for this to work.)
- A tuple pattern `⟨p1, p2, p3⟩`, which matches a constructor with many arguments, or a series
  of nested conjunctions or existentials. For example if the active hypothesis is `a ∧ b ∧ c`,
  then the conjunction will be destructured, and `p1` will be matched against `a`, `p2` against `b`
  and so on.
- A `@` before a tuple pattern as in `@⟨p1, p2, p3⟩` will bind all arguments in the constructor,
  while leaving the `@` off will only use the patterns on the explicit arguments.
- An alternation pattern `p1 | p2 | p3`, which matches an inductive type with multiple constructors,
  or a nested disjunction like `a ∨ b ∨ c`.

A pattern like `⟨a, b, c⟩ | ⟨d, e⟩` will do a split over the inductive datatype,
naming the first three parameters of the first constructor as `a,b,c` and the
first two of the second constructor `d,e`. If the list is not as long as the
number of arguments to the constructor or the number of constructors, the
remaining variables will be automatically named. If there are nested brackets
such as `⟨⟨a⟩, b | c⟩ | d` then these will cause more case splits as necessary.
If there are too many arguments, such as `⟨a, b, c⟩` for splitting on
`∃ x, ∃ y, p x`, then it will be treated as `⟨a, ⟨b, c⟩⟩`, splitting the last
parameter as necessary.

`[rcases]](#manual-rcases)` also has special support for quotient types: quotient induction into Prop works like
matching on the constructor `quot.mk`.

`[rcases]](#manual-rcases) h : e [with]](#manual-rcases) PAT` will do the same as `[rcases]](#manual-rcases) e [with]](#manual-rcases) PAT` with the exception that an
assumption `h : e = PAT` will be added to the context.

tactic

```lean
[fun_cases]](#manual-fun_cases)
```

The `fun_cases` tactic is a convenience wrapper of the `[cases]](#manual-cases)` tactic when using a functional
cases principle.

The tactic invocation

```
fun_cases f x ... y ...`
```

is equivalent to

```
cases y, ... using f.fun_cases_unfolding x ...
```

where the arguments of `f` are used as arguments to `f.fun_cases_unfolding` or targets of the case
analysis, as appropriate.

The form

```lean
fun_cases f
```

(with no arguments to `f`) searches the goal for a unique eligible application of `f`, and uses
these arguments. An application of `f` is eligible if it is saturated and the arguments that will
become targets are free variables.

The form `fun_cases f x y with | case1 => tac₁ | case2 x' ih => tac₂` works like with `[cases]](#manual-cases)`.

Under `set_option tactic.fun_induction.unfolding true` (the default), `[fun_induction]](#manual-fun_induction)` uses the
`f.fun_cases_unfolding` theorem, which will try to automatically unfold the call to `f` in
the goal. With `set_option tactic.fun_induction.unfolding false`, it uses `f.fun_cases` instead.

tactic

```lean
[induction]](#manual-induction)
```

Assuming `x` is a variable in the local context with an inductive type,
`[induction]](#manual-induction) x` applies induction on `x` to the main goal,
producing one goal for each constructor of the inductive type,
in which the target is replaced by a general instance of that constructor
and an inductive hypothesis is added for each recursive argument to the constructor.
If the type of an element in the local context depends on `x`,
that element is reverted and reintroduced afterward,
so that the inductive hypothesis incorporates that hypothesis as well.

For example, given `n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` and a goal with a hypothesis `h : P n` and target `Q n`,
`[induction]](#manual-induction) n` produces one goal with hypothesis `h : P 0` and target `Q 0`,
and one goal with hypotheses `h : P (Nat.succ a)` and `ih₁ : P a → Q a` and target `Q (Nat.succ a)`.
Here the names `a` and `ih₁` are chosen automatically and are not accessible.
You can use `with` to provide the variables names for each constructor.

- `[induction]](#manual-induction) e`, where `e` is an expression instead of a variable,
  generalizes `e` in the goal, and then performs induction on the resulting variable.
- `[induction]](#manual-induction) e [using]](#manual-induction) r` allows the user to specify the principle of induction that should be used.
  Here `r` should be a term whose result type must be of the form `C t`,
  where `C` is a bound variable and `t` is a (possibly empty) sequence of bound variables
- `[induction]](#manual-induction) e [generalizing]](#manual-induction) z₁ ... zₙ`, where `z₁ ... zₙ` are variables in the local context,
  generalizes over `z₁ ... zₙ` before applying the induction but then introduces them in each goal.
  In other words, the net effect is that each inductive hypothesis is generalized.
- Given `x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, `induction x with | zero => tac₁ | succ x' ih => tac₂`
  uses tactic `tac₁` for the `zero` case, and `tac₂` for the `succ` case.

tactic

```lean
[fun_induction]](#manual-fun_induction)
```

The `[fun_induction]](#manual-fun_induction)` tactic is a convenience wrapper around the `[induction]](#manual-induction)` tactic to use the
functional induction principle.

The tactic invocation

```lean
fun_induction f x₁ ... xₙ y₁ ... yₘ
```

where `f` is a function defined by non-mutual structural or well-founded recursion, is equivalent to

```
induction y₁, ... yₘ using f.induct_unfolding x₁ ... xₙ
```

where the arguments of `f` are used as arguments to `f.induct_unfolding` or targets of the
induction, as appropriate.

The form

```lean
fun_induction f
```

(with no arguments to `f`) searches the goal for a unique eligible application of `f`, and uses
these arguments. An application of `f` is eligible if it is saturated and the arguments that will
become targets are free variables.

The forms `[fun_induction]](#manual-fun_induction) f x y [generalizing]](#manual-fun_induction) z₁ ... zₙ` and
`fun_induction f x y with | case1 => tac₁ | case2 x' ih => tac₂` work like with `[induction]](#manual-induction).`

Under `set_option tactic.fun_induction.unfolding true` (the default), `[fun_induction]](#manual-fun_induction)` uses the
`f.induct_unfolding` induction principle, which will try to automatically unfold the call to `f` in
the goal. With `set_option tactic.fun_induction.unfolding false`, it uses `f.induct` instead.

tactic

```lean
[nofun]](#manual-nofun)
```

The tactic `[nofun]](#manual-nofun)` is shorthand for `[exact]](#manual-exact) [nofun]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___nofun)`: it introduces the assumptions, then performs an
empty pattern match, closing the goal if the introduced pattern is impossible.

tactic

```lean
[nomatch]](#manual-nomatch)
```

The tactic `[nomatch]](#manual-nomatch) h` is shorthand for `[exact]](#manual-exact) [nomatch]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___nomatch) h`.

### 14.5.16. Library Search {#manual-tactic-ref-search}

The library search tactics are intended for interactive use.
When run, they search the Lean library for lemmas or rewrite rules that could be applicable in the current situation, and suggests a new tactic.
These tactics should not be left in a proof; rather, their suggestions should be incorporated.

tactic

```lean
[exact?]](#manual-exact___)
```

Searches environment for definitions or theorems that can solve the goal using `[exact]](#manual-exact)`
with conditions resolved by `[solve_by_elim]](#manual-solve_by_elim)`.

The optional `using` clause provides identifiers in the local context that must be
used by `[exact?]](#manual-exact___)` when closing the goal. This is most useful if there are multiple
ways to resolve the goal, and one wants to guide which lemma is used.

Use `+grind` to enable `[grind]](#manual-grind)` as a fallback discharger for subgoals.
Use `+try?` to enable `try?` as a fallback discharger for subgoals.
Use `-star` to disable fallback to star-indexed lemmas (like `[Empty.elim](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Empty-Type/#Empty___elim)`, `[And.left](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro)`).
Use `+all` to collect all successful lemmas instead of stopping at the first.

tactic

```lean
[apply?]](#manual-apply___)
```

Searches environment for definitions or theorems that can refine the goal using `[apply]](#manual-apply)`
with conditions resolved when possible with `[solve_by_elim]](#manual-solve_by_elim)`.

The optional `using` clause provides identifiers in the local context that must be
used when closing the goal.

Use `+grind` to enable `[grind]](#manual-grind)` as a fallback discharger for subgoals.
Use `+try?` to enable `try?` as a fallback discharger for subgoals.
Use `-star` to disable fallback to star-indexed lemmas.
Use `+all` to collect all successful lemmas instead of stopping at the first.

In this proof state:

i:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)j:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)k:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h1:i [<]](#manual-LT___mk) jh2:j [<]](#manual-LT___mk) k⊢ i [<]](#manual-LT___mk) k

invoking `[apply?]](#manual-apply___)All goals completed! 🐙` suggests:

```lean
Try this:
  [apply] exact Nat.lt_trans h1 h2
```

tactic

```lean
[rw?]](#manual-rw___)
```

`[rw?]](#manual-rw___)` tries to find a lemma which can rewrite the goal.

`[rw?]](#manual-rw___)` should not be left in proofs; it is a search tool, like `[apply?]](#manual-apply___)`.

Suggestions are printed as `[rw]](#manual-rw) [h]` or `[rw]](#manual-rw) [← h]`.

You can use `[rw?]](#manual-rw___) [-my_lemma, -my_theorem]` to prevent `[rw?]](#manual-rw___)` using the named lemmas.

### 14.5.17. Case Analysis {#manual-tactic-ref-cases}

tactic

```lean
[split]](#manual-split)
```

The `[split]](#manual-split)` tactic is useful for breaking nested if-then-else and `[match]](#manual-match)` expressions into separate cases.
For a `[match]](#manual-match)` expression with `n` cases, the `[split]](#manual-split)` tactic generates at most `n` subgoals.

For example, given `n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, and a target `[if]](#manual-termIfThenElse) n = 0 [then]](#manual-termIfThenElse) Q [else]](#manual-termIfThenElse) R`, `[split]](#manual-split)` will generate
one goal with hypothesis `n = 0` and target `Q`, and a second goal with hypothesis
`¬n = 0` and target `R`. Note that the introduced hypothesis is unnamed, and is commonly
renamed using the `[case]](#manual-case)` or `[next]](#manual-next)` tactics.

- `[split]](#manual-split)` will split the goal (target).
- `[split]](#manual-split) at h` will split the hypothesis `h`.

tactic

```lean
[by_cases]](#manual-by_cases)
```

`by_cases (h :)? p` splits the main goal into two cases, assuming `h : p` in the first branch, and `h : ¬ p` in the second branch.

### 14.5.18. Decision Procedures {#manual-tactic-ref-decision}

tactic

```lean
[decide]](#manual-decide)
```

`[decide]](#manual-Decidable___decide)` attempts to prove the main goal (with target type `p`) by synthesizing an instance of `[Decidable]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse) p`
and then reducing that instance to evaluate the truth value of `p`.
If it reduces to `[isTrue]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse) h`, then `h` is a proof of `p` that closes the goal.

The target is not allowed to contain local variables or metavariables.
If there are local variables, you can first try using the `[revert]](#manual-revert)` tactic with these local variables to move them into the target,
or you can use the `+revert` option, described below.

Options:

- `[decide]](#manual-decide) +revert` begins by reverting local variables that the target depends on,
  after cleaning up the local context of irrelevant variables.
  A variable is *relevant* if it appears in the target, if it appears in a relevant variable,
  or if it is a proposition that refers to a relevant variable.
- `[decide]](#manual-decide) +kernel` uses kernel for reduction instead of the elaborator.
  It has two key properties: (1) since it uses the kernel, it ignores transparency and can unfold everything,
  and (2) it reduces the `[Decidable]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse)` instance only once instead of twice.
- `[decide]](#manual-decide) +native` uses the native code compiler (`#eval`) to evaluate the `[Decidable]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse)` instance,
  admitting the result via an axiom.
  This can be significantly more efficient than using reduction, but it is at the cost of increasing the size
  of the trusted code base.
  Namely, it depends on the correctness of the Lean compiler and all definitions with an `@[implemented_by]` attribute.
  Like with `+kernel`, the `[Decidable]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse)` instance is evaluated only once.

Limitation: In the default mode or `+kernel` mode, since `[decide]](#manual-Decidable___decide)` uses reduction to evaluate the term,
`[Decidable]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse)` instances defined by well-founded recursion might not work because evaluating them requires reducing proofs.
Reduction can also get stuck on `[Decidable]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse)` instances with `Eq.rec` terms.
These can appear in instances defined using tactics (such as `[rw]](#manual-rw)` and `[simp]](#manual-simp)`).
To avoid this, create such instances using definitions such as `decidable_of_iff` instead.

**Examples**

Proving inequalities:

```lean
example : 2 + 2 ≠ 5 := by⊢ 2 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 2 ≠ 5 [decide]](#manual-decide)All goals completed! 🐙
```

Trying to prove a false proposition:

```
example : 1 ≠ 1 := by decide
/-
tactic 'decide' proved that the proposition
  1 ≠ 1
is false
-/
```

Trying to prove a proposition whose `[Decidable]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse)` instance fails to reduce

```
opaque unknownProp : Prop

open scoped Classical in
example : unknownProp := by decide
/-
tactic 'decide' failed for proposition
  unknownProp
since its 'Decidable' instance reduced to
  Classical.choice ⋯
rather than to the 'isTrue' constructor.
-/
```

**Properties and relations**

For equality goals for types with decidable equality, usually `[rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)` can be used in place of `[decide]](#manual-Decidable___decide)`.

```lean
example : 1 + 1 = 2 := by⊢ 1 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 1 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 2 [decide]](#manual-decide)All goals completed! 🐙
example : 1 + 1 = 2 := by⊢ 1 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 1 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 2 [rfl]](#manual-rfl)All goals completed! 🐙
```

tactic

```lean
[native_decide]](#manual-native_decide)
```

`[native_decide]](#manual-native_decide)` is a synonym for `[decide]](#manual-decide) +native`.
It will attempt to prove a goal of type `p` by synthesizing an instance
of `[Decidable]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse) p` and then evaluating it to `[isTrue]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse) ..`. Unlike `[decide]](#manual-Decidable___decide)`, this
uses `#eval` to evaluate the decidability instance.

This should be used with care because it adds the entire lean compiler to the trusted
part, and a new axiom will show up in `#print axioms` for theorems using
this method or anything that transitively depends on them. Nevertheless, because it is
compiled, this can be significantly more efficient than using `[decide]](#manual-Decidable___decide)`, and for very
large computations this is one way to run external programs and trust the result.

```lean
example : ([List.range](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___range) 1000).[length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length) = 1000 := by⊢ ([List.range](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___range) 1000).[length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 1000 [native_decide]](#manual-native_decide)All goals completed! 🐙
```

tactic

```lean
[omega]](#manual-omega)
```

The `[omega]](#manual-omega)` tactic, for resolving integer and natural linear arithmetic problems.

It is not yet a full decision procedure (no "dark" or "grey" shadows),
but should be effective on many problems.

We handle hypotheses of the form `x = y`, `x < y`, `x ≤ y`, and `k ∣ x` for `x y` in `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` or `[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)`
(and `k` a literal), along with negations of these statements.

We decompose the sides of the inequalities as linear combinations of atoms.

If we encounter `x / k` or `x % k` for literal integers `k` we introduce new auxiliary variables
and the relevant inequalities.

On the first pass, we do not perform case splits on natural subtraction.
If `[omega]](#manual-omega)` fails, we recursively perform a case split on
a natural subtraction appearing in a hypothesis, and try again.

The options

```
omega +splitDisjunctions +splitNatSub +splitNatAbs +splitMinMax
```

can be used to:

- `splitDisjunctions`: split any disjunctions found in the context,
  if the problem is not otherwise solvable.
- `splitNatSub`: for each appearance of `((a - b : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat))`, split on `a ≤ b` if necessary.
- `splitNatAbs`: for each appearance of `[Int.natAbs](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___natAbs) a`, split on `0 ≤ a` if necessary.
- `splitMinMax`: for each occurrence of `[min]](#manual-Min___mk) a b`, split on `[min]](#manual-Min___mk) a b = a ∨ [min]](#manual-Min___mk) a b = b`

Currently, all of these are on by default.

tactic

```lean
[bv_omega]](#manual-bv_omega)
```

`[bv_omega]](#manual-bv_omega)` is `[omega]](#manual-omega)` with an additional preprocessor that turns statements about `[BitVec](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Bitvectors/#BitVec___ofFin)` into statements about `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`.
Currently the preprocessor is implemented as `[try]](#manual-try) [simp]](#manual-simp) [only]](#manual-simp) [bitvec_to_nat] at *`.
`bitvec_to_nat` is a `@[simp]` attribute that you can (cautiously) add to more theorems.

#### 14.5.18.1. SAT Solver Integration {#manual-tactic-ref-sat}

tactic

```lean
[bv_decide]](#manual-bv_decide)
```

Close fixed-width `[BitVec](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Bitvectors/#BitVec___ofFin)` and `[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` goals by obtaining a proof from an external SAT solver and
verifying it inside Lean. The solvable goals are currently limited to

- the Lean equivalent of [`QF_BV`](https://smt-lib.org/logics-all.shtml#QF_BV)
- automatically splitting up `structure`s that contain information about `[BitVec](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Bitvectors/#BitVec___ofFin)` or `[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`

```lean
example : ∀ (a b : [BitVec](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Bitvectors/#BitVec___ofFin) 64), (a &&& b) + (a ^^^ b) = a ||| b := by⊢ ∀ (a b : [BitVec](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Bitvectors/#BitVec___ofFin) 64), [(]](#manual-HAnd___mk)a [&&&]](#manual-HAnd___mk) b[)]](#manual-HAnd___mk) [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) [(]](#manual-HXor___mk)a [^^^]](#manual-HXor___mk) b[)]](#manual-HXor___mk) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) a [|||]](#manual-HOr___mk) b
[intros]](#manual-intros)a✝:[BitVec](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Bitvectors/#BitVec___ofFin) 64b✝:[BitVec](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Bitvectors/#BitVec___ofFin) 64⊢ [(]](#manual-HAnd___mk)a✝ [&&&]](#manual-HAnd___mk) b✝[)]](#manual-HAnd___mk) [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) [(]](#manual-HXor___mk)a✝ [^^^]](#manual-HXor___mk) b✝[)]](#manual-HXor___mk) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) a✝ [|||]](#manual-HOr___mk) b✝
[bv_decide]](#manual-bv_decide)All goals completed! 🐙
```

If `[bv_decide]](#manual-bv_decide)` encounters an unknown definition it will be treated like an unconstrained `[BitVec](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Bitvectors/#BitVec___ofFin)`
variable. Sometimes this enables solving goals despite not understanding the definition because
the precise properties of the definition do not matter in the specific proof.

If `[bv_decide]](#manual-bv_decide)` fails to close a goal it provides a counter-example, containing assignments for all
terms that were considered as variables.

In order to avoid calling a SAT solver every time, the proof can be cached with `[bv_decide?]](#manual-bv_decide___)`.

If solving your problem relies inherently on using associativity or commutativity, consider enabling
the `bv.ac_nf` option.

`bv_decide types [T₁, ..., Tₙ]` restricts the analysis of structures and enum inductives to
`T₁, ..., Tₙ`, treating all other ones as opaque variables.

Note: `[bv_decide]](#manual-bv_decide)` trusts the correctness of the code generator and adds a axioms asserting its result.

Note: include `import Std.Tactic.BVDecide`

tactic

```lean
[bv_normalize]](#manual-bv_normalize)
```

Run the normalization procedure of `[bv_decide]](#manual-bv_decide)` only. Sometimes this is enough to solve basic
`[BitVec](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Bitvectors/#BitVec___ofFin)` goals already.

Note: include `import Std.Tactic.BVDecide`

tactic

```lean
[bv_check]](#manual-bv_check)
```

This tactic works just like `[bv_decide]](#manual-bv_decide)` but skips calling a SAT solver by using a proof that is
already stored on disk. It is called with the name of an LRAT file in the same directory as the
current Lean file:

```lean
bv_check "proof.lrat"
```

tactic

```lean
[bv_decide?]](#manual-bv_decide___)
```

Suggest a proof script for a `[bv_decide]](#manual-bv_decide)` tactic call. Useful for caching LRAT proofs.

Note: include `import Std.Tactic.BVDecide`

### 14.5.19. Call-by-Value Evaluation {#manual-tactic-ref-cbv}

The `[cbv]](#manual-cbv)` tactic simulates call-by-value evaluation to reduce terms.
In call-by-value evaluation, the arguments to a function are reduced to values before the function call is reduced.
Roughly speaking, *values* are either functions or applications of constructors to values; the body of a function does not need to be a value for the function itself to count as a value.
This evaluation strategy matches the execution order of code produced by the Lean compiler, which makes it a good match for code that is written to perform well at run time.

`[cbv]](#manual-cbv)` unfolds definitions using their [equational lemmas]](#manual---tech-term-equational-lemmas) and applies similar theorems that are automatically proved for [matcher functions]](#manual---tech-term-matcher-functions), producing propositional equality proofs at each step.
Because the unfolding is propositional rather than definitional, `[cbv]](#manual-cbv)` can reduce functions defined via [well-founded recursion]](#manual-well-founded-recursion) or [partial fixpoints]](#manual-partial-fixpoint).
In general, these functions are not definitionally equal to their unfoldings, so the kernel's definitional reduction does not reduce their recursive calls.

The proofs produced by `[cbv]](#manual-cbv)` only use the three standard axioms (`[propext]](#manual-propext)`, `[Quot.sound]](#manual-Quot___sound)`, and `Classical.choice`).
In particular, they do not require trust in the correctness of the code generator, unlike `[native_decide]](#manual-native_decide)`.

Because `[cbv]](#manual-cbv)` rewrites subterms via `[congrArg](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#congrArg)` and `[congrFun](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#congrFun)`, it cannot rewrite subterms that appear in dependent positions.
Rewriting the argument of a dependent function would change the type of subsequent arguments, and even with heterogeneous equality there are no suitable congruence lemmas for arbitrary dependent functions.

When reducing constant applications, `[cbv]](#manual-cbv)` tries the following strategies in order:

1. Custom `cbv_eval` rewrite rules
2. [Equational lemmas]](#manual---tech-term-equational-lemmas) (e.g., `foo.eq_1`, `foo.eq_2`)
3. Unfolding equations
4. Kernel matcher reduction

Declarations marked with `cbv_opaque` are never unfolded unless a matching `cbv_eval` rewrite rule is provided.

syntaxCall-by-Value Evaluation

```lean
tactic ::= ...
    | cbv (at (term | locationType)*)?
```

tactic

```lean
[cbv]](#manual-cbv)
```

`[cbv]](#manual-cbv)` performs simplification that closely mimics call-by-value evaluation.
It reduces terms by unfolding definitions using their defining equations and
applying matcher equations. The unfolding is propositional, so `[cbv]](#manual-cbv)` also works
with functions defined via well-founded recursion or partial fixpoints.

`[cbv]](#manual-cbv)` reduces the goal type (and optionally hypothesis types) using call-by-value
evaluation. For equation goals (`lhs = rhs`), `[cbv]](#manual-cbv)` automatically attempts `refl`
after reduction to close the goal.

`[cbv]](#manual-cbv)` supports the standard `at` location syntax:

- `[cbv]](#manual-cbv)` — reduce the goal target
- `[cbv]](#manual-cbv) at h` — reduce hypothesis `h`
- `[cbv]](#manual-cbv) at h |-` — reduce hypothesis `h` and the goal target
- `[cbv]](#manual-cbv) at *` — reduce the goal target and all non-dependent propositional hypotheses

If a hypothesis reduces to `[False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)`, the goal is closed immediately.

`[cbv]](#manual-cbv)` is not a finishing tactic in general: it may leave a new (simpler) goal.

The proofs produced by `[cbv]](#manual-cbv)` only use the three standard axioms.
In particular, they do not require trust in the correctness of the code
generator.

**Example: Reducing Well-Founded Recursive Functions**

The function `[countdown]](#manual-countdown-_LPAR_in-Reducing-Well-Founded-Recursive-Functions_RPAR_)` is defined using well-founded recursion, so it is not definitionally equal to its unfolding.
Ordinary `[rfl]](#manual-rfl)` cannot close the goal:

```lean
def countdown (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[match]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match) n [with]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| 0 => [0]
| n + 1 => (n + 1) :: [countdown]](#manual-countdown-_LPAR_in-Reducing-Well-Founded-Recursive-Functions_RPAR_) n
termination_by n
```

```lean
example : [countdown]](#manual-countdown-_LPAR_in-Reducing-Well-Founded-Recursive-Functions_RPAR_) 3 = [3, 2, 1, 0] := by⊢ [countdown]](#manual-countdown-_LPAR_in-Reducing-Well-Founded-Recursive-Functions_RPAR_) 3 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)3[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 2[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 1[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 0[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [rfl]](#manual-rfl)⊢ [countdown]](#manual-countdown-_LPAR_in-Reducing-Well-Founded-Recursive-Functions_RPAR_) 3 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)3[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 2[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 1[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 0[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
```

```lean
Tactic `rfl` failed: The left-hand side
  [countdown]](#manual-countdown-_LPAR_in-Reducing-Well-Founded-Recursive-Functions_RPAR_) 3
is not definitionally equal to the right-hand side
  [[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)3[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 2[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 1[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 0[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)

⊢ [countdown]](#manual-countdown-_LPAR_in-Reducing-Well-Founded-Recursive-Functions_RPAR_) 3 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)3[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 2[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 1[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 0[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
```

The `[cbv]](#manual-cbv)` tactic can reduce `[countdown]](#manual-countdown-_LPAR_in-Reducing-Well-Founded-Recursive-Functions_RPAR_) 3` via propositional rewriting and then close the equation goal via `[rfl]](#manual-rfl)`:

```lean
example : [countdown]](#manual-countdown-_LPAR_in-Reducing-Well-Founded-Recursive-Functions_RPAR_) 3 = [3, 2, 1, 0] := by⊢ [countdown]](#manual-countdown-_LPAR_in-Reducing-Well-Founded-Recursive-Functions_RPAR_) 3 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)3[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 2[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 1[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 0[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
[cbv]](#manual-cbv)All goals completed! 🐙
```

**Example: Reducing Hypotheses**

The `[cbv]](#manual-cbv)` tactic supports the standard `at` location syntax.
When used with `at h`, it reduces the type of hypothesis `h`.
When used with `at *`, it reduces all non-dependent propositional
hypotheses and the goal target.

```lean
def countdown (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[match]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match) n [with]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| 0 => [0]
| n + 1 => (n + 1) :: [countdown]](#manual-countdown-_LPAR_in-Reducing-Hypotheses_RPAR_) n
termination_by n
```

**Example: cbv as a Non-Finishing Tactic**

Unlike `[decide]](#manual-decide)`, `[cbv]](#manual-cbv)` is not a terminal tactic.
It simplifies the goal as much as possible but may leave a goal that requires further reasoning.
Here, `[cbv]](#manual-cbv)` reduces the call to `[countdown]](#manual-countdown-_LPAR_in-cbv--as-a-Non-Finishing-Tactic_RPAR_)` but leaves the membership goal:

```lean
def countdown (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[match]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match) n [with]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| 0 => [0]
| n + 1 => (n + 1) :: [countdown]](#manual-countdown-_LPAR_in-cbv--as-a-Non-Finishing-Tactic_RPAR_) n
termination_by n
```

```lean
example : 1 ∈ [countdown]](#manual-countdown-_LPAR_in-cbv--as-a-Non-Finishing-Tactic_RPAR_) 2 := by⊢ 1 ∈ [countdown]](#manual-countdown-_LPAR_in-cbv--as-a-Non-Finishing-Tactic_RPAR_) 2
[cbv]](#manual-cbv)⊢ [List.Mem](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___Mem___head) 1 [[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)2[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 1[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 0[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
```

**Example: Dependent Positions**

The function `[wfLength]](#manual-wfLength-_LPAR_in-Dependent-Positions_RPAR_)` is a version of `[List.length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length)` that is defined via [well-founded recursion]](#manual---tech-term-well-founded-recursion) instead of [structural recursion]](#manual-structural-recursion).
As a result, it is [irreducible]](#manual---tech-term-Irreducible):

```lean
def wfLength : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| [] => 0
| _ :: xs => [wfLength]](#manual-wfLength-_LPAR_in-Dependent-Positions_RPAR_) xs + 1
termination_by xs => xs
```

In a non-dependent `[Std.TreeMap](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Maps-and-Sets/#Std___TreeMap)`, `[cbv]](#manual-cbv)` can reduce the computed key `[wfLength]](#manual-wfLength-_LPAR_in-Dependent-Positions_RPAR_) [1, 2]`:

```lean

[.empty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Maps-and-Sets/#Std___TreeMap___empty) |>.[insert](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Maps-and-Sets/#Std___TreeMap___insert) ([wfLength]](#manual-wfLength-_LPAR_in-Dependent-Positions_RPAR_) [1, 2]) 42
example : [myTreeMap]](#manual-myTreeMap-_LPAR_in-Dependent-Positions_RPAR_).[toList](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Maps-and-Sets/#Std___TreeMap___toList) = [⟨2, 42⟩] := by⊢ [myTreeMap]](#manual-myTreeMap-_LPAR_in-Dependent-Positions_RPAR_).[toList](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Maps-and-Sets/#Std___TreeMap___toList) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)[(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)2[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) 42[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
[cbv]](#manual-cbv)All goals completed! 🐙
```
