#### 14.5.19.1. `[decide_cbv]](#manual-decide_cbv)` {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Tactic-Proofs--Tactic-Reference--Call-by-Value-Evaluation--decide_cbv}

tactic

```lean
[decide_cbv]](#manual-decide_cbv)
```

`[decide_cbv]](#manual-decide_cbv)` is a finishing tactic that closes goals of the form `p`, where `p`
is a `[Decidable]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse)` proposition. It proceeds in two steps:

1. Apply `of_decide_eq_true` to transform the goal into `[decide]](#manual-Decidable___decide) p = [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`.
2. Reduce `[decide]](#manual-Decidable___decide) p` via call-by-value normalization. If the result is
   definitionally equal to `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`, the goal is closed.

`[decide_cbv]](#manual-decide_cbv)` fails with an error if `[decide]](#manual-Decidable___decide) p` does not reduce to `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`.
Unlike `[cbv]](#manual-cbv)`, `[decide_cbv]](#manual-decide_cbv)` is a terminal tactic: it either closes the goal or
fails.

The proofs produced by `[decide_cbv]](#manual-decide_cbv)` only use the three standard axioms.
In particular, they do not require trust in the correctness of the code
generator.

**Example: decide\_cbv**

The `[decide_cbv]](#manual-decide_cbv)` tactic closes goals that are decidable propositions by reducing the `[Decidable]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse)` instance via [call-by-value evaluation]](#manual---tech-term-call-by-value-evaluation):

```lean
example : 2 + 3 = 5 ∧ 10 < 20 := by⊢ 2 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 3 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 5 [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) 10 [<]](#manual-LT___mk) 20
[decide_cbv]](#manual-decide_cbv)All goals completed! 🐙
```

Unlike `[native_decide]](#manual-native_decide)`, `[decide_cbv]](#manual-decide_cbv)` does not require trust in the code generator.
Unlike `[decide]](#manual-decide)`, which uses definitional reduction, `[decide_cbv]](#manual-decide_cbv)` can handle functions defined by [well-founded recursion]](#manual-well-founded-recursion):

```lean
def isAllPositive : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| [] => [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| x :: xs => x > 0 && [isAllPositive]](#manual-isAllPositive-_LPAR_in-decide_cbv_RPAR_) xs
termination_by xs => xs
example : [isAllPositive]](#manual-isAllPositive-_LPAR_in-decide_cbv_RPAR_) [1, 2, 3] = [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) := by⊢ [isAllPositive]](#manual-isAllPositive-_LPAR_in-decide_cbv_RPAR_) [[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)1[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 2[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 3[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
[decide_cbv]](#manual-decide_cbv)All goals completed! 🐙
```

**Example: Prime Power Testing with decide\_cbv**

Because `[decide_cbv]](#manual-decide_cbv)` uses propositional unfolding, it can evaluate complex decision procedures involving [well-founded recursive]](#manual-well-founded-recursion) functions.
Here, `[Nat.minFac]](#manual-Nat___minFac-_LPAR_in-Prime-Power-Testing-with--decide_cbv_RPAR_)` finds the smallest divisor of a number, while the helper `[minFacAux]](#manual-minFacAux-_LPAR_in-Prime-Power-Testing-with--decide_cbv_RPAR_)` searches for the smallest odd divisor:

```lean
def minFacAux (n k : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[if]](#manual-termDepIfThenElse) h : n < k * k [then]](#manual-termDepIfThenElse) n
[else]](#manual-termDepIfThenElse)
[if]](#manual-termDepIfThenElse) h' : k ∣ n [then]](#manual-termDepIfThenElse) k
[else]](#manual-termDepIfThenElse)
have : k ≤ n := byn:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)k:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h:[¬](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)n [<]](#manual-LT___mk) k [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) kh':[¬](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)k [∣]](#manual-Dvd___mk) n⊢ k [≤]](#manual-LE___mk) n
[have]](#manual-have) := Nat.le_mul_self kn:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)k:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h:[¬](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)n [<]](#manual-LT___mk) k [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) kh':[¬](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)k [∣]](#manual-Dvd___mk) nthis:k [≤]](#manual-LE___mk) k [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) k⊢ k [≤]](#manual-LE___mk) n; [grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
[minFacAux]](#manual-minFacAux-_LPAR_in-Prime-Power-Testing-with--decide_cbv_RPAR_) n (k + 2)
termination_by n + 2 - k
def Nat.minFac (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[if]](#manual-termIfThenElse) 2 ∣ n [then]](#manual-termIfThenElse) 2 [else]](#manual-termIfThenElse) [minFacAux]](#manual-minFacAux-_LPAR_in-Prime-Power-Testing-with--decide_cbv_RPAR_) n 3
```

`[Nat.log]](#manual-Nat___log-_LPAR_in-Prime-Power-Testing-with--decide_cbv_RPAR_) b n` computes the floor of the base-`b` logarithm of `n` by repeated squaring:

```lean
def Nat.log (b n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[if]](#manual-termIfThenElse) b ≤ 1 [then]](#manual-termIfThenElse) 0 [else]](#manual-termIfThenElse) ([go]](#manual-Nat___log___go-_LPAR_in-Prime-Power-Testing-with--decide_cbv_RPAR_) b n).[2](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) where
go : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) × [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| _, 0 => (n, 0)
| b, fuel + 1 =>
[if]](#manual-termIfThenElse) n < b [then]](#manual-termIfThenElse) (n, 0)
[else]](#manual-termIfThenElse)
let (q, e) := [go]](#manual-Nat___log___go-_LPAR_in-Prime-Power-Testing-with--decide_cbv_RPAR_) (b * b) fuel
[if]](#manual-termIfThenElse) q < b [then]](#manual-termIfThenElse)
(q, 2 * e)
[else]](#manual-termIfThenElse)
(q / b, 2 * e + 1)
```

#### 14.5.19.2. Controlling `[cbv]](#manual-cbv)` Behavior {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Tactic-Proofs--Tactic-Reference--Call-by-Value-Evaluation--Controlling--cbv--Behavior}

attributeCustom `cbv` Rewrite Rules

The `cbv_eval` attribute registers a theorem as a custom rewrite rule that `[cbv]](#manual-cbv)` applies before trying [equational lemmas]](#manual---tech-term-equational-lemmas).
The theorem must be an unconditional equality; one side (generally the left-hand side) must be an application of a constant.

```lean
attr ::= ...
    | cbv_eval
```

The `←` modifier instructs `[cbv]](#manual-cbv)` to apply the rule from right to left:

```lean
attr ::= ...
    | cbv_eval ←
```

**Example: cbv\_eval**

Custom rewrite rules can be used to control how `[cbv]](#manual-cbv)` evaluates specific functions.
For instance, the naïve definition of reversal, `[slowReverse]](#manual-slowReverse-_LPAR_in-cbv_eval_RPAR_)`, has quadratic complexity due to repeated use of `[List.append](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___append)`.
By providing a tail-recursive characterization via `[fastReverse]](#manual-fastReverse-_LPAR_in-cbv_eval_RPAR_)`, `[cbv]](#manual-cbv)` can evaluate `[slowReverse]](#manual-slowReverse-_LPAR_in-cbv_eval_RPAR_)` efficiently:

```lean

| [] => []
| x :: xs => [slowReverse]](#manual-slowReverse-_LPAR_in-cbv_eval_RPAR_) xs ++ [x]
def fastReverse (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[go]](#manual-fastReverse___go-_LPAR_in-cbv_eval_RPAR_) [] xs
```

attributeOpaque Declarations for `cbv`

The `cbv_opaque` attribute prevents `[cbv]](#manual-cbv)` from unfolding a declaration using its [equational lemmas]](#manual---tech-term-equational-lemmas) or unfold theorems.
However, `cbv_eval` rewrite rules always take priority over `cbv_opaque`: if a matching `cbv_eval` rule exists for a declaration, it will be applied even if the declaration is marked `cbv_opaque`.
This allows replacing the default unfolding behavior with a controlled set of evaluation rules.

```lean
attr ::= ...
    | cbv_opaque
```

**Example: Opaque Definitions with @[cbv\_opaque]**

Marking `[countdown]](#manual-countdown-_LPAR_in-Opaque-Definitions-with--____LSQ_cbv_opaque_RSQ__RPAR_)` as `cbv_opaque` prevents `[cbv]](#manual-cbv)` from unfolding it, so the goal that was previously closed by `[cbv]](#manual-cbv)` now remains unsolved:

```lean
def countdown (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[match]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match) n [with]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| 0 => [0]
| n + 1 => (n + 1) :: [countdown]](#manual-countdown-_LPAR_in-Opaque-Definitions-with--____LSQ_cbv_opaque_RSQ__RPAR_) n
termination_by n
```

```lean
[attribute]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___attribute) [cbv_opaque] [countdown]](#manual-countdown-_LPAR_in-Opaque-Definitions-with--____LSQ_cbv_opaque_RSQ__RPAR_)
```

```lean
example : [countdown]](#manual-countdown-_LPAR_in-Opaque-Definitions-with--____LSQ_cbv_opaque_RSQ__RPAR_) 3 = [3, 2, 1, 0] := by⊢ [countdown]](#manual-countdown-_LPAR_in-Opaque-Definitions-with--____LSQ_cbv_opaque_RSQ__RPAR_) 3 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)3[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 2[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 1[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 0[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
[cbv]](#manual-cbv)⊢ [countdown]](#manual-countdown-_LPAR_in-Opaque-Definitions-with--____LSQ_cbv_opaque_RSQ__RPAR_) 3 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)3[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 2[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 1[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 0[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
```

##### 14.5.19.2.1. Custom Simplification Procedures {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Tactic-Proofs--Tactic-Reference--Call-by-Value-Evaluation--Controlling--cbv--Behavior--Custom-Simplification-Procedures}

A cbv simplification procedure (`[cbv]](#manual-cbv)` simproc) is a user-defined metaprogram that `[cbv]](#manual-cbv)` invokes on subexpressions matching a given pattern.
While `cbv_eval` rules are limited to static equality, `[cbv]](#manual-cbv)` simprocs can perform arbitrary computation to decide how to rewrite a subexpression.
Common use cases include defining procedures for evaluating functions on literal values or short-circuiting control flow.

The simprocs used by `[cbv]](#manual-cbv)` have type `Lean.Meta.Sym.Simp.Simproc`, which is distinct from the `Lean.Meta.Simp.Simproc` type used by the `[simp]](#manual-simp)` tactic.
The two systems are independent: registering a `[cbv]](#manual-cbv)` simproc has no effect on `[simp]](#manual-simp)`, and vice versa.

syntaxCustom `cbv` Simplification Procedures

The body must have type `Simproc` (that is, `Expr → SimpM Result`).
The pattern is an expression with holes (`_`) that determines which subexpressions trigger the procedure.
Patterns are matched agains subexpressions structurally after unfolding reducible definitions and applying [β]](#manual---tech-term-___)-, [η]](#manual---tech-term-___-equivalence)-, and [ζ]](#manual---tech-term-___-next-next-next)-reduction to both sides.
Matching is modulo α-equivalence (bound variable names are ignored), and proof and instance arguments in the pattern are treated as wildcards.
An optional phase specifier controls when the procedure fires during normalization.
When no phase is specified, the default is `↑` (post).

`↓` (pre)
:   Fires on each subexpression *before* `[cbv]](#manual-cbv)` reduces it. The arguments are still unreduced. Use this phase to override `[cbv]](#manual-cbv)`'s default call-by-value evaluation order. A typical use case would be to evaluate arguments lazily or to short-circuit evaluation (as the built-in `ite` and `[Or](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl)` procedures do).

`cbv_eval` (eval)
:   Fires *after* arguments have been reduced to values, but *before* the function is unfolded. Use this phase to provide efficient ground evaluation procedures.

`↑` (post, default)
:   Fires *after* `[cbv]](#manual-cbv)` has attempted standard reduction (equation lemmas, unfolding, kernel matching). Use this phase when standard reduction should be tried first.

```lean
command ::= ...
    | cbv_simproc name (pattern) := body
```

An optional phase specifier can be placed before the name:

```lean
command ::= ...
    | cbv_simproc ↓ name (pattern) := body
```

```lean
command ::= ...
    | cbv_simproc cbv_eval name (pattern) := body
```

The `cbv_simproc_decl` variant declares the procedure without activating it.
It can be activated later with `cbv_simproc`.

```lean
command ::= ...
    | cbv_simproc_decl name (pattern) := body
```

attributeSimplification Procedure Attribute for `cbv`

The `cbv_simproc` attribute activates a previously declared simplification procedure (defined with `cbv_simproc_decl`) for use by `[cbv]](#manual-cbv)`.
An optional phase specifier controls when the procedure fires during normalization.

```lean
attr ::= ...
    | cbv_simproc
```

Phase specifiers control when the procedure fires:

```lean
attr ::= ...
    | cbv_simproc ↓
```

```lean
attr ::= ...
    | cbv_simproc ↑
```

```lean
attr ::= ...
    | cbv_simproc cbv_eval
```

**Example: Declaring a cbv\_simproc**

A simplification procedure is declared by providing a pattern and a body of type `Lean.Meta.Sym.Simp.Simproc`.
The pattern is an expression with holes (`_`) that determines which subexpressions trigger the procedure.
Here, the pattern is (`myConst _`), which matches any application of `[myConst]](#manual-myConst-_LPAR_in-Declaring-a--cbv_simproc_RPAR_)`.
The procedure (`fun _e => [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do) return .rfl`) ignores the expression, returning a result that indicates that no rewriting is to be performed.

```lean
opaque myConst : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
[open]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___open) Lean Meta Sym.Simp [in]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___in)
cbv_simproc evalMyConst ([myConst]](#manual-myConst-_LPAR_in-Declaring-a--cbv_simproc_RPAR_) _) := fun _e => [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
-- A real simproc would inspect `e`, compute a result,
-- and return `.step result proof`.
return .rfl
```

The [`cbv_simproc_decl`]](#manual-Lean___Parser____FLQQ_command_Cbv_simproc_decl__LPAR___RPAR_________FLQQ_) variant declares the procedure without activating it.
The `cbv_simproc` attribute can be used to activate it later, optionally at a specific phase:

```lean
[open]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___open) Lean Meta Sym.Simp [in]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___in)
[cbv_simproc_decl]](#manual-Lean___Parser____FLQQ_command_Cbv_simproc_decl__LPAR___RPAR_________FLQQ_) evalMyConst2 ([myConst]](#manual-myConst-_LPAR_in-Declaring-a--cbv_simproc_RPAR_) _) := fun _e =>
return .rfl
[attribute]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___attribute) [cbv_simproc cbv_eval] [evalMyConst2]](#manual-evalMyConst2-_LPAR_in-Declaring-a--cbv_simproc_RPAR_)
```

**Example: Lazy evaluation of a head of the list**

This is an example of a pre-phase simplification procedure that breaks the conventional call-by-value order of evaluation to achieve laziness.
The `↓` modifier ensures that `[evalListHead]](#manual-evalListHead-_LPAR_in-Lazy-evaluation-of-a-head-of-the-list_RPAR_)` fires before the arguments to `[List.head?](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___head___)` are evaluated.
It rewrites `[List.head?](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___head___) (a :: as)` to `[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) a` using `List.head?_cons`, discarding the tail `as` without evaluating it.
Only the head element `a` is subsequently reduced by `[cbv]](#manual-cbv)`.

```lean
cbv_simproc ↓ evalListHead ([List.head?](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___head___) _) := fun e => [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let_expr [List.head?](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___head___) α listExpr := e | return .rfl
let_expr [List.cons](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) _ a as := listExpr | return .rfl
let Level.succ u ← Sym.getLevel α | return .rfl
let result ← Sym.share <| mkApp2 (mkConst ``[Option.some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [u]) α a
let proof := mkApp3 (mkConst ``List.head?_cons [u]) α a as
return .step result proof
theorem cbv_simproc_test : [5 + 5,6].[head?](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___head___) = [.some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) 10 := by⊢ [[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)5 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 5[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 6[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil).[head?](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___head___) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) 10 [cbv]](#manual-cbv)All goals completed! 🐙
```

Inspecting the proof term confirms that the simplification procedure fired: `List.head?_cons` appears directly in the proof, showing that `[cbv]](#manual-cbv)` used the simproc's rewrite rather than reducing `[List.head?](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___head___)` by unfolding its definition.

```lean
theorem cbv_simproc_test : [[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)5 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 5[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 6[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil).[head?](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___head___) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) 10 :=
of_eq_true
  ([Eq.trans](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___trans) (congrFun' ([congrArg](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#congrArg) [Eq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) ([Eq.trans](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___trans) List.head?_cons ([congrArg](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#congrArg) [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) ([Eq.refl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 10)))) ([some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) 10))
    (eq_self ([some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) 10)))
```

Lean includes a number of built-in simplification procedures for `[cbv]](#manual-cbv)`.
These handle control flow (`ite`, `dite`, `cond`, `Decidable.decide`, `Decidable.rec`), logical connectives (`Or`, `And`), and data structure operations (array indexing, string operations).
The control flow procedures use the `↓` (pre) phase to enable short-circuit evaluation, while the array and string procedures use the `cbv_eval` phase to reduce ground applications directly.

#### 14.5.19.3. Options {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Tactic-Proofs--Tactic-Reference--Call-by-Value-Evaluation--Options}

option

```lean
cbv.maxSteps
```

Default value: `100000`

Controls the maximum number of steps for the `[cbv]](#manual-cbv)` tactic.

option

```lean
cbv.warning
```

Default value: `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`

When enabled, displays a warning that the `[cbv]](#manual-cbv)` tactic is being used.

### 14.5.20. Controlling Reduction {#manual-tactic-reducibility}

tactic

```lean
with_reducible
```

`with_reducible tacs` executes `tacs` using the reducible transparency setting.
In this setting only definitions tagged as `[reducible]` are unfolded.

tactic

```lean
with_reducible_and_instances
```

`with_reducible_and_instances tacs` executes `tacs` using the `.instances` transparency setting.
In this setting only definitions tagged as `[reducible]` or type class instances are unfolded.

tactic

```lean
with_unfolding_all
```

`with_unfolding_all tacs` executes `tacs` using the `.all` transparency setting.
In this setting all definitions that are not opaque are unfolded.

tactic

```lean
[with_unfolding_none]](#manual-with_unfolding_none)
```

`with_unfolding_none tacs` executes `tacs` using the `.none` transparency setting.
In this setting no definitions are unfolded.

### 14.5.21. Control Flow {#manual-tactic-ref-control}

tactic

```lean
[skip]](#manual-skip)
```

`[skip]](#manual-skip)` does nothing.

tactic

```lean
[guard_hyp]](#manual-guard_hyp)
```

Tactic to check that a named hypothesis has a given type and/or value.

- `[guard_hyp]](#manual-guard_hyp) h : t` checks the type up to reducible defeq,
- `[guard_hyp]](#manual-guard_hyp) h :~ t` checks the type up to default defeq,
- `[guard_hyp]](#manual-guard_hyp) h :ₛ t` checks the type up to syntactic equality,
- `[guard_hyp]](#manual-guard_hyp) h :ₐ t` checks the type up to alpha equality.
- `[guard_hyp]](#manual-guard_hyp) h := v` checks value up to reducible defeq,
- `[guard_hyp]](#manual-guard_hyp) h :=~ v` checks value up to default defeq,
- `[guard_hyp]](#manual-guard_hyp) h :=ₛ v` checks value up to syntactic equality,
- `[guard_hyp]](#manual-guard_hyp) h :=ₐ v` checks the value up to alpha equality.

The value `v` is elaborated using the type of `h` as the expected type.

tactic

```lean
[guard_target]](#manual-guard_target)
```

Tactic to check that the target agrees with a given expression.

- `[guard_target]](#manual-guard_target) = e` checks that the target is defeq at reducible transparency to `e`.
- `[guard_target]](#manual-guard_target) =~ e` checks that the target is defeq at default transparency to `e`.
- `[guard_target]](#manual-guard_target) =ₛ e` checks that the target is syntactically equal to `e`.
- `[guard_target]](#manual-guard_target) =ₐ e` checks that the target is alpha-equivalent to `e`.

The term `e` is elaborated with the type of the goal as the expected type, which is mostly
useful within `conv` mode.

tactic

```lean
[guard_expr]](#manual-guard_expr)
```

Tactic to check equality of two expressions.

- `[guard_expr]](#manual-guard_expr) e = e'` checks that `e` and `e'` are defeq at reducible transparency.
- `[guard_expr]](#manual-guard_expr) e =~ e'` checks that `e` and `e'` are defeq at default transparency.
- `[guard_expr]](#manual-guard_expr) e =ₛ e'` checks that `e` and `e'` are syntactically equal.
- `[guard_expr]](#manual-guard_expr) e =ₐ e'` checks that `e` and `e'` are alpha-equivalent.

Both `e` and `e'` are elaborated then have their metavariables instantiated before the equality
check. Their types are unified (using `isDefEqGuarded`) before synthetic metavariables are
processed, which helps with default instance handling.

tactic

```lean
[done]](#manual-done)
```

`[done]](#manual-done)` succeeds iff there are no remaining goals.

tactic

```lean
[sleep]](#manual-sleep)
```

The tactic `sleep ms` sleeps for `ms` milliseconds and does nothing.
It is used for debugging purposes only.

tactic

```lean
[stop]](#manual-stop)
```

`[stop]](#manual-stop)` is a helper tactic for "discarding" the rest of a proof:
it is defined as `[repeat]](#manual-repeat) [sorry]](#manual-sorry)`.
It is useful when working on the middle of a complex proofs,
and less messy than commenting the remainder of the proof.

### 14.5.22. Term Elaboration Backends {#manual-tactic-ref-term-helpers}

These tactics are used during elaboration of terms to satisfy obligations that arise.

tactic

```lean
[decreasing_with]](#manual-decreasing_with)
```

Constructs a proof of decreasing along a well founded relation, by simplifying, then applying
lexicographic order lemmas and finally using `ts` to solve the base case. If it fails,
it prints a message to help the user diagnose an ill-founded recursive definition.

tactic

```lean
[get_elem_tactic]](#manual-get_elem_tactic)
```

`[get_elem_tactic]](#manual-get_elem_tactic)` is the tactic automatically called by the notation `arr[i]`
to prove any side conditions that arise when constructing the term
(e.g. the index is in bounds of the array). It just delegates to
`get_elem_tactic_extensible` and gives a diagnostic error message otherwise;
users are encouraged to extend `get_elem_tactic_extensible` instead of this tactic.

tactic

```lean
[get_elem_tactic_trivial]](#manual-get_elem_tactic_trivial)
```

`[get_elem_tactic_trivial]](#manual-get_elem_tactic_trivial)` has been deprecated in favour of `get_elem_tactic_extensible`.

### 14.5.23. Debugging Utilities {#manual-tactic-ref-debug}

tactic

```lean
[sorry]](#manual-sorry)
```

The `[sorry]](#manual-sorry)` tactic is a temporary placeholder for an incomplete tactic proof,
closing the main goal using `[exact]](#manual-exact) sorry`.

This is intended for stubbing-out incomplete parts of a proof while still having a syntactically correct proof skeleton.
Lean will give a warning whenever a proof uses `[sorry]](#manual-sorry)`, so you aren't likely to miss it,
but you can double check if a theorem depends on `[sorry]](#manual-sorry)` by looking for `sorryAx` in the output
of the `#print axioms my_thm` command, the axiom used by the implementation of `[sorry]](#manual-sorry)`.

tactic

```lean
[admit]](#manual-admit)
```

`[admit]](#manual-admit)` is a synonym for `[sorry]](#manual-sorry)`.

tactic

```lean
[dbg_trace]](#manual-dbg_trace)
```

`[dbg_trace]](#manual-dbg_trace) "foo"` prints `foo` when elaborated.
Useful for debugging tactic control flow:

```lean
example : [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False) ∨ [True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro) := by⊢ [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False) [∨](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) [True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro)
[first]](#manual-first)
| [apply]](#manual-apply) [Or.inl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl)⊢ [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False); [trivial]](#manual-trivial)⊢ [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False); [dbg_trace]](#manual-dbg_trace) "left"
| [apply]](#manual-apply) [Or.inr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl)⊢ [True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro); [trivial]](#manual-trivial)All goals completed! 🐙; [dbg_trace]](#manual-dbg_trace) "right"
```

tactic

```lean
[trace_state]](#manual-trace_state)
```

`[trace_state]](#manual-trace_state)` displays the current state in the info view.

tactic

```lean
[trace]](#manual-trace)
```

`trace msg` displays `msg` in the info view.

### 14.5.24. Suggestions {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Tactic-Proofs--Tactic-Reference--Suggestions}

tactic

```lean
[∎]](#manual-___-next)
```

`∎` (typed as `\qed`) is a macro that expands to `try?` in tactic mode.

tactic

```lean
[suggestions]](#manual-suggestions)
```

`#suggestions` will suggest relevant theorems from the library for the current goal,
using the currently registered library suggestion engine.

The suggestions are printed in the order of their confidence, from highest to lowest.

### 14.5.25. Other {#manual-tactic-ref-other}

tactic

```lean
[trivial]](#manual-trivial)
```

`trivial` tries different simple tactics (e.g., `[rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)`, `[contradiction]](#manual-contradiction)`, ...)
to close the current goal.
You can use the command `macro_rules` to extend the set of tactics used. Example:

```lean
[macro_rules](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Macros/#Lean___Parser___Command___macro_rules) | `(tactic| [trivial]](#manual-trivial)) => `(tactic| [simp]](#manual-simp))
```

tactic

```lean
[solve]](#manual-solve)
```

Similar to `[first]](#manual-first)`, but succeeds only if one the given tactics solves the current goal.

tactic

```lean
[and_intros]](#manual-and_intros)
```

`[and_intros]](#manual-and_intros)` applies `[And.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro)` until it does not make progress.

tactic

```lean
[infer_instance]](#manual-infer_instance)
```

`[infer_instance]](#manual-infer_instance)` is an abbreviation for `[exact]](#manual-exact) inferInstance`.
It synthesizes a value of any target type by typeclass inference.

tactic

```lean
[expose_names]](#manual-expose_names)
```

`[expose_names]](#manual-expose_names)` renames all inaccessible variables with accessible names, making them available
for reference in generated tactics. However, this renaming introduces machine-generated names
that are not fully under user control. `[expose_names]](#manual-expose_names)` is primarily intended as a preamble for
auto-generated end-game tactic scripts. It is also useful as an alternative to
`set_option tactic.hygienic false`. If explicit control over renaming is needed in the
middle of a tactic script, consider using structured tactic scripts with
`match .. with`, `induction .. with`, or `[intro]](#manual-intro)` with explicit user-defined names,
as well as tactics such as `[next]](#manual-next)`, `[case]](#manual-case)`, and `[rename_i]](#manual-rename_i)`.

tactic

```lean
[unhygienic]](#manual-unhygienic)
```

`unhygienic tacs` runs `tacs` with name hygiene disabled.
This means that tactics that would normally create inaccessible names will instead
make regular variables. **Warning**: Tactics may change their variable naming
strategies at any time, so code that depends on autogenerated names is brittle.
Users should try not to use `unhygienic` if possible.

```lean
example : ∀ x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero), x = x := by⊢ ∀ (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)), x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) x [unhygienic]](#manual-unhygienic)
[intro]](#manual-intro)x:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) x -- x would normally be intro'd as inaccessible
[exact]](#manual-exact) [Eq.refl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) xAll goals completed! 🐙 -- refer to x
```

tactic

```lean
[run_tac]](#manual-run_tac)
```

The `[run_tac]](#manual-run_tac) doSeq` tactic executes code in `TacticM Unit`.

### 14.5.26. Verification Condition Generation {#manual-tactic-ref-mvcgen}

tactic

```lean
[mvcgen]](#manual-mvcgen)
```

`mvcgen` will break down a Hoare triple proof goal like `⦃P⦄ prog ⦃Q⦄` into verification conditions,
provided that all functions used in `prog` have specifications registered with `@[[spec](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--mvcgen--tactic/Predicate-Transformers/#Lean___Parser___Attr___spec)]`.

**Verification Conditions and specifications**

A verification condition is an entailment in the stateful logic of `[Std.Do.SPred](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--mvcgen--tactic/Predicate-Transformers/#Std___Do___SPred)`
in which the original program `prog` no longer occurs.
Verification conditions are introduced by the `mspec` tactic; see the `mspec` tactic for what they
look like.
When there's no applicable `mspec` spec, `mvcgen` will try and rewrite an application
`prog = f a b c` with the simp set registered via `@[[spec](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--mvcgen--tactic/Predicate-Transformers/#Lean___Parser___Attr___spec)]`.

**Features**

When used like `mvcgen +noLetElim [foo_spec, bar_def, instBEqFloat]`, `mvcgen` will additionally

- add a Hoare triple specification `foo_spec : ... → ⦃P⦄ foo ... ⦃Q⦄` to `[spec](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--mvcgen--tactic/Predicate-Transformers/#Lean___Parser___Attr___spec)` set for a
  function `foo` occurring in `prog`,
- unfold a definition `def bar_def ... := ...` in `prog`,
- unfold any method of the `instBEqFloat : [BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk) [Float](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Floating-Point-Numbers/#Float___ofModel)` instance in `prog`.
- it will no longer substitute away `[let]](#manual-let)`-expressions that occur at most once in `P`, `Q` or `prog`.

**Config options**

`+noLetElim` is just one config option of many. Check out `Lean.Elab.Tactic.Do.VCGen.Config` for all
options. Of particular note is `stepLimit = [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) 42`, which is useful for bisecting bugs in
`mvcgen` and tracing its execution.

**Extended syntax**

Often, `mvcgen` will be used like this:

```
mvcgen [...]
case inv1 => exact I1
case inv2 => exact I2
all_goals (mleave; try grind)
```

There is special syntax for this:

```
mvcgen [...] invariants
· I1
· I2
with grind
```

When `I1` and `I2` need to refer to inaccessibles (`mvcgen` will introduce a lot of them for program
variables), you can use case label syntax:

```
mvcgen [...] invariants
| inv1 _ acc _ => I1 acc
| _ => I2
with grind
```

This is more convenient than the equivalent `· by rename_i _ acc _; exact I1 acc`.

**Invariant suggestions**

`mvcgen` will suggest invariants for you if you use the `invariants?` keyword.

```
mvcgen [...] invariants?
```

This is useful if you do not recall the exact syntax to construct invariants.
Furthermore, it will suggest a concrete invariant encoding "this holds at the start of the loop and
this must hold at the end of the loop" by looking at the corresponding VCs.
Although the suggested invariant is a good starting point, it is too strong and requires users to
interpolate it such that the inductive step can be proved. Example:

```
def mySum (l : List Nat) : Nat := Id.run do
  let mut acc := 0
  for x in l do
    acc := acc + x
  return acc

/--
info: Try this:
  invariants
    · ⇓⟨xs, letMuts⟩ => ⌜xs.prefix = [] ∧ letMuts = 0 ∨ xs.suffix = [] ∧ letMuts = l.sum⌝
-/
#guard_msgs (info) in
theorem mySum_suggest_invariant (l : List Nat) : mySum l = l.sum := by
  generalize h : mySum l = r
  apply Id.of_wp_run_eq h
  mvcgen invariants?
  all_goals admit
```

#### 14.5.26.1. Tactics for Stateful Goals in `Std.Do.SPred` {#manual-tactic-ref-spred}

##### 14.5.26.1.1. Starting and Stopping the Proof Mode {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Tactic-Proofs--Tactic-Reference--Verification-Condition-Generation--Tactics-for-Stateful-Goals-in--Std___Do___SPred--Starting-and-Stopping-the-Proof-Mode}

tactic

```lean
[mstart]](#manual-mstart)
```

Start the stateful proof mode of `[Std.Do.SPred](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--mvcgen--tactic/Predicate-Transformers/#Std___Do___SPred)`.
This will transform a stateful goal of the form `H ⊢ₛ T` into `⊢ₛ H → T`
upon which `mintro` can be used to re-introduce `H` and give it a name.
It is often more convenient to use `mintro` directly, which will
try `mstart` automatically if necessary.

tactic

```lean
[mstop]](#manual-mstop)
```

Stops the stateful proof mode of `[Std.Do.SPred](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--mvcgen--tactic/Predicate-Transformers/#Std___Do___SPred)`.
This will simply forget all the names given to stateful hypotheses and pretty-print
a bit differently.

tactic

```lean
[mleave]](#manual-mleave)
```

Leaves the stateful proof mode of `[Std.Do.SPred](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--mvcgen--tactic/Predicate-Transformers/#Std___Do___SPred)`, tries to eta-expand through all definitions
related to the logic of the `[Std.Do.SPred](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--mvcgen--tactic/Predicate-Transformers/#Std___Do___SPred)` and gently simplifies the resulting pure Lean
proposition. This is often the right thing to do after `mvcgen` in order for automation to prove
the goal.

##### 14.5.26.1.2. Proving a Stateful Goal {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Tactic-Proofs--Tactic-Reference--Verification-Condition-Generation--Tactics-for-Stateful-Goals-in--Std___Do___SPred--Proving-a-Stateful-Goal}

tactic

```lean
[mspec]](#manual-mspec)
```

`mspec` is an `[apply]](#manual-apply)`-like tactic that applies a Hoare triple specification to the target of the
stateful goal.

Given a stateful goal `H ⊢ₛ wp⟦prog⟧ Q'`, `mspec foo_spec` will instantiate
`foo_spec : ... → ⦃P⦄ foo ⦃Q⦄`, match `foo` against `prog` and produce subgoals for
the verification conditions `?pre : H ⊢ₛ P` and `?post : Q ⊢ₚ Q'`.

- If `prog = x >>= f`, then `mspec Specs.bind` is tried first so that `foo` is matched against `x`
  instead. Tactic `mspec_no_bind` does not attempt to do this decomposition.
- If `?pre` or `?post` follow by `.[rfl]](#manual-rfl)`, then they are discharged automatically.
- `?post` is automatically simplified into constituent `⊢ₛ` entailments on
  success and failure continuations.
- `?pre` and `?post.*` goals introduce their stateful hypothesis under an inaccessible name.
  You can give it a name with the `mrename_i` tactic.
- Any uninstantiated MVar arising from instantiation of `foo_spec` becomes a new subgoal.
- If the target of the stateful goal looks like `fun s => _` then `mspec` will first `mintro ∀s`.
- If `P` has schematic variables that can be instantiated by doing `mintro ∀s`, for example
  `foo_spec : ∀(n:Nat), ⦃fun s => ⌜n = s⌝⦄ foo ⦃Q⦄`, then `mspec` will do `mintro ∀s` first to
  instantiate `n = s`.
- Right before applying the spec, the `mframe` tactic is used, which has the following effect:
  Any hypothesis `Hᵢ` in the goal `h₁:H₁, h₂:H₂, ..., hₙ:Hₙ ⊢ₛ T` that is
  pure (i.e., equivalent to some `⌜φᵢ⌝`) will be moved into the pure context as `hᵢ:φᵢ`.

Additionally, `mspec` can be used without arguments or with a term argument:

- `mspec` without argument will try and look up a spec for `x` registered with `@[[spec](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--mvcgen--tactic/Predicate-Transformers/#Lean___Parser___Attr___spec)]`.
- `mspec (foo_spec blah ?bleh)` will elaborate its argument as a term with expected type
  `⦃?P⦄ x ⦃?Q⦄` and introduce `?bleh` as a subgoal.
  This is useful to pass an invariant to e.g., `Specs.forIn_list` and leave the inductive step
  as a hole.

tactic

```lean
[mintro]](#manual-mintro)
```

Like `[intro]](#manual-intro)`, but introducing stateful hypotheses into the stateful context of the `[Std.Do.SPred](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--mvcgen--tactic/Predicate-Transformers/#Std___Do___SPred)`
proof mode.
That is, given a stateful goal `(hᵢ : Hᵢ)* ⊢ₛ P → T`, `mintro h` transforms
into `(hᵢ : Hᵢ)*, (h : P) ⊢ₛ T`.

Furthermore, `mintro ∀s` is like `[intro]](#manual-intro) s`, but preserves the stateful goal.
That is, `mintro ∀s` brings the topmost state variable `s:σ` in scope and transforms
`(hᵢ : Hᵢ)* ⊢ₛ T` (where the entailment is in `[Std.Do.SPred](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--mvcgen--tactic/Predicate-Transformers/#Std___Do___SPred) (σ::σs)`) into
`(hᵢ : Hᵢ s)* ⊢ₛ T s` (where the entailment is in `[Std.Do.SPred](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--mvcgen--tactic/Predicate-Transformers/#Std___Do___SPred) σs`).

Beyond that, `mintro` supports the full syntax of `mcases` patterns
(`mintro pat = (mintro h; mcases h with pat`), and can perform multiple
introductions in sequence.

```
example (Q : SPred σs) : Q ⊢ₛ Q := by
  mstart
  mintro HQ
  mexact HQ
```

It specializes a hypothesis from the stateful context with hypotheses from either the pure
or stateful context or pure terms.

```
example (P Q : SPred σs) : P ⊢ₛ (P → Q) → Q := by
  mintro HP HPQ
  mspecialize HPQ HP
  mexact HPQ

example (y : Nat) (P Q : SPred σs) (Ψ : Nat → SPred σs) (hP : ⊢ₛ P) : ⊢ₛ Q → (∀ x, P → Q → Ψ x) → Ψ (y + 1) := by
  mintro HQ HΨ
  mspecialize HΨ (y + 1) hP HQ
  mexact HΨ
```

```lean
[mspecialize_pure]](#manual-mspecialize_pure)
```

`mspecialize_pure` is like `mspecialize`, but it specializes a hypothesis from the
*pure* context with hypotheses from either the pure or stateful context or pure terms.

```
example (y : Nat) (P Q : SPred σs) (Ψ : Nat → SPred σs) (hP : ⊢ₛ P) (hΨ : ∀ x, ⊢ₛ P → Q → Ψ x) : ⊢ₛ Q → Ψ (y + 1) := by
  mintro HQ
  mspecialize_pure (hΨ (y + 1)) hP HQ => HΨ
  mexact HΨ
```

```lean
[mcases]](#manual-mcases)
```

Like `[rcases]](#manual-rcases)`, but operating on stateful `[Std.Do.SPred](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--mvcgen--tactic/Predicate-Transformers/#Std___Do___SPred)` goals.
Example: Given a goal `h : (P ∧ (Q ∨ R) ∧ (Q → R)) ⊢ₛ R`,
`mcases h with ⟨-, ⟨hq | hr⟩, hqr⟩` will yield two goals:
`(hq : Q, hqr : Q → R) ⊢ₛ R` and `(hr : R) ⊢ₛ R`.

That is, `mcases h with pat` has the following semantics, based on `pat`:

- `pat=□h'` renames `h` to `h'` in the stateful context, regardless of whether `h` is pure
- `pat=⌜h'⌝` introduces `h' : φ` to the pure local context if `h : ⌜φ⌝`
  (c.f. `Lean.Elab.Tactic.Do.ProofMode.IsPure`)
- `pat=h'` is like `pat=⌜h'⌝` if `h` is pure
  (c.f. `Lean.Elab.Tactic.Do.ProofMode.IsPure`), otherwise it is like `pat=□h'`.
- `pat=_` renames `h` to an inaccessible name
- `pat=-` discards `h`
- `⟨pat₁, pat₂⟩` matches on conjunctions and existential quantifiers and recurses via
  `pat₁` and `pat₂`.
- `⟨pat₁ | pat₂⟩` matches on disjunctions, matching the left alternative via `pat₁` and the right
  alternative via `pat₂`.

tactic

```lean
[mrename_i]](#manual-mrename_i)
```

`mrename_i` is like `[rename_i]](#manual-rename_i)`, but names inaccessible stateful hypotheses in a `[Std.Do.SPred](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--mvcgen--tactic/Predicate-Transformers/#Std___Do___SPred)` goal.

tactic

```lean
[mpure]](#manual-mpure)
```

`mpure` moves a pure hypothesis from the stateful context into the pure context.

```
example (Q : SPred σs) (ψ : φ → ⊢ₛ Q): ⌜φ⌝ ⊢ₛ Q := by
  mintro Hφ
  mpure Hφ
  mexact (ψ Hφ)
```

tactic

```lean
[mframe]](#manual-mframe)
```

`mframe` infers which hypotheses from the stateful context can be moved into the pure context.
This is useful because pure hypotheses "survive" the next application of modus ponens
(`Std.Do.SPred.mp`) and transitivity (`Std.Do.SPred.entails.trans`).

It is used as part of the `mspec` tactic.

```
example (P Q : SPred σs) : ⊢ₛ ⌜p⌝ ∧ Q ∧ ⌜q⌝ ∧ ⌜r⌝ ∧ P ∧ ⌜s⌝ ∧ ⌜t⌝ → Q := by
  mintro _
  mframe
  /- `h : p ∧ q ∧ r ∧ s ∧ t` in the pure context -/
  mcases h with hP
  mexact h
```

## Tactic Proofs — 14.6. Targeted Rewriting with `[conv](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Targeted-Rewriting-with--conv/#conv-next)` {#manual-tactic-proofs-146-targeted-rewriting-with}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Targeted-Rewriting-with--conv/

## 14.6. Targeted Rewriting with `[conv]](#manual-conv-next)`

The `[conv]](#manual-conv-next)`, or conversion, tactic allows targeted rewriting within a goal.
The argument to `[conv]](#manual-conv-next)` is written in a separate language that interoperates with the main tactic language; it features commands to navigate to specific subterms within the goal along with commands that allow these subterms to be rewritten.
`[conv]](#manual-conv-next)` is useful when rewrites should only be applied in part of a goal (e.g. only on one side of an equality), rather than across the board, or when rewrites should be applied underneath a binder that prevents tactics like `[rw]](#manual-rw)` from accessing the term.

The conversion tactic language is very similar to the main tactic language: it uses the same proof states, tactics work primarily on the main goal and may either fail or succeed with a sequence of new goals, and macro expansion is interleaved with tactic execution.
Unlike the main tactic language, in which tactics are intended to eventually solve goals, the `[conv]](#manual-conv-next)` tactic is used to *change* a goal so that it becomes amenable to further processing in the main tactic language.
Goals that are intended to be rewritten with `[conv]](#manual-conv-next)` are shown with a vertical bar instead of a turnstile.

tactic

```lean
[conv]](#manual-conv-next)
```

`conv => ...` allows the user to perform targeted rewriting on a goal or hypothesis,
by focusing on particular subexpressions.

See [https://lean-lang.org/theorem\_proving\_in\_lean4/conv.html](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/conv.html) for more details.

Basic forms:

- `conv => cs` will rewrite the goal with conv tactics `cs`.
- `conv at h => cs` will rewrite hypothesis `h`.
- `conv in pat => cs` will rewrite the first subexpression matching `pat` (see `pattern`).

**Example: Navigation and Rewriting with conv**

In this example, there are multiple instances of addition, and `[rw]](#manual-rw)` would by default rewrite the first instance that it encounters.
Using `[conv]](#manual-conv-next)` to navigate to the specific subterm before rewriting leaves `[rw]](#manual-rw)` no choice but to rewrite the correct term.

**Example: Rewriting Under Binders with conv**

In this example, addition occurs under binders, so `[rw]](#manual-rw)` can't be used.
However, after using `[conv]](#manual-conv-next)` to navigate to the function body, it succeeds.
The nested use of `[conv]](#manual-conv-next)` causes control to return to the current position in the term after performing further conversions on one of its subterms.
Because the goal is a reflexive equation after rewriting, `[conv]](#manual-conv-next)` automatically closes it.

### 14.6.1. Control Structures {#manual-conv-control}

conv tactic

```lean
[first]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___first)
```

`first | conv | ...` runs each `conv` until one succeeds, or else fails.

conv tactic

```lean
[try]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___convTry_)
```

`try tac` runs `tac` and succeeds even if `tac` failed.

conv tactic

```lean
[<;>]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv____FLQQ_conv__LT__SEMI__GT___FLQQ_)
```

`tac <;> tac'` runs `tac` on the main goal and `tac'` on each produced goal, concatenating all goals
produced by `tac'`.

conv tactic

```lean
[repeat]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___convRepeat_)
```

`repeat convs` runs the sequence `convs` repeatedly until it fails to apply.

conv tactic

```lean
[skip]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___skip)
```

`[skip]](#manual-skip)` does nothing.

conv tactic

```lean
[{ ... }]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___nestedConv)
```

`{ convs }` runs the list of `convs` on the current target, and any subgoals that
remain are trivially closed by `[skip]](#manual-skip)`.

conv tactic

```lean
[( ... )]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___paren)
```

`(convs)` runs the `convs` in sequence on the current list of targets.
This is pure grouping with no added effects.

conv tactic

```lean
[done]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___convDone)
```

`[done]](#manual-done)` succeeds iff there are no goals remaining.

### 14.6.2. Goal Selection {#manual-conv-goals}

conv tactic

```lean
[all_goals]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___allGoals)
```

`all_goals tac` runs `tac` on each goal, concatenating the resulting goals, if any.

conv tactic

```lean
[any_goals]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___anyGoals)
```

`any_goals tac` applies the tactic `tac` to every goal, and succeeds if at
least one application succeeds.

conv tactic

```lean
[case ... => ...]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___case)
```

- `case tag => tac` focuses on the goal with case name `tag` and solves it using `tac`,
  or else fails.
- `case tag x₁ ... xₙ => tac` additionally renames the `n` most recent hypotheses
  with inaccessible names to the given names.
- `case tag₁ | tag₂ => tac` is equivalent to `(case tag₁ => tac); (case tag₂ => tac)`.

conv tactic

```lean
[case' ... => ...]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___case___)
```

`[case']](#manual-case___)` is similar to the `case tag => tac` tactic, but does not ensure the goal
has been solved after applying `tac`, nor admits the goal if `tac` failed.
Recall that `[case]](#manual-case)` closes the goal using `[sorry]](#manual-sorry)` when `tac` fails, and
the tactic execution is not interrupted.

conv tactic

```lean
[next ... => ...]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv____FLQQ_convNext______GT___FLQQ_)
```

`next => tac` focuses on the next goal and solves it using `tac`, or else fails.
`next x₁ ... xₙ => tac` additionally renames the `n` most recent hypotheses with
inaccessible names to the given names.

conv tactic

```lean
[focus]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___focus)
```

`focus tac` focuses on the main goal, suppressing all other goals, and runs `tac` on it.
Usually `· tac`, which enforces that the goal is closed by `tac`, should be preferred.

conv tactic

```lean
[· ...]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv____FLQQ_conv_____FLQQ_)
```

`· conv` focuses on the main conv goal and tries to solve it using `s`.

conv tactic

```lean
[fail_if_success]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___failIfSuccess)
```

`fail_if_success t` fails if the tactic `t` succeeds.

### 14.6.3. Navigation {#manual-conv-nav}

conv tactic

```lean
[lhs]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___lhs)
```

Traverses into the left subterm of a binary operator.

In general, for an `n`-ary operator, it traverses into the second to last argument.
It is a synonym for `arg -2`.

conv tactic

```lean
[rhs]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___rhs)
```

Traverses into the right subterm of a binary operator.

In general, for an `n`-ary operator, it traverses into the last argument.
It is a synonym for `arg -1`.

conv tactic

```lean
[fun]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___fun)
```

Traverses into the function of a (unary) function application.
For example, `| f a b` turns into `| f a`. (Use `arg 0` to traverse into `f`.)

conv tactic

```lean
[congr]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___congr)
```

Performs one step of "congruence", which takes a term and produces
subgoals for all the function arguments. For example, if the target is `f x y` then
`[congr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#congr-next)` produces two subgoals, one for `x` and one for `y`.

conv tactic

```lean
[arg [@]i](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Targeted-Rewriting-with--conv/#Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___arg)
```

- `arg i` traverses into the `i`'th argument of the target. For example if the
  target is `f a b c d` then `arg 1` traverses to `a` and `arg 3` traverses to `c`.
  The index may be negative; `arg -1` traverses into the last argument,
  `arg -2` into the second-to-last argument, and so on.
- `arg @i` is the same as `arg i` but it counts all arguments instead of just the
  explicit arguments.
- `arg 0` traverses into the function. If the target is `f a b c d`, `arg 0` traverses into `f`.

syntaxArguments to `enter`

```lean
enterArg ::= ...
    | num
```

```lean
enterArg ::= ...
    | @num
```

```lean
enterArg ::= ...
    | ident
```

conv tactic

```lean
[enter]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___enter)
```

`enter [arg, ...]` is a compact way to describe a path to a subterm.
It is a shorthand for other conv tactics as follows:

- `enter [i]` is equivalent to `arg i`.
- `enter [@i]` is equivalent to `arg @i`.
- `enter [x]` (where `x` is an identifier) is equivalent to `[ext]](#manual-ext) x`.
- `enter [in e]` (where `e` is a term) is equivalent to `pattern e`.
  Occurrences can be specified with `enter [in (occs := ...) e]`.
  For example, given the target `f (g a (fun x => x b))`, `enter [1, 2, x, 1]`
  will traverse to the subterm `b`.

conv tactic

```lean
[pattern]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___pattern)
```

- `pattern pat` traverses to the first subterm of the target that matches `pat`.
- `pattern (occs := *) pat` traverses to every subterm of the target that matches `pat`
  which is not contained in another match of `pat`. It generates one subgoal for each matching
  subterm.
- `pattern (occs := 1 2 4) pat` matches occurrences `1, 2, 4` of `pat` and produces three subgoals.
  Occurrences are numbered left to right from the outside in.

Note that skipping an occurrence of `pat` will traverse inside that subexpression, which means
it may find more matches and this can affect the numbering of subsequent pattern matches.
For example, if we are searching for `f _` in `f (f a) = f b`:

- `occs := 1 2` (and `occs := *`) returns `| f (f a)` and `| f b`
- `occs := 2` returns `| f a`
- `occs := 2 3` returns `| f a` and `| f b`
- `occs := 1 3` is an error, because after skipping `f b` there is no third match.

conv tactic

```lean
[ext]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___ext)
```

`[ext]](#manual-ext) x` traverses into a binder (a `fun x => e` or `∀ x, e` expression)
to target `e`, introducing name `x` in the process.

conv tactic

```lean
[args]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___convArgs)
```

`args` traverses into all arguments. Synonym for `[congr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#congr-next)`.

conv tactic

```lean
[left]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___convLeft)
```

`[left]](#manual-left)` traverses into the left argument. Synonym for `lhs`.

conv tactic

```lean
[right]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___convRight)
```

`[right]](#manual-right)` traverses into the right argument. Synonym for `rhs`.

conv tactic

```lean
[intro]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___convIntro___)
```

`[intro]](#manual-intro)` traverses into binders. Synonym for `[ext]](#manual-ext)`.

### 14.6.4. Changing the Goal {#manual-conv-change}

#### 14.6.4.1. Reduction {#manual-conv-reduction}

conv tactic

```lean
[cbv]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___cbv)
```

`[cbv]](#manual-cbv)` performs simplification that closely mimics call-by-value evaluation.
It reduces the target term by unfolding definitions using their defining equations and
applying matcher equations. The unfolding is propositional, so `[cbv]](#manual-cbv)` also works
with functions defined via well-founded recursion or partial fixpoints.

The proofs produced by `[cbv]](#manual-cbv)` only use the three standard axioms.
In particular, they do not require trust in the correctness of the code
generator.

**Example: The cbv Tactic**

The `[cbv]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___cbv)` tactic can be used to reduce functions, including ones that are defined via [well-founded recursion]](#manual-well-founded-recursion), which are otherwise irreducible.
Ordinarily, `[f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-The--cbv--Tactic_RPAR_)` is only propositionally equal to its unfolding, so `[rfl]](#manual-rfl)` can't prove the equality `[f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-The--cbv--Tactic_RPAR_) 5 = 5`:

```lean
def f (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) :=
[match]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match) n [with]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| 0 => 0
| n + 1 => [f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-The--cbv--Tactic_RPAR_) n + 1
termination_by (n,0)
```

```lean
example : [f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-The--cbv--Tactic_RPAR_) 5 = 5 := by⊢ [f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-The--cbv--Tactic_RPAR_) 5 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 5 [rfl]](#manual-rfl)⊢ [f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-The--cbv--Tactic_RPAR_) 5 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 5
```

```lean
Tactic `rfl` failed: The left-hand side
  [f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-The--cbv--Tactic_RPAR_) 5
is not definitionally equal to the right-hand side
  5

⊢ [f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-The--cbv--Tactic_RPAR_) 5 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 5
```

Using `[cbv]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___cbv)` on the left-hand side of the equality, the statement can be made true:

```lean
example : [f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-The--cbv--Tactic_RPAR_) 5 = 5 := by⊢ [f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-The--cbv--Tactic_RPAR_) 5 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 5
conv =>| [f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-The--cbv--Tactic_RPAR_) 5 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 5
[lhs]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___lhs)| [f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-The--cbv--Tactic_RPAR_) 5
[cbv]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___cbv)| 5
```

conv tactic

```lean
[whnf]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___whnf)
```

Reduces the target to Weak Head Normal Form. This reduces definitions
in "head position" until a constructor is exposed. For example, `[List.map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___map) f [a, b, c]`
weak head normalizes to `f a :: [List.map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___map) f [b, c]`.

conv tactic

```lean
[reduce]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___reduce)
```

Puts term in normal form, this tactic is meant for debugging purposes only.

conv tactic

```lean
[zeta]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___zeta)
```

Expands let-declarations and let-variables.

conv tactic

```lean
[delta]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___delta)
```

`delta id1 id2 ...` unfolds all occurrences of `id1`, `id2`, ... in the target.
Like the `[delta]](#manual-delta)` tactic, this ignores any definitional equations and uses
primitive delta-reduction instead, which may result in leaking implementation details.
Users should prefer `[unfold]](#manual-unfold)` for unfolding definitions.

conv tactic

```lean
[unfold]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___unfold)
```

- `[unfold]](#manual-unfold) id` unfolds all occurrences of definition `id` in the target.
- `unfold id1 id2 ...` is equivalent to `unfold id1; unfold id2; ...`.

Definitions can be either global or local definitions.

For non-recursive global definitions, this tactic is identical to `[delta]](#manual-delta)`.
For recursive global definitions, it uses the "unfolding lemma" `id.eq_def`,
which is generated for each recursive definition, to unfold according to the recursive definition given by the user.
Only one level of unfolding is performed, in contrast to `[simp]](#manual-simp) [only]](#manual-simp) [id]`, which unfolds definition `id` recursively.

This is the `conv` version of the `[unfold]](#manual-unfold)` tactic.

#### 14.6.4.2. Simplification {#manual-conv-simp}

conv tactic

```lean
[simp]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___simp)
```

`[simp]](#manual-simp) [thm]` performs simplification using `thm` and marked `@[simp]` lemmas.
See the `[simp]](#manual-simp)` tactic for more information.

conv tactic

```lean
[dsimp]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___dsimp)
```

`[dsimp]](#manual-dsimp)` is the definitional simplifier in `conv`-mode. It differs from `[simp]](#manual-simp)` in that it only
applies theorems that hold by reflexivity.

Examples:

```lean
example (a : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)): (0 + 0) = a - a := bya:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ 0 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 0 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) a [-]](#manual-HSub___mk) a
conv =>a:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)| 0 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 0 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) a [-]](#manual-HSub___mk) a
[lhs]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___lhs)a:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)| 0 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 0
[dsimp]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___dsimp)a:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)| 0
[rw]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___convRw__) [← Nat.sub_self a]a:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)| a [-]](#manual-HSub___mk) a
```

conv tactic

```lean
[simp_match]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___simpMatch)
```

`simp_match` simplifies match expressions. For example,

```lean
[match]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match) [a, b] [with]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [] => 0
| hd :: tl => hd
```

simplifies to `a`.

#### 14.6.4.3. Rewriting {#manual-conv-rw}

conv tactic

```lean
[change]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___change)
```

`[change]](#manual-change) t'` replaces the target `t` with `t'`,
assuming `t` and `t'` are definitionally equal.

conv tactic


`[rw]](#manual-rw) [thm]` rewrites the target using `thm`. See the `[rw]](#manual-rw)` tactic for more information.

conv tactic

See the `[rw]](#manual-rw)` tactic for more information.

conv tactic


`[erw]](#manual-erw) [rules]` is a shorthand for `[rw]](#manual-rw) (transparency := .default) [rules]`.
This does rewriting up to unfolding of regular definitions (by comparison to regular `[rw]](#manual-rw)`
which only unfolds `@[reducible]` definitions).

conv tactic

```lean
[apply]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___convApply_)
```

The `[apply]](#manual-apply) thm` conv tactic is the same as `[apply]](#manual-apply) thm` the tactic.
There are no restrictions on `thm`, but strange results may occur if `thm`

## Tactic Proofs — 14.7. Naming Bound Variables {#manual-tactic-proofs-147-naming-bound-variables}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Naming-Bound-Variables/

When the [simplifier](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The-Simplifier/#the-simplifier) or the `[rw]](#manual-rw)` tactic introduce new binding forms such as function parameters, they select a name for the bound variable based on the one in the statement of the rewrite rule being applied.
This name is made unique if necessary.
In some situations, such as [preprocessing definitions for termination proofs that use well-founded recursion]](#manual-well-founded-preprocessing), the names that appear in termination proof obligations should be the corresponding names written in the original function definition.

The `[binderNameHint]](#manual-binderNameHint)` [gadget]](#manual---tech-term-gadgets) can be used to indicate that a bound variable should be named according to the variables bound in some other term.
By convention, the term `()` is used to indicate that a name should *not* be taken from the original definition.

def

```lean
[binderNameHint.{u, v, w}]](#manual-binderNameHint) {α : Sort u} {β : Sort v} {γ : Sort w} (v : α)
  (binder : β) (e : γ) : γ



[binderNameHint.{u, v, w}]](#manual-binderNameHint) {α : Sort u}
  {β : Sort v} {γ : Sort w} (v : α)
  (binder : β) (e : γ) : γ
```

The expression `[binderNameHint]](#manual-binderNameHint) v binder e` defined to be `e`.

If it is used on the right-hand side of an equation that is used for rewriting by `[rw]](#manual-rw)` or `[simp]](#manual-simp)`,
and `v` is a local variable, and `binder` is an expression that (after beta-reduction) is a binder
(`fun w => …` or `∀ w, …`), then it will rename `v` to the name used in that binder, and remove
the `[binderNameHint]](#manual-binderNameHint)`.

A typical use of this gadget would be as follows; the gadget ensures that after rewriting, the local
variable is still `name`, and not `x`:

```
theorem all_eq_not_any_not (l : List α) (p : α → Bool) :
    l.all p = !l.any fun x => binderNameHint x p (!p x) := sorry

example (names : List String) : names.all (fun name => "Waldo".isPrefixOf name) = true := by
  rw [all_eq_not_any_not]
  -- ⊢ (!names.any fun name => !"Waldo".isPrefixOf name) = true
```

If `binder` is not a binder, then the name of `v` attains a macro scope. This only matters when the
resulting term is used in a non-hygienic way, e.g. in termination proofs for well-founded recursion.

This gadget is supported by

- `[simp]](#manual-simp)`, `[dsimp]](#manual-dsimp)` and `[rw]](#manual-rw)` in the right-hand-side of an equation
- `[simp]](#manual-simp)` in the assumptions of congruence rules

It is ineffective in other positions (hypotheses of rewrite rules) or when used by other tactics
(e.g. `[apply]](#manual-apply)`).

## Tactic Proofs — 14.8. Custom Tactics {#manual-tactic-proofs-148-custom-tactics}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Tactic-Proofs/Custom-Tactics/

Tactics are productions in the syntax category `tactic`.
Given the syntax of a tactic, the tactic interpreter is responsible for carrying out actions in the tactic monad `TacticM`, which is a wrapper around Lean's term elaborator that keeps track of the additional state needed to execute tactics.
A custom tactic consists of an extension to the `tactic` category along with either:

- a [macro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Macros/#--tech-term-Macros) that translates the new syntax into existing syntax, or
- an elaborator that carries out `TacticM` actions to implement the tactic.

### 14.8.1. Tactic Macros {#manual-tactic-macros}

The easiest way to define a new tactic is as a [macro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Macros/#--tech-term-Macros) that expands into already-existing tactics.
Macro expansion is interleaved with tactic execution.
The tactic interpreter first expands tactic macros just before they are to be interpreted.
Because tactic macros are not fully expanded prior to running a tactic script, they can use recursion; as long as the recursive occurrence of the macro syntax is beneath a tactic that can be executed, there will not be an infinite chain of expansion.

**Example: Recursive tactic macro**

This recursive implementation of a tactic akin to `[repeat]](#manual-repeat)` is defined via macro expansion.
When the argument `$t` fails, the recursive occurrence of `rep` is never invoked, and is thus never macro expanded.

```lean
[syntax](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Defining-New-Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Command___syntax) "rep" tactic : tactic
[macro_rules](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Macros/#Lean___Parser___Command___macro_rules)
| `(tactic|rep $t) =>
`(tactic|
[first]](#manual-first)
| $t; rep $t
| [skip]](#manual-skip))
example : 0 ≤ 4 := by⊢ 0 [≤]](#manual-LE___mk) 4
rep ([apply]](#manual-apply) [Nat.le.step](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___le___refl)⊢ [Nat.le](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___le___refl) 0 0)
[apply]](#manual-apply) [Nat.le.refl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___le___refl)All goals completed! 🐙
```

Like other Lean macros, tactic macros are [hygienic](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Macros/#--tech-term-hygienic).
References to global names are resolved when the macro is defined, and names introduced by the tactic macro cannot capture names from its invocation site.

When defining a tactic macro, it's important to specify that the syntax being matched or constructed is for the syntax category `tactic`.
Otherwise, the syntax will be interpreted as that of a term, which will match against or construct an incorrect AST for tactics.

#### 14.8.1.1. Extensible Tactic Macros {#manual-tactic-macro-extension}

Because macro expansion can fail, multiple macros can match the same syntax, allowing backtracking.
Tactic macros take this further: even if a tactic macro expands successfully, if the expansion fails when interpreted, the tactic interpreter will attempt the next expansion.
This is used to make a number of Lean's built-in tactics extensible—new behavior can be added to a tactic by adding a [`macro_rules`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Macros/#Lean___Parser___Command___macro_rules) declaration.

**Example: Extending trivial**

The `[trivial]](#manual-trivial)`, which is used by many other tactics to quickly dispatch subgoals that are not worth bothering the user with, is designed to be extended through new macro expansions.
Lean's default `trivial` can't solve `[IsEmpty]](#manual-IsEmpty-_LPAR_in-Extending--trivial_RPAR_) []` goals:

```lean
def IsEmpty (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : Prop :=
¬ xs ≠ []
```

```lean
example (α : Type u) : [IsEmpty]](#manual-IsEmpty-_LPAR_in-Extending--trivial_RPAR_) (α := α) [] := byα:Type u⊢ [IsEmpty]](#manual-IsEmpty-_LPAR_in-Extending--trivial_RPAR_) [[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [trivial]](#manual-trivial)α:Type u⊢ [IsEmpty]](#manual-IsEmpty-_LPAR_in-Extending--trivial_RPAR_) [[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
```

The error message is an artifact of `[trivial]](#manual-trivial)` trying `[assumption]](#manual-assumption)` last.
Adding another expansion allows `[trivial]](#manual-trivial)` to take care of these goals:

```lean
def emptyIsEmpty : [IsEmpty]](#manual-IsEmpty-_LPAR_in-Extending--trivial_RPAR_) (α := α) [] := byα:Type u_1⊢ [IsEmpty]](#manual-IsEmpty-_LPAR_in-Extending--trivial_RPAR_) [[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [simp]](#manual-simp) [[IsEmpty]](#manual-IsEmpty-_LPAR_in-Extending--trivial_RPAR_)]All goals completed! 🐙
[macro_rules](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Macros/#Lean___Parser___Command___macro_rules) | `(tactic|[trivial]](#manual-trivial)) => `(tactic|[exact]](#manual-exact) emptyIsEmpty)
example (α : Type u) : [IsEmpty]](#manual-IsEmpty-_LPAR_in-Extending--trivial_RPAR_) (α := α) [] := byα:Type u⊢ [IsEmpty]](#manual-IsEmpty-_LPAR_in-Extending--trivial_RPAR_) [[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
[trivial]](#manual-trivial)All goals completed! 🐙
```

**Example: Expansion Backtracking**

Macro expansion can induce backtracking when the failure arises from any part of the expanded syntax.
An infix version of `[first]](#manual-first)` can be defined by providing multiple expansions in separate [`macro_rules`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Macros/#Lean___Parser___Command___macro_rules) declarations:

```lean
[syntax](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Defining-New-Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Command___syntax) tactic "<|||>" tactic : tactic
[macro_rules](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Macros/#Lean___Parser___Command___macro_rules)
| `(tactic|$t1 <|||> $t2) => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) t1
[macro_rules](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Macros/#Lean___Parser___Command___macro_rules)
| `(tactic|$t1 <|||> $t2) => [pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) t2
example : 2 = 2 := by⊢ 2 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 2
[rfl]](#manual-rfl)All goals completed! 🐙 <|||> [apply]](#manual-apply) And.intro
example : 2 = 2 := by⊢ 2 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 2
[apply]](#manual-apply) And.intro <|||> [rfl]](#manual-rfl)All goals completed! 🐙
```

Multiple [`macro_rules`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Macros/#Lean___Parser___Command___macro_rules) declarations are needed because each defines a pattern-matching function that will always take the first matching alternative.
Backtracking is at the granularity of [`macro_rules`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Notations-and-Macros/Macros/#Lean___Parser___Command___macro_rules) declarations, not their individual cases.

## The Simplifier {#manual-the-simplifier}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The-Simplifier/

The simplifier is one of the most-used features of Lean.
It performs inside-out rewriting of terms based on a database of simplification rules.
The simplifier is highly configurable, and a number of tactics use it in different ways.

1. [15.1. Invoking the Simplifier](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The-Simplifier/Invoking-the-Simplifier/#simp-tactic-naming)
2. [15.2. Rewrite Rules](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The-Simplifier/Rewrite-Rules/#simp-rewrites)
3. [15.3. Simp sets](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The-Simplifier/Simp-sets/#simp-sets)
4. [15.4. Simp Normal Forms](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The-Simplifier/Simp-Normal-Forms/#simp-normal-forms)
5. [15.5. Terminal vs Non-Terminal Positions](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The-Simplifier/Terminal-vs-Non-Terminal-Positions/#terminal-simp)
6. [15.6. Configuring Simplification](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The-Simplifier/Configuring-Simplification/#simp-config)
7. [15.7. Simplification vs Rewriting](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The-Simplifier/Simplification-vs-Rewriting/#simp-vs-rw)
