## The Simplifier — 15.1. Invoking the Simplifier {#manual-the-simplifier-151-invoking-the-simplifier}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The-Simplifier/Invoking-the-Simplifier/

Lean's simplifier can be invoked in a variety of ways.
The most common patterns are captured in a set of tactics.
The [tactic reference]](#manual-simp-tactics) contains a complete list of simplification tactics.

Simplification tactics all contain `simp` in their name.
Aside from that, they are named according to a system of prefixes and suffixes that describe their functionality:

`-!` suffix
:   Sets the `[autoUnfold](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The-Simplifier/Configuring-Simplification/#Lean___Meta___Simp___Config___mk)` configuration option to `true`, causing the simplifier to unfold all definitions

`-?` suffix
:   Causes the simplifier to keep track of which rules it employed during simplification and suggest a minimal [simp set](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The-Simplifier/Simp-sets/#--tech-term-simp-set) as an edit to the tactic script

`-_arith` suffix
:   Enables the use of linear arithmetic simplification rules

`d-` prefix
:   Causes the simplifier to simplify only with rewrites that hold definitionally

`-_all` suffix
:   Causes the simplifier to repeatedly simplify all assumptions and the conclusion of the goal, taking as many hypotheses into account as possible, until no further simplification is possible

There are two further simplification tactics, `[simpa]](#manual-simpa)` and `[simpa!]](#manual-simpa___)`, which are used to simultaneously simplify a goal and either a proof term or an assumption before discharging the goal.
This simultaneous simplification makes proofs more robust to changes in the [simp set](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The-Simplifier/Simp-sets/#--tech-term-simp-set).

### 15.1.1. Parameters {#manual-simp-tactic-params}

The simplification tactics have the following grammar:

syntaxSimplification Tactics

```lean
tactic ::= ...
    | simp [optConfig]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Tactic___optConfig-next) only? ([ (simpStar | simpErase | simpLemma),* ] )? (at (term | locationType)*)?
```

In other words, an invocation of a simplification tactic takes the following modifiers, in order, all of which are optional:

- A set of [configuration options]](#manual-tactic-config), which should include the fields of `[Lean.Meta.Simp.Config](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The-Simplifier/Configuring-Simplification/#Lean___Meta___Simp___Config___mk)` or `[Lean.Meta.DSimp.Config](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The-Simplifier/Configuring-Simplification/#Lean___Meta___DSimp___Config___mk)`, depending on whether the simplifier being invoked is a version of `[simp]](#manual-simp)` or a version of `[dsimp]](#manual-dsimp)`.
- The [`only`]](#manual-simp) modifier excludes the default simp set, instead beginning with an emptyTechnically, the simp set always includes `eq_self` and `iff_self` in order to discharge reflexive cases. simp set.
- The lemma list adds or removes lemmas from the simp set. There are three ways to specify lemmas in the lemma list:

  - `*`, which adds all assumptions in the proof state to the simp set
  - `-` followed by a lemma, which removes the lemma from the simp set
  - A lemma specifier, consisting of the following in sequence:

    - An optional `↓` or `↑`, which respectively cause the lemma to be applied before or after entering a subterm (`↑` is the default). The simplifier typically simplifies subterms before attempting to simplify parent terms, as simplified arguments often make more rules applicable; `↓` causes the parent term to be simplified with the rule prior to the simplification of subterms.
    - An optional `←`, which causes equational lemmas to be used from right to left rather than from left to right.
    - A mandatory lemma, which can be a simp set name, a lemma name, or a term. Terms are treated as if they were named lemmas with fresh names.
- A location specifier, preceded by [`at`]](#manual-simp), which consists of a sequence of locations. Locations may be:

  - The name of an assumption, indicating that its type should be simplified
  - An asterisk `*`, indicating that all assumptions and the conclusion should be simplified
  - A turnstile `⊢`, indicating that the conclusion should be simplified

  By default, only the conclusion is simplified.

**Example: Location specifiers for simp**

In this proof state,

p:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Propx:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h:p [(]](#manual-HAdd___mk)x [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 5 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 2[)]](#manual-HAdd___mk)h':p [(]](#manual-HAdd___mk)3 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) x [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 9[)]](#manual-HAdd___mk)⊢ p [(]](#manual-HAdd___mk)6 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) x [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 1[)]](#manual-HAdd___mk)

the tactic `[simp]](#manual-simp) +[arith](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The-Simplifier/Configuring-Simplification/#Lean___Meta___Simp___Config___mk)p:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Propx:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h:p [(]](#manual-HAdd___mk)x [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 5 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 2[)]](#manual-HAdd___mk)h':p [(]](#manual-HAdd___mk)3 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) x [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 9[)]](#manual-HAdd___mk)⊢ p [(]](#manual-HAdd___mk)x [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 7[)]](#manual-HAdd___mk)` simplifies only the goal:

p:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Propx:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h:p [(]](#manual-HAdd___mk)x [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 5 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 2[)]](#manual-HAdd___mk)h':p [(]](#manual-HAdd___mk)3 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) x [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 9[)]](#manual-HAdd___mk)⊢ p [(]](#manual-HAdd___mk)x [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 7[)]](#manual-HAdd___mk)

Invoking `[simp]](#manual-simp) +[arith](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The-Simplifier/Configuring-Simplification/#Lean___Meta___Simp___Config___mk) at hp:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Propx:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h':p [(]](#manual-HAdd___mk)3 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) x [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 9[)]](#manual-HAdd___mk)h:p [(]](#manual-HAdd___mk)x [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 7[)]](#manual-HAdd___mk)⊢ p [(]](#manual-HAdd___mk)6 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) x [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 1[)]](#manual-HAdd___mk)` yields a goal in which the hypothesis `h` has been simplified:

## The Simplifier — 15.2. Rewrite Rules {#manual-the-simplifier-152-rewrite-rules}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The-Simplifier/Rewrite-Rules/

The simplifier has three kinds of rewrite rules:

Declarations to unfold
:   The simplifier will only unfold [reducible]](#manual---tech-term-Reducible) definitions by default.
    However, a rewrite rule can be added for any [semireducible]](#manual---tech-term-Semireducible) or [irreducible]](#manual---tech-term-Irreducible) definition that causes the simplifier to unfold it as well.
    When the simplifier is running in definitional mode (`[dsimp]](#manual-dsimp)` and its variants), definition unfolding only replaces the defined name with its value; otherwise, it also uses the equational lemmas produced by the equation compiler.

Equational lemmas
:   The simplifier can treat equality proofs as rewrite rules, in which case the left side of the equality will be replaced with the right. These equational lemmas may have any number of parameters. The simplifier instantiates parameters to make the left side of the equality match the goal, and it performs a proof search to instantiate any additional parameters.

Simplification procedures
:   The simplifier supports simplification procedures, known as *simprocs*, that use Lean metaprogramming to perform rewrites that can't be efficiently specified using equations. Lean includes simprocs for the most important operations on built-in types.

Due to [propositional extensionality]](#manual---tech-term-Extensionality), equational lemmas can rewrite propositions to simpler, logically equivalent propositions.
When the simplifier rewrites a proof goal to `[True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro)`, it automatically closes it.
As a special case of equational lemmas, propositions other than equality can be tagged as rewrite rules
They are preprocessed into rules that rewrite the proposition to `[True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro)`.

**Example: Rewriting Propositions**

When asked to simplify an equality of pairs:

α:Typeβ:Typew:αy:αx:βz:β⊢ [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)w[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) x[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)y[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) z[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)

`[simp]](#manual-simp)α:Typeβ:Typew:αy:αx:βz:β⊢ w [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) y [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) z` yields a conjunction of equalities:

α:Typeβ:Typew:αy:αx:βz:β⊢ w [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) y [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) z

The default simp set contains `Prod.mk.injEq`, which shows the equivalence of the two statements:

```lean
Prod.mk.injEq.{u, v} {α : Type u} {β : Type v} (fst : α) (snd : β) :
∀ (fst_1 : α) (snd_1 : β),
((fst, snd) = (fst_1, snd_1)) = (fst = fst_1 ∧ snd = snd_1)
```

In addition to rewrite rules, `[simp]](#manual-simp)` has a number of built-in reduction rules, [controlled by the `config` parameter](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The-Simplifier/Configuring-Simplification/#simp-config).
Even when the simp set is empty, `[simp]](#manual-simp)` can replace `let`-bound variables with their values, reduce [`match`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match) expressions whose [discriminants]](#manual---tech-term-match-discriminants) are constructor applications, reduce structure projections applied to constructors, or apply lambdas to their arguments.

---



## The Simplifier — 15.3. Simp sets {#manual-the-simplifier-153-simp-sets}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The-Simplifier/Simp-sets/

A collection of rules used by the simplifier is called a *simp set*.
A simp set is specified in terms of modifications from a *default simp set*.
These modifications can include adding rules, removing rules, or adding a set of rules.
The `only` modifier to the `[simp]](#manual-simp)` tactic causes it to start with an empty simp set, rather than the default one.
Rules are added to the default simp set using the `simp` attribute.

attributeRegistering `simp` Lemmas

The `simp` attribute adds a declaration to the default simp set.
If the declaration is a definition, the definition is marked for unfolding; if it is a theorem, then the theorem is registered as a rewrite rule.

```lean
attr ::= ...
    | simp
```

```lean
attr ::= ...
    | simp ↑ prio?
```

```lean
attr ::= ...
    | simp ↓ prio?
```

```lean
attr ::= ...
    | simp prio
```

*Custom simp sets* are created with `[registerSimpAttr]](#manual-Lean___Meta___registerSimpAttr)`, which must be run during [initialization]](#manual---tech-term-initialization) by placing it in an `initialize` block.
As a side effect, it creates a new attribute with the same interface as `simp` that adds rules to the custom simp set.
The returned value is a `[SimpExtension]](#manual-Lean___Meta___SimpExtension)`, which can be used to programmatically access the contents of the custom simp set.
The `[simp]](#manual-simp)` tactics can be instructed to use the new simp set by including its attribute name in the rule list.

def

```lean
[Lean.Meta.registerSimpAttr]](#manual-Lean___Meta___registerSimpAttr) (attrName : Lean.Name) (attrDescr : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray))
  (ref : Lean.Name := by exact decl_name%) : [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [Lean.Meta.SimpExtension]](#manual-Lean___Meta___SimpExtension)



[Lean.Meta.registerSimpAttr]](#manual-Lean___Meta___registerSimpAttr)
  (attrName : Lean.Name)
  (attrDescr : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray))
  (ref : Lean.Name := by
    exact decl_name%) :
  [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [Lean.Meta.SimpExtension]](#manual-Lean___Meta___SimpExtension)
```

Registers the given name as a custom simp set. Applying the name as an attribute to a name adds it
to the simp set, and using the name as a parameter to the `[simp]](#manual-simp)` tactic causes `[simp]](#manual-simp)` to use the
included lemmas.

Custom simp sets must be registered during [initialization](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0-rc1/find/?domain=Verso.Genre.Manual.section&name=initialization).

The description should be a short, singular noun phrase that describes the contents of the custom
simp set.

def

```lean
[Lean.Meta.SimpExtension]](#manual-Lean___Meta___SimpExtension) : Type



[Lean.Meta.SimpExtension]](#manual-Lean___Meta___SimpExtension) : Type
```

The environment extension that contains a simp set, returned by `[Lean.Meta.registerSimpAttr]](#manual-Lean___Meta___registerSimpAttr)`.

Use the simp set's attribute or `Lean.Meta.addSimpTheorem` to add theorems to the simp set. Use
`Lean.Meta.SimpExtension.getTheorems` to get the contents.

## The Simplifier — 15.4. Simp Normal Forms {#manual-the-simplifier-154-simp-normal-forms}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The-Simplifier/Simp-Normal-Forms/

The default [simp set]](#manual---tech-term-simp-set) contains all the theorems and simplification procedures marked with the `simp` attribute.
The *simp normal form* of an expression is the result of applying the default simp set via the `[simp]](#manual-simp)` tactic until no more rules can be applied.
When an expression is in simp normal form, it is as reduced as possible according to the default simp set, often making it easier to work with in proofs.

The `[simp]](#manual-simp)` tactic **does not guarantee confluence**, which means that the simp normal form of an expression may depend on the order in which the elements of the default simp set are applied.
The order in which the rules are applied can be changed by assigning priorities when setting the `simp` attribute.

When designing a Lean library, it's important to think about what the appropriate simp normal form for the various combinations of the library's operators is.
This can serve as a guide when selecting which rules the library should add to the default simp set.
In particular, the right-hand side of simp lemmas should be in simp normal form; this helps ensure that simplification terminates.
Additionally, each concept in the library should be expressed through one simp normal form, even if there are multiple equivalent ways to state it.
If a concept is stated in two different ways in different simp lemmas, then some desired simplifications may not occur because the simplifier does not connect them.

Even though simplification doesn't need to be confluent, striving for confluence is helpful because it makes the library more predictable and tends to reveal missing or poorly chosen simp lemmas.
The default simp set is as much a part of a library's interface as the type signatures of the constants that it exports.

Libraries should not add rules to the default simp set that don't mention at least one constant defined in the library.
Otherwise, importing a library could change the behavior of `[simp]](#manual-simp)` for some unrelated library.
If a library relies on additional simplification rules for definitions or declarations from other libraries, please create a custom simp set and either instruct users to use it or provide a dedicated tactic.

## The Simplifier — 15.5. Terminal vs Non-Terminal Positions {#manual-the-simplifier-155-terminal-vs-non-terminal-positions}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The-Simplifier/Terminal-vs-Non-Terminal-Positions/

To write maintainable proofs, avoid using `[simp]](#manual-simp)` without [`only`]](#manual-simp) unless it closes the goal.
Such uses of `[simp]](#manual-simp)` that do not close a goal are referred to as *non-terminal simps*.
This is because additions to the default simp set may make `[simp]](#manual-simp)` more powerful or just cause it to select a different sequence of rewrites and arrive at a different simp normal form.
When [`only`]](#manual-simp) is specified, additional lemmas will not affect that invocation of the tactic.
In practice, terminal uses of `[simp]](#manual-simp)` are not nearly as likely to be broken by the addition of new simp lemmas, and when they are, it's easier to understand the issue and fix it.

When working in non-terminal positions, `[simp?]](#manual-simp___-next)` (or one of the other simplification tactics with `?` in their names) can be used to generate an appropriate invocation with [`only`]](#manual-simp).
Just as `[apply?]](#manual-apply___)` or `[rw?]](#manual-rw___)` suggest the use of relevant lemmas, `[simp?]](#manual-simp___-next)` suggests an invocation of `[simp]](#manual-simp)` with a minimal simp set that was used to reach the normal form.

**Example: Using simp?**

The non-terminal `[simp?]](#manual-simp___-next)` in this proof suggests a smaller `[simp]](#manual-simp)` with [`only`]](#manual-simp):

```lean
example (xs : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit)) : xs.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size) = 2 → xs = #[(), ()] := byxs:[Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit)⊢ xs.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 2 → xs [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [#[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___toArray)[(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit___unit)[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit___unit)[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit___unit)[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit___unit)[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___toArray)
[intros]](#manual-intros)xs:[Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit)a✝:xs.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 2⊢ xs [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [#[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___toArray)[(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit___unit)[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit___unit)[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit___unit)[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit___unit)[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___toArray)
[ext]](#manual-ext)h₁xs:[Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit)a✝:xs.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 2⊢ xs.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [#[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___toArray)[(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit___unit)[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit___unit)[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit___unit)[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit___unit)[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___toArray).[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size)
[simp?]](#manual-simp___-next)h₁xs:[Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit)a✝:xs.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 2⊢ xs.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 2
[assumption]](#manual-assumption)All goals completed! 🐙
```

The suggested rewrite is:

```lean
Try this:
  [apply] simp only [List.size_toArray, List.length_cons, List.length_nil, Nat.zero_add, Nat.reduceAdd]
```

which results in the more maintainable proof:

## The Simplifier — 15.6. Configuring Simplification {#manual-the-simplifier-156-configuring-simplification}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The-Simplifier/Configuring-Simplification/

`[simp]](#manual-simp)` is primarily configured via a configuration parameter, passed as a named argument called `config`.

structure

```lean
[Lean.Meta.Simp.Config]](#manual-Lean___Meta___Simp___Config___mk) : Type



[Lean.Meta.Simp.Config]](#manual-Lean___Meta___Simp___Config___mk) : Type
```

The configuration for `[simp]](#manual-simp)`.
Passed to `[simp]](#manual-simp)` using, for example, the `[simp]](#manual-simp) +contextual` or `[simp]](#manual-simp) (maxSteps := 100000)` syntax.

See also `[Lean.Meta.Simp.neutralConfig]](#manual-Lean___Meta___Simp___neutralConfig)` and `[Lean.Meta.DSimp.Config]](#manual-Lean___Meta___DSimp___Config___mk)`.

Constructor

```lean
[Lean.Meta.Simp.Config.mk]](#manual-Lean___Meta___Simp___Config___mk)
```

Fields

```lean
maxSteps : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

The maximum number of subexpressions to visit when performing simplification.
The default is 100000.

```lean
maxDischargeDepth : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

When simp discharges side conditions for conditional lemmas, it can recursively apply simplification.
The `maxDischargeDepth` (default: 2) is the maximum recursion depth when recursively applying simplification to side conditions.

```lean
contextual : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

When `contextual` is true (default: `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`) and simplification encounters an implication `p → q`
it includes `p` as an additional simp lemma when simplifying `q`.

```lean
memoize : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

When true (default: `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`) then the simplifier caches the result of simplifying each sub-expression, if possible.

```lean
singlePass : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

When `singlePass` is `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` (default: `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`), the simplifier runs through a single round of simplification,
which consists of running pre-methods, recursing using congruence lemmas, and then running post-methods.
Otherwise, when it is `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`, it iteratively applies this simplification procedure.

```lean
zeta : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

When `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` (default: `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`), performs zeta reduction of `[let]](#manual-let)` and `[have]](#manual-have)` expressions.
That is, `let x := v; e[x]` reduces to `e[v]`.
If `zetaHave` is `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` then `[have]](#manual-have)` expressions are not zeta reduced.
See also `zetaDelta`.

```lean
beta : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

When `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` (default: `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`), performs beta reduction of applications of `fun` expressions.
That is, `(fun x => e[x]) v` reduces to `e[v]`.

```lean
eta : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

TODO (currently unimplemented). When `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` (default: `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`), performs eta reduction for `fun` expressions.
That is, `(fun x => f x)` reduces to `f`.

```lean
etaStruct : Lean.Meta.EtaStructMode
```

Configures how to determine definitional equality between two structure instances.
See documentation for `Lean.Meta.EtaStructMode`.

```lean
iota : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

When `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` (default: `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`), reduces `[match]](#manual-match)` expressions applied to constructors.

```lean
proj : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

When `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` (default: `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`), reduces projections of structure constructors.

```lean
decide : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

When `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` (default: `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`), rewrites a proposition `p` to `[True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro)` or `[False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)` by inferring
a `[Decidable]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse) p` instance and reducing it.

```lean
arith : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

When `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` (default: `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`), simplifies simple arithmetic expressions.

```lean
autoUnfold : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

When `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` (default: `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`), unfolds applications of functions defined by pattern matching, when one of the patterns applies.
This can be enabled using the `[simp!]](#manual-simp___)` syntax.

```lean
dsimp : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

When `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` (default: `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`) then switches to `dsimp` on dependent arguments
if there is no congruence theorem that would allow `[simp]](#manual-simp)` to visit them.
When `dsimp` is `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`, then the argument is not visited.

```lean
failIfUnchanged : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

If `failIfUnchanged` is `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` (default: `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`), then calls to `[simp]](#manual-simp)`, `dsimp`, or `[simp_all]](#manual-simp_all)`
will fail if they do not make progress.

```lean
ground : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

If `ground` is `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` (default: `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`), then ground terms are reduced.
A term is ground when it does not contain free or meta variables.
Reduction is interrupted at a function application `f ...` if `f` is marked to not be unfolded.
Ground term reduction applies `@[seval]` lemmas.

```lean
unfoldPartialApp : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

If `unfoldPartialApp` is `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` (default: `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`), then calls to `[simp]](#manual-simp)`, `dsimp`, or `[simp_all]](#manual-simp_all)`
will unfold even partial applications of `f` when we request `f` to be unfolded.

```lean
zetaDelta : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

When `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` (default: `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`), local definitions are unfolded.
That is, given a local context containing `x : t := e`, then the free variable `x` reduces to `e`.
Otherwise, `x` must be provided as a `[simp]](#manual-simp)` argument.

```lean
index : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

When `index` (default : `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`) is `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`, `[simp]](#manual-simp)` will only use the root symbol
to find candidate `[simp]](#manual-simp)` theorems. It approximates Lean 3 `[simp]](#manual-simp)` behavior.

```lean
implicitDefEqProofs : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

If `implicitDefEqProofs := true`, `[simp]](#manual-simp)` does not create proof terms when the
input and output terms are definitionally equal.

```lean
zetaUnused : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

When `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` (default : `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`), then `[simp]](#manual-simp)` removes unused `[let]](#manual-let)` and `[have]](#manual-have)` expressions:
`let x := v; e` simplifies to `e` when `x` does not occur in `e`.
This option takes precedence over `zeta` and `zetaHave`.

```lean
catchRuntime : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

When `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` (default : `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`), then `[simp]](#manual-simp)` catches runtime exceptions and
converts them into `[simp]](#manual-simp)` exceptions.

```lean
zetaHave : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

When `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` (default: `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`), then disables zeta reduction of `[have]](#manual-have)` expressions.
If `zeta` is `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`, then this option has no effect.
Unused `[have]](#manual-have)`s are still removed if `zeta` or `zetaUnused` are true.

```lean
letToHave : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

When `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` (default : `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`), then `[simp]](#manual-simp)` will attempt to transform `[let]](#manual-let)`s into `[have]](#manual-have)`s
if they are non-dependent. This only applies when `zeta := false`.

```lean
congrConsts : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

When `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` (default: `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`), `[simp]](#manual-simp)` tries to realize constant `f.congr_simp`
when constructing an auxiliary congruence proof for `f`.
This option exists because the termination prover uses `[simp]](#manual-simp)` and `withoutModifyingEnv`
while constructing the termination proof. Thus, any constant realized by `[simp]](#manual-simp)`
is deleted.

```lean
bitVecOfNat : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

## The Simplifier — 15.7. Simplification vs Rewriting {#manual-the-simplifier-157-simplification-vs-rewriting}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The-Simplifier/Simplification-vs-Rewriting/

Both `[simp]](#manual-simp)` and `[rw]](#manual-rw)`/`[rewrite]](#manual-rewrite)` use equational lemmas to replace parts of terms with equivalent alternatives.
Their intended uses and their rewriting strategies differ, however.
Tactics in the `[simp]](#manual-simp)` family are primarily used to reformulate a problem in a standardized way, making it more amenable to both human understanding and further automation.
In particular, simplification should never render an otherwise-provable goal impossible.
Tactics in the `[rw]](#manual-rw)` family are primarily used to apply hand-selected transformations that do not always preserve provability nor place terms in standardized forms.
These different emphases are reflected in the differences of behavior between the two families of tactics.

The `[simp]](#manual-simp)` tactics primarily rewrite from the inside out.
The smallest possible expressions are simplified first so that they can unlock further simplification opportunities for the surrounding expressions.
The `[rw]](#manual-rw)` tactics select the leftmost outermost subterm that matches the pattern, rewriting it a single time.
Both tactics allow their strategy to be overridden: when adding a lemma to a simp set, the `↓` modifier causes it to be applied prior to the simplification of subterms, and the `[occs]](#manual-Lean___Meta___Rewrite___Config___mk)` field of `[rw]](#manual-rw)`'s configuration parameter allows a different occurrence to be selected, either via a whitelist or a blacklist.

## The grind tactic {#manual-the-grind-tactic}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/

## 16. The `grind` tactic

## Tutorials

- [Using `grind` for Ordered Maps](https://lean-lang.org/doc/tutorials/4.34.0-rc1//#grind-index-map)

The `[grind]](#manual-grind)` tactic uses techniques inspired by modern SMT solvers to automatically construct proofs.
It produces proofs by incrementally collecting sets of facts, deriving new facts from the existing ones using a set of cooperating techniques.
Behind the scenes, all proofs are by contradiction, so there is no operational distinction between the expected conclusion and the premises; `[grind]](#manual-grind)` always attempts to derive a contradiction.

Picture a virtual whiteboard.
Every time `[grind]](#manual-grind)` discovers a new equality, inequality, or Boolean literal it writes that fact on the board, merges equivalent terms into buckets, and invites each engine to read from—and add back to—the shared whiteboard.
In particular, because all true propositions are equal to `[True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro)` and all false propositions are equal to `[False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)`, `[grind]](#manual-grind)` tracks a set of known facts as part of tracking equivalence classes.

The cooperating engines are:

- [congruence closure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Congruence-Closure/#--tech-term-Congruence-closure),
- [constraint propagation](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Constraint-Propagation/#--tech-term-Constraint-propagation),
- [E‑matching](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/E___matching/#--tech-term-E-matching),
- guided [case analysis](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Case-Analysis/#grind-split), and
- a suite of satellite theory solvers, including both [linear integer arithmetic](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Linear-Integer-Arithmetic/#cutsat) and [commutative rings](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Algebraic-Solver-_LPAR_Commutative-Rings___-Fields_RPAR_/#grind-ring).

Like other tactics, `[grind]](#manual-grind)` produces ordinary Lean proof terms for every fact it adds.
Lean’s standard library is already annotated with `@[grind]` attributes, so common lemmas are discovered automatically.

`[grind]](#manual-grind)` is **not** designed for goals whose search space explodes combinatorially—think large‑`n` pigeonhole instances, graph‑coloring reductions, high‑order N‑queens boards, or a 200‑variable Sudoku encoded as Boolean constraints.
Such encodings require thousands (or millions) of case‑splits that overwhelm `[grind]](#manual-grind)`’s branching search.
For bit‑level or pure Boolean combinatorial problems, use `[bv_decide]](#manual-bv_decide)`. The `[bv_decide]](#manual-bv_decide)` tactic calls a state‑of‑the‑art SAT solver (e.g. CaDiCaL or Kissat) and then returns a compact, machine‑checkable certificate.
All heavy search happens outside Lean; the certificate is replayed and verified inside Lean, so trust is preserved (verification time scales with certificate size).

**Example: Congruence Closure**

This proof succeeds instantly using [congruence closure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Congruence-Closure/#--tech-term-Congruence-closure), which discovers sets of equal terms.

```lean
example (a b c : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (h₁ : a = b) (h₂ : b = c) :
a = c := bya:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)b:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)c:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h₁:a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) bh₂:b [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) c⊢ a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) c
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

**Example: Finite-Field Reasoning**

Arithmetic operations on `[Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk)` overflow, wrapping around to `0` when the result would be outside the bound.
`[grind]](#manual-grind)` can use this fact to prove theorems such as this:

```lean
example (x y : [Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) 11) :
x ^ 2 * y = 1 →
x * y ^ 2 = y →
y * x = 1 := byx:[Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) 11y:[Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) 11⊢ x [^]](#manual-HPow___mk) 2 [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) y [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 1 → x [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) y [^]](#manual-HPow___mk) 2 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) y → y [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 1
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

## The grind tactic — 16.1. Error Messages {#manual-the-grind-tactic-161-error-messages}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Error-Messages/

When `[grind]](#manual-grind)` fails, it prints the remaining subgoal followed by all the information returned by its subsystems—the contents of the “shared whiteboard.”
In particular, it presents equivalence classes of terms that it has determined to be equal.
The two largest classes are shown as `True propositions` and `False propositions`, listing every literal currently known to be provable or refutable.
Inspect these lists to spot missing facts or contradictory assumptions.

---



## The grind tactic — 16.2. Minimizing `grind` calls {#manual-the-grind-tactic-162-minimizing-calls}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Minimizing--grind--calls/

The `grind only [...]` tactic invokes `[grind]](#manual-grind)` with a limited set of theorems, which can improve performance.
Calls to `grind only` can be conveniently constructed using `[grind?]](#manual-grind___)`, which automatically records the theorems used by `[grind]](#manual-grind)` and suggests a suitable `grind only`.

These theorems will typically include a symbol prefix such as `=`, `←`, or `→`, indicating the
pattern that triggered the instantiation. See the [section on E-matching](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/E___matching/#e-matching) for details.
Some theorems may be labelled with a `usr` prefix, which indicates that a custom pattern was used.

---



## The grind tactic — 16.3. Congruence Closure {#manual-the-grind-tactic-163-congruence-closure}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Congruence-Closure/

*Congruence closure* maintains equivalence classes of terms under the reflexive, symmetric, and transitive closure of “is equal to” *and* the rule that equal arguments yield equal function results.
Formally, if `a = a'` and `b = b'`, then `f a b = f a' b'` is added.
The algorithm merges equivalence classes until a fixed point is reached.
If a contradiction is discovered, then the goal can be closed immediately.

Using the analogy of the shared whiteboard:

1. Every hypothesis `h : t₁ = t₂` writes a line connecting `t₁` and `t₂`.
2. Whenever two terms are connected by one or more lines, they're considered to be equal.
   Soon, whole constellations (`f a`, `g (f a)`, …) are connected.
3. If two different constructors of the same inductive type are connected by one or more lines, then a contradiction is discovered and the goal is closed.
   For example, equating `[True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro)` and `[False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)` or `[none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` and `[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) 1` would be a contradiction.

**Example: Congruence Closure**

This theorem is proved using congruence closure:

```lean
example {α} (f g : α → α) (x y : α)
(h₁ : x = y) (h₂ : f y = g y) :
f x = g x := byα:Sort u_1f:α → αg:α → αx:αy:αh₁:x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) yh₂:f y [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) g y⊢ f x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) g x
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

Initially, `f y`, `g y`, `x`, and `y` are in separate equivalence classes.
The congruence closure engine uses `h₁` to merge `x` and `y`, after which the equivalence classes are `{x, y}`, `f y`, and `g y`.
Next, `h₂` is used to merge `f y` and `g y`, after which the classes are `{x, y}` and `{f y, g y}`.
This is sufficient to prove that `f x = g x`, because `y` and `x` are in the same class.

Similar reasoning is used for constructors:

```lean
example (a b c : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (h : a = b) : (a, c) = (b, c) := bya:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)b:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)c:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h:a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) b⊢ [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)a[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) c[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)b[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) c[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

Because the pair constructor `[Prod.mk](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)` obeys congruence, the tuples become equal as soon as `a` and `b` are placed in the same class.

### 16.3.1. Congruence Closure vs. Simplification {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--The--grind--tactic--Congruence-Closure--Congruence-Closure-vs___-Simplification}

Congruence closure is a fundamentally different operation from simplification:

- `[simp]](#manual-simp)` *rewrites* a goal, replacing occurrences of `t₁` with `t₂` as soon as it sees `h : t₁ = t₂`.
  The rewrite is directional and destructive.
- `[grind]](#manual-grind)` *accumulates* equalities bidirectionally. No term is rewritten; instead, both representatives live in the same class. All other engines ([E‑matching](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/E___matching/#--tech-term-E-matching), theory solvers, [propagation](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Constraint-Propagation/#--tech-term-Constraint-propagation)) can query these classes and add new facts, then the closure updates incrementally.

This makes congruence closure especially robust in the presence of symmetrical reasoning, mutual recursion, and large nestings of constructors where rewriting would duplicate work.

---



## The grind tactic — 16.4. Constraint Propagation {#manual-the-grind-tactic-164-constraint-propagation}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Constraint-Propagation/

Constraint propagation works on the `[True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro)` and `[False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)` buckets of the whiteboard.
Whenever a term is added to one of those buckets, `[grind]](#manual-grind)` fires dozens of small *forward rules* that derive further information from its logical consequences:

Boolean connectives
:   The truth tables of the Boolean connectives can be used to derive further true and false facts.
    For example:

    - If `A` is `[True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro)`, then `A ∨ B` becomes `[True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro)`.
    - If `A ∧ B` is `[True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro)`, then both `A` and `B` become `[True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro)`.
    - If `A ∧ B` is `[False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)`, at least one of `A`, `B` becomes `[False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)`.

Inductive Types
:   If terms formed by applications of two different constructors of the same [inductive type]](#manual---tech-term-Inductive-types) (e.g. `[none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` and `[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`) are placed in the same equivalence class, a contradiction is derived.
    If two terms formed by applications of the same constructor are placed in the same equivalence class, then their arguments are also made equal.

Projections
:   From `h : (x, y) = (x', y')` we derive `x = x'` and `y = y'`.

Casts
:   Any term `[cast](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#cast) h a : β` is equated with `a : α` immediately (using [heterogeneous equality](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#--tech-term-Heterogeneous-equality)).

Reduction
:   Definitional reduction is propagated, so `(a, b).[1](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)` is equated with `a`.

Below is a *representative slice* of the propagators that demonstrates their overall style.
Each follows the same skeleton.

1. It inspect the truth value of sub‑expressions.
2. If further facts can be derived, it either equates terms (connecting them on the metaphorical whiteboard) using (`pushEq`), or it indicates truth values using (`pushEqTrue` / `pushEqFalse`).
   These steps produce proof terms using internal helper lemmas such as `Grind.and_eq_of_eq_true_left`.
3. If a contradiction arises, the goal is closed using (`closeGoal`).

*Upward propagation* derives facts about a term from facts about sub-terms, while *downward propagation* derives facts about sub-terms from facts about a term.

```lean
/-- Propagate equalities *upwards* for conjunctions. -/
builtin_grind_propagator propagateAndUp ↑And := fun e => [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
let_expr [And](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) a b := e | return ()
if (← isEqTrue a) then
-- a = True ⇒ (a ∧ b) = b
pushEq e b <|
mkApp3 (mkConst ``Grind.and_eq_of_eq_true_left)
a b (← mkEqTrueProof a)
else if (← isEqTrue b) then
-- b = True ⇒ (a ∧ b) = a
pushEq e a <|
mkApp3 (mkConst ``Grind.and_eq_of_eq_true_right)
a b (← mkEqTrueProof b)
else if (← isEqFalse a) then
-- a = False ⇒ (a ∧ b) = False
pushEqFalse e <|
mkApp3 (mkConst ``Grind.and_eq_of_eq_false_left)
a b (← mkEqFalseProof a)
else if (← isEqFalse b) then
-- b = False ⇒ (a ∧ b) = False
pushEqFalse e <|
mkApp3 (mkConst ``Grind.and_eq_of_eq_false_right)
a b (← mkEqFalseProof b)
/--
Truth flows *down* when the whole `And` is proven `True`.
-/
builtin_grind_propagator propagateAndDown ↓And :=
fun e => [do](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do)
if (← isEqTrue e) then
let_expr [And](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) a b := e | return ()
let h ← mkEqTrueProof e
-- (a ∧ b) = True ⇒ a = True
pushEqTrue a <| mkApp3
(mkConst ``Grind.eq_true_of_and_eq_true_left) a b h
-- (a ∧ b) = True ⇒ b = True
pushEqTrue b <| mkApp3
(mkConst ``Grind.eq_true_of_and_eq_true_right) a b h
```

Other frequently‑triggered propagators follow the same pattern:

| Propagator | Handles | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `propagateOrUp` / `propagateOrDown` | `A ∨ B` | Uses the truth table for disjunction to derive further truth values |
| `propagateNotUp` / `propagateNotDown` | `¬ A` | Ensures that `¬ A` and `A` have opposite truth values |
| `propagateEqUp` / `propagateEqDown` | `a = b` | Bridges Booleans, detects constructor clash |
| `propagateIte` / `propagateDIte` | `ite` / `dite` | Equates the term with the chosen branch once the condition's truth value is known |
| `propagateEtaStruct` | Values of structures tagged `[grind ext]` | Generates η‑expansion `a = ⟨a.1, …⟩` |

Many specialized variants for `[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` mirror these rules exactly (e.g. `propagateBoolAndUp`).

### 16.4.1. Propagation‑Only Examples {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--The--grind--tactic--Constraint-Propagation--Propagation___Only-Examples}

These goals are closed **purely** by constraint propagation—no case splits, no theory solvers:

```lean
-- Boolean connective: a && !a is always false.
example (a : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) : (a && !a) = [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) := bya:[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)⊢ [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___and)a [&&](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___and) [!](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___not)a[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___and) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
-- Conditional (ite):
-- once the condition is true, ite picks the 'then' branch.
example (c : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) (t e : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (h : c = [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) :
([if]](#manual-termIfThenElse) c [then]](#manual-termIfThenElse) t [else]](#manual-termIfThenElse) e) = t := byc:[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)t:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)e:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h:c [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)⊢ (if c [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) then t else e) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) t
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
-- Negation propagates truth downwards.
example (a : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) (h : (!a) = [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) : a = [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) := bya:[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)h:[(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___not)[!](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___not)a[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___not) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)⊢ a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

These snippets run instantly because the relevant propagators (`propagateBoolAndUp`, `propagateIte`, `propagateBoolNotDown`) fire as soon as the hypotheses are internalized.
Setting the option `trace.grind.eqc` to `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` causes `[grind]](#manual-grind)` to print a line every time two equivalence classes merge, which is handy for seeing propagation in action.

The set of propagation rules is expanded and refined over time, so the InfoView will show increasingly rich `[True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro)` and `[False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)` buckets.
The full equivalence classes are displayed automatically *only when `[grind]](#manual-grind)` fails*, and only for the first subgoal that it could not close—use this output to inspect missing facts and understand why the subgoal remains open.

**Example: Identifying Missing Facts**

In this example, `[grind]](#manual-grind)` fails:

```lean
example :
x = y ∧ y = z →
w = x ∨ w = v →
w = z := byα✝:Sort u_1x:α✝y:α✝z:α✝w:α✝v:α✝⊢ x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) y [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) y [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) z → w [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) x [∨](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) w [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) v → w [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) z
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

The resulting error message includes the identified equivalence classes along with the true and false propositions:

```lean
`grind` failed
grindα:Sort u_1x y z w v:αleft:x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) yright:y [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) zh_1:w [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) x [∨](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) w [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) vh_2:[¬](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)w [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) z⊢ [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)
[grind] Goal diagnostics

- [facts] Asserted facts
  - [prop] x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) y
  - [prop] y [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) z
  - [prop] w [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) x [∨](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) w [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) v
  - [prop] [¬](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)w [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) z
- [eqc] True propositions
  - [prop] w [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) x [∨](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) w [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) v
  - [prop] w [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) v
- [eqc] False propositions
  - [prop] w [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) x
  - [prop] w [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) z
- [eqc] Equivalence classes
  - [eqc] {x, y, z}
  - [eqc] {w, v}
```

Both `x = y` and `y = z` were discovered by constraint propagation from the `x = y ∧ y = z` premise.
In this proof, `[grind]](#manual-grind)` performed a case split on `w = x ∨ w = v`.
In the second branch, it could not place `w` and `z` in the same equivalence class.

---



## The grind tactic — 16.5. Case Analysis {#manual-the-grind-tactic-165-case-analysis}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Case-Analysis/

In addition to congruence closure and constraint propagation, `[grind]](#manual-grind)` performs case analysis.
During case analysis, `[grind]](#manual-grind)` considers each possible way that a term could have been built, or each possible value of a particular term, in a manner similar to the `[cases]](#manual-cases)` and `[split]](#manual-split)` tactics.
This case analysis is not exhaustive: `[grind]](#manual-grind)` only recursively splits cases up to a configured depth limit, and configuration options and annotations control which terms are candidates for splitting.

### 16.5.1. Selection Heuristics {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--The--grind--tactic--Case-Analysis--Selection-Heuristics}

`[grind]](#manual-grind)` decides which sub‑term to split on by combining three sources of signal:

Structural flags
:   These configuration flags determine whether `[grind]](#manual-grind)` performs certain case splits:

    `splitIte` (default `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`)
    :   Every `if`-term should be split, as if by the `[split]](#manual-split)` tactic.

    `splitMatch` (default `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`)
    :   Every [`match`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match)-term should be split, as if by the `[split]](#manual-split)` tactic.

    `splitImp` (default `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`)
    :   Hypotheses of the form `A → B` whose antecedent `A` is **propositional** are split by considering all possibilities for `A`.
        Arithmetic antecedents are special‑cased: if `A` is an arithmetic literal (that is, a proposition formed by operators such as `≤`, `=`, `¬`, `[Dvd]](#manual-Dvd___mk)`, …) then `[grind]](#manual-grind)` will split *even when `splitImp := false`* so the integer solver can propagate facts.

Global limits
:   The `[grind]](#manual-grind)` option `splits := n` caps the depth of the search tree.
    Once a branch performs `n` splits `[grind]](#manual-grind)` stops splitting further in that branch; if the branch cannot be closed it reports that the split threshold has been reached.

Manual annotations
:   Inductive predicates or structures may be tagged with the `grind cases` attribute.
    `[grind]](#manual-grind)` treats every instance of that predicate as a candidate for splitting.

attributeCase Analysis

```lean
attr ::= ...
    | grind cases
```

The `[cases]](#manual-cases)` modifier marks inductively-defined predicates as suitable for case splitting.

attributeEager Case Analysis

```lean
attr ::= ...
    | grind cases eager
```

The `[cases]](#manual-cases) eager` modifier marks inductively-defined predicates as suitable for case splitting,
and instructs `[grind]](#manual-grind)` to perform it eagerly while preprocessing hypotheses.

**Example: Splitting Conditional Expressions**

In this example, `[grind]](#manual-grind)` proves the theorem by considering both cases for the conditional:

```lean
example (c : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) (x y : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
(h : ([if]](#manual-termIfThenElse) c [then]](#manual-termIfThenElse) x [else]](#manual-termIfThenElse) y) = 0) :
x = 0 ∨ y = 0 := byc:[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)x:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)y:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h:(if c [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) then x else y) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0⊢ x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0 [∨](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) y [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

**Example: Splitting Predicates**

`[Not30]](#manual-Not30-_LPAR_in-Splitting-Predicates_RPAR_)` is a somewhat verbose way to state that a number is not `30`:

```lean
inductive Not30 : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Prop where
| gt : x > 30 → [Not30]](#manual-Not30-_LPAR_in-Splitting-Predicates_RPAR_) x
| lt : x < 30 → [Not30]](#manual-Not30-_LPAR_in-Splitting-Predicates_RPAR_) x
```

By default, `[grind]](#manual-grind)` cannot show that `[Not30]](#manual-Not30-_LPAR_in-Splitting-Predicates_RPAR_)` implies that a number is, in fact, not `30`:

```lean
example : [Not30]](#manual-Not30-_LPAR_in-Splitting-Predicates_RPAR_) n → n ≠ 30 := byn:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ [Not30]](#manual-Not30-_LPAR_in-Splitting-Predicates_RPAR_) n → n ≠ 30 [grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

This is because `[grind]](#manual-grind)` does not consider both cases for `[Not30]](#manual-Not30-_LPAR_in-Splitting-Predicates_RPAR_)`

| zero : [Even]](#manual-Even___zero-next) 0
| step : [Even]](#manual-Even___zero-next) n → [Even]](#manual-Even___zero-next) (n + 2)
