### 16.5.2. Performance {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--The--grind--tactic--Case-Analysis--Performance}

Case analysis is powerful, but computationally expensive: each level of case splitting multiplies the search space.
It's important to be judicious and not perform unnecessary splits.
In particular:

- Increase `splits` **only** when the goal genuinely needs deeper branching; each extra level multiplies the search space.
- Disable `splitMatch` when large pattern‑matching definitions explode the tree; this can be observed by setting the `[trace.grind.split]](#manual-trace___grind___split)`.
- Flags can be combined, e.g. `by grind -splitMatch (splits := 10) +splitImp`.
- The `grind cases` attribute is [*scoped*]](#manual-scoped-attributes).
  The modifiers `local` and `scoped` restrict extra splitting to a section or namespace.

option

```lean
trace.grind.split
```

Default value: `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`

enable/disable tracing for the given module and submodules

---



## The grind tactic — 16.6. E‑matching {#manual-the-grind-tactic-166-ematching}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/E___matching/

*E-matching* is a procedure for efficiently instantiating quantified theorem statements with ground terms.
It is widely employed in SMT solvers, and `[grind]](#manual-grind)` uses it to instantiate theorems efficiently.
It is especially effective when combined with [congruence closure]](#manual---tech-term-Congruence-closure), enabling `[grind]](#manual-grind)` to discover non-obvious consequences of equalities and annotated theorems automatically.

E-matching adds new facts to the metaphorical whiteboard, based on an index of theorems.
When the whiteboard contains terms that match the index, the E-matching engine instantiates the corresponding theorems, and the resulting terms can feed further rounds of [congruence closure]](#manual---tech-term-Congruence-closure), [constraint propagation]](#manual---tech-term-Constraint-propagation), and theory-specific solvers.
Each fact added to the whiteboard by E-matching is referred to as an *instance*.
Annotating theorems for E-matching, thus adding them to the index, is essential for enabling `[grind]](#manual-grind)` to make effective use of a library.

In addition to user-specified theorems, `[grind]](#manual-grind)` uses automatically generated equations for [`match`]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match)-expressions as E-matching theorems.
Behind the scenes, the [elaborator]](#manual---tech-term-elaborator) generates auxiliary functions that implement pattern matches, along with equational theorems that specify their behavior.
Using these equations with E-matching enables `[grind]](#manual-grind)` to reduce these instances of pattern matching.

### 16.6.1. Patterns {#manual-e-matching-patterns}

The E-matching index is a table of *patterns*.
When a term matches one of the patterns in the table, `[grind]](#manual-grind)` attempts to instantiate and apply the corresponding theorem, giving rise to further facts and equalities.
Selecting appropriate patterns is an important part of using `[grind]](#manual-grind)` effectively: if the patterns are too restrictive, then useful theorems may not be applied; if they are too general, performance may suffer.

**Example: E-matching Patterns**

Consider the following functions and theorems:

```lean
def f (a : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
a + 1
def g (a : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
a - 1
@[grind =]
theorem gf (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [g]](#manual-g-_LPAR_in-E-matching-Patterns_RPAR_) ([f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-E-matching-Patterns_RPAR_) x) = x := byx:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ [g]](#manual-g-_LPAR_in-E-matching-Patterns_RPAR_) ([f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-E-matching-Patterns_RPAR_) x) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) x
[simp]](#manual-simp) [[f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-E-matching-Patterns_RPAR_), [g]](#manual-g-_LPAR_in-E-matching-Patterns_RPAR_)]All goals completed! 🐙
```

The theorem `[gf]](#manual-gf-_LPAR_in-E-matching-Patterns_RPAR_)` asserts that `[g]](#manual-g-_LPAR_in-E-matching-Patterns_RPAR_) ([f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-E-matching-Patterns_RPAR_) x) = x` for all natural numbers `x`.
The attribute `grind =` instructs `[grind]](#manual-grind)` to use the left-hand side of the equation, `[g]](#manual-g-_LPAR_in-E-matching-Patterns_RPAR_) ([f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-E-matching-Patterns_RPAR_) x)`, as a pattern for heuristic instantiation via E-matching.

This proof goal does not include an instance of `[g]](#manual-g-_LPAR_in-E-matching-Patterns_RPAR_) ([f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-E-matching-Patterns_RPAR_) x)`, but `[grind]](#manual-grind)` is nonetheless able to solve it:

```lean
example {a b} (h : [f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-E-matching-Patterns_RPAR_) b = a) : [g]](#manual-g-_LPAR_in-E-matching-Patterns_RPAR_) a = b := byx:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)a✝:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)b✝:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)a:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)b:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h:[f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-E-matching-Patterns_RPAR_) b [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) a⊢ [g]](#manual-g-_LPAR_in-E-matching-Patterns_RPAR_) a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) b
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

Although `[g]](#manual-g-_LPAR_in-E-matching-Patterns_RPAR_) a` is not an instance of the pattern `[g]](#manual-g-_LPAR_in-E-matching-Patterns_RPAR_) ([f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-E-matching-Patterns_RPAR_) x)`, it becomes one modulo the equation `[f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-E-matching-Patterns_RPAR_) b = a`.
By substituting `a` with `[f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-E-matching-Patterns_RPAR_) b` in `[g]](#manual-g-_LPAR_in-E-matching-Patterns_RPAR_) a`, we obtain the term `[g]](#manual-g-_LPAR_in-E-matching-Patterns_RPAR_) ([f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-E-matching-Patterns_RPAR_) b)`, which matches the pattern `[g]](#manual-g-_LPAR_in-E-matching-Patterns_RPAR_) ([f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-E-matching-Patterns_RPAR_) x)` with the assignment `x := b`.
Thus, the theorem `[gf]](#manual-gf-_LPAR_in-E-matching-Patterns_RPAR_)` is instantiated with `x := b`, and the new equality `[g]](#manual-g-_LPAR_in-E-matching-Patterns_RPAR_) ([f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-E-matching-Patterns_RPAR_) b) = b` is asserted.
`[grind]](#manual-grind)` then uses congruence closure to derive the implied equality `[g]](#manual-g-_LPAR_in-E-matching-Patterns_RPAR_) a = [g]](#manual-g-_LPAR_in-E-matching-Patterns_RPAR_) ([f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-E-matching-Patterns_RPAR_) b)` and completes the proof.

The `grind_pattern` command can be used to manually select an E-matching pattern for a theorem.
Enabling the option `[trace.grind.ematch.instance]](#manual-trace___grind___ematch___instance)` causes `[grind]](#manual-grind)` print a trace message for each theorem instance it generates, which can be helpful when determining E-matching patterns.

syntaxE-matching Pattern Selection

```lean
command ::= ...
    | grind_pattern ident => term,*
```

Associates a theorem with one or more patterns.
When multiple patterns are provided in a single `grind_pattern` command, *all* of them must match a term before `[grind]](#manual-grind)` will attempt to instantiate the theorem.

```lean
command ::= ...
    | grind_pattern ident => term,* where (isValue
       | isStrictValue
       | notValue
       | notStrictValue
       | isGround
       | sizeLt
       | depthLt
       | genLt
       | maxInsts
       | guard
       | check
       | notDefEq
       | defEq)
```

The optional `where` clause specifies constraints that must be satisfied before `[grind]](#manual-grind)` attempts to instantiate the theorem.
Each constraint has the form `variable =/= value`, preventing instantiation when the pattern variable would be assigned the specified value.
This is useful to avoid unbounded or excessive instantiations with problematic terms.

**Example: Selecting Patterns**

The `grind =` attribute uses the left side of the equality as the E-matching pattern for `[gf]](#manual-gf-_LPAR_in-Selecting-Patterns_RPAR_)`:

```lean
def f (a : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
a + 1
def g (a : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
a - 1
@[grind =]
theorem gf (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [g]](#manual-g-_LPAR_in-Selecting-Patterns_RPAR_) ([f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-Selecting-Patterns_RPAR_) x) = x := byx:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ [g]](#manual-g-_LPAR_in-Selecting-Patterns_RPAR_) ([f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-Selecting-Patterns_RPAR_) x) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) x
[simp]](#manual-simp) [[f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-Selecting-Patterns_RPAR_), [g]](#manual-g-_LPAR_in-Selecting-Patterns_RPAR_)]All goals completed! 🐙
```

For example, the pattern `g (f x)` is too restrictive in the following case:
the theorem `gf` will not be instantiated because the goal does not even
contain the function symbol `g`.

In this example, `[grind]](#manual-grind)` fails because the pattern is too restrictive: the goal does not contain the function symbol `[g]](#manual-g-_LPAR_in-Selecting-Patterns_RPAR_)`.

```lean
example (h₁ : [f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-Selecting-Patterns_RPAR_) b = a) (h₂ : [f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-Selecting-Patterns_RPAR_) c = a) : b = c := byb:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)a:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)c:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h₁:[f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-Selecting-Patterns_RPAR_) b [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) ah₂:[f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-Selecting-Patterns_RPAR_) c [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) a⊢ b [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) c
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

```lean
`grind` failed
grindb a c:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h₁:[f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-Selecting-Patterns_RPAR_) b [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) ah₂:[f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-Selecting-Patterns_RPAR_) c [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) ah:[¬](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)b [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) c⊢ [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)
[grind] Goal diagnostics

- [facts] Asserted facts
  - [prop] [f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-Selecting-Patterns_RPAR_) b [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) a
  - [prop] [f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-Selecting-Patterns_RPAR_) c [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) a
  - [prop] [¬](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)b [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) c

```

Using just `f x` as the pattern allows `[grind]](#manual-grind)` to solve the goal automatically:

```lean
grind_pattern [gf]](#manual-gf-_LPAR_in-Selecting-Patterns_RPAR_) => [f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-Selecting-Patterns_RPAR_) x
example {a b c} (h₁ : [f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-Selecting-Patterns_RPAR_) b = a) (h₂ : [f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-Selecting-Patterns_RPAR_) c = a) : b = c := bya:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)b:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)c:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h₁:[f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-Selecting-Patterns_RPAR_) b [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) ah₂:[f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-Selecting-Patterns_RPAR_) c [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) a⊢ b [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) c
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

Enabling `[trace.grind.ematch.instance]](#manual-trace___grind___ematch___instance)` makes it possible to see the equalities found by E-matching:

```lean
example (h₁ : [f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-Selecting-Patterns_RPAR_) b = a) (h₂ : [f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-Selecting-Patterns_RPAR_) c = a) : b = c := byb:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)a:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)c:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h₁:[f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-Selecting-Patterns_RPAR_) b [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) ah₂:[f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-Selecting-Patterns_RPAR_) c [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) a⊢ b [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) c
[set_option]](#manual-set_option) [trace.grind.ematch.instance]](#manual-trace___grind___ematch___instance) [true]](#manual-set_option) [in]](#manual-set_option)
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

```lean
[grind.ematch.instance] [gf]](#manual-gf-_LPAR_in-Selecting-Patterns_RPAR_): [g]](#manual-g-_LPAR_in-Selecting-Patterns_RPAR_) ([f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-Selecting-Patterns_RPAR_) c) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) c[grind.ematch.instance] [gf]](#manual-gf-_LPAR_in-Selecting-Patterns_RPAR_): [g]](#manual-g-_LPAR_in-Selecting-Patterns_RPAR_) ([f]](#manual-f-_LPAR_in-Selecting-Patterns_RPAR_) b) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) b
```

After E-matching, the proof succeeds because congruence closure equates `g (f c)` with `g (f b)`, because both `f b` and `f c` are equal to `a`.
Thus, `b` and `c` must be in the same equivalence class.

When multiple patterns are specified together, all of them must match in the current context before `[grind]](#manual-grind)` attempts to instantiate the theorem.
This is referred to as a *multi-pattern*.
This is useful for lemmas such as transitivity rules, where multiple premises must be simultaneously present for the rule to apply.
A single theorem may be associated with multiple separate patterns by using multiple invocations of `grind_pattern` or the `[@[]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)grind _=_[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Attributes/#Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)` attribute.
If *any* of these separate patterns match, the theorem will be instantiated.

**Example: Multi-Patterns**

`[R]](#manual-R-_LPAR_in-Multi-Patterns_RPAR_)` is a transitive binary relation over `[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)`:

```lean
opaque R : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) → [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) → Prop
[axiom]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___axiom-next) Rtrans {x y z : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)} : [R]](#manual-R-_LPAR_in-Multi-Patterns_RPAR_) x y → [R]](#manual-R-_LPAR_in-Multi-Patterns_RPAR_) y z → [R]](#manual-R-_LPAR_in-Multi-Patterns_RPAR_) x z
```

To use the fact that `[R]](#manual-R-_LPAR_in-Multi-Patterns_RPAR_)` is transitive, `[grind]](#manual-grind)` must already be able to satisfy both premises.
This is represented using a [multi-pattern]](#manual---tech-term-multi-pattern):

```lean
grind_pattern [Rtrans]](#manual-Rtrans-_LPAR_in-Multi-Patterns_RPAR_) => [R]](#manual-R-_LPAR_in-Multi-Patterns_RPAR_) x y, [R]](#manual-R-_LPAR_in-Multi-Patterns_RPAR_) y z
example {a b c d} : [R]](#manual-R-_LPAR_in-Multi-Patterns_RPAR_) a b → [R]](#manual-R-_LPAR_in-Multi-Patterns_RPAR_) b c → [R]](#manual-R-_LPAR_in-Multi-Patterns_RPAR_) c d → [R]](#manual-R-_LPAR_in-Multi-Patterns_RPAR_) a d := bya:[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)b:[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)c:[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)d:[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)⊢ [R]](#manual-R-_LPAR_in-Multi-Patterns_RPAR_) a b → [R]](#manual-R-_LPAR_in-Multi-Patterns_RPAR_) b c → [R]](#manual-R-_LPAR_in-Multi-Patterns_RPAR_) c d → [R]](#manual-R-_LPAR_in-Multi-Patterns_RPAR_) a d
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

The multi-pattern `R x y, R y z` instructs `[grind]](#manual-grind)` to instantiate `[Rtrans]](#manual-Rtrans-_LPAR_in-Multi-Patterns_RPAR_)` only when both `[R]](#manual-R-_LPAR_in-Multi-Patterns_RPAR_) x y` and `[R]](#manual-R-_LPAR_in-Multi-Patterns_RPAR_) y z` are available in the context.
In the example, `[grind]](#manual-grind)` applies `[Rtrans]](#manual-Rtrans-_LPAR_in-Multi-Patterns_RPAR_)` to derive `[R]](#manual-R-_LPAR_in-Multi-Patterns_RPAR_) a c` from `[R]](#manual-R-_LPAR_in-Multi-Patterns_RPAR_) a b` and `[R]](#manual-R-_LPAR_in-Multi-Patterns_RPAR_) b c`, and can then repeat the same reasoning to deduce `[R]](#manual-R-_LPAR_in-Multi-Patterns_RPAR_) a d` from `[R]](#manual-R-_LPAR_in-Multi-Patterns_RPAR_) a c` and `[R]](#manual-R-_LPAR_in-Multi-Patterns_RPAR_) c d`.

**Example: Pattern Constraints**

Certain combinations of theorems can lead to unbounded instantiation, where E-matching repeatedly generates longer and longer terms.
Consider theorems about `[List.flatMap](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___flatMap)` and `[List.reverse](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___reverse)`.
If `List.flatMap_def`, `List.flatMap_reverse`, and `List.reverse_flatMap` are all annotated with `[@[]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)grind =[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Attributes/#Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)`, then as soon as `List.flatMap_reverse` is instantiated, the following chain of instantiations occurs, creating progressively longer function compositions with `[List.reverse](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___reverse)`.
This can be observed using the `#grind_lint` command:

```
attribute [local grind =] List.reverse_flatMap

set_option trace.grind.ematch.instance true in
#grind_lint inspect List.flatMap_reverse
```

The trace output shows the unbounded instantiation:

```
[grind.ematch.instance] List.flatMap_def: List.flatMap (List.reverse ∘ f) l = (List.map (List.reverse ∘ f) l).flatten
[grind.ematch.instance] List.flatMap_def: List.flatMap f l.reverse = (List.map f l.reverse).flatten
[grind.ematch.instance] List.flatMap_reverse: List.flatMap f l.reverse = (List.flatMap (List.reverse ∘ f) l).reverse
[grind.ematch.instance] List.reverse_flatMap: (List.flatMap (List.reverse ∘ f) l).reverse =
  List.flatMap (List.reverse ∘ List.reverse ∘ f) l.reverse
[grind.ematch.instance] List.flatMap_def: List.flatMap (List.reverse ∘ List.reverse ∘ f) l.reverse =
  (List.map (List.reverse ∘ List.reverse ∘ f) l.reverse).flatten
```

This pattern continues indefinitely, with each iteration adding another `[List.reverse](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___reverse)` to the composition.
The `where` clause prevents this by excluding problematic instantiations:

```
grind_pattern reverse_flatMap => (l.flatMap f).reverse where
  f =/= List.reverse ∘ _
```

This instructs `[grind]](#manual-grind)` to use the pattern `(l.flatMap f).reverse`, but only when `f` is not a composition with `[List.reverse](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___reverse)`, preventing the unbounded chain of instantiations.

You can use `#grind_lint check` to look for problematic patterns, or `#grind_lint check in List` or `#grind_lint check in module Std.Data` to look in specific namespaces or modules.

The `grind` attribute automatically generates an E-matching pattern or multi-pattern using a heuristic, instead of using `grind_pattern` to explicitly specify a pattern.
It includes a number of variants that select different heuristics.
The `grind?` attribute displays an info message showing the pattern which was selected—this is very helpful for debugging!

Patterns are subexpressions of theorem statements.
A subexpression is *indexable* if it has an indexable constant as its head, and it is said to *cover* one of the theorem's arguments if it fixes the argument's value.
Indexable constants are all constants other than `[Eq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl)`, `[HEq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#HEq___refl)`, `[Iff](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Iff___intro)`, `[And](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro)`, `[Or](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl)`, and `[Not](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)`.
The set of arguments that are covered by a pattern or multi-pattern is referred to as its *coverage*.
Some constants are lower priority than others; in particular, the arithmetic operators `[HAdd.hAdd]](#manual-HAdd___mk)`, `[HSub.hSub]](#manual-HSub___mk)`, `[HMul.hMul]](#manual-HMul___mk)`, `[Dvd.dvd]](#manual-Dvd___mk)`, `[HDiv.hDiv]](#manual-HDiv___mk)`, and `[HMod.hMod]](#manual-HMod___mk)` have low priority.
An indexable subexpression is *minimal* if there is no smaller indexable subexpression whose head constant has at least as high priority.

attributeGrind Patterns

When the `grind` attribute is added to a definition, it causes `grind` to unfold that definition to its body whenever it is encountered.
When using the module system, if the body of the definition is not visible (e.g. via `[@[]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)expose[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Attributes/#Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)`), then the `grind` attribute is ignored.

```lean
attr ::= ...
    | grind grindMod?
```

The `grind` attribute automatically generates an E-matching pattern for a theorem, using a strategy determined by the provided modifier.
If no modifier is provided, then `grind` suggests suitable modifiers, displaying the resulting patterns.

```lean
attr ::= ...
    | grind! grindMod?
```

The `grind!` attribute automatically generates an E-matching pattern for a theorem, using a strategy determined by the provided modifier.
It additionally enforces the condition that the selected pattern(s) should be minimal indexable subexpressions.

```lean
attr ::= ...
    | grind? grindMod?
```

The `grind?` displays the pattern that was generated.

```lean
attr ::= ...
    | grind!? grindMod?
```

The `grind!?` attribute is equivalent to `grind!`, except it displays the resulting pattern for inspection.

Without any modifier, `[@[]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)grind[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Attributes/#Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)` traverses the conclusion and then the hypotheses from left to right, adding patterns as they increase the coverage, stopping when all arguments are covered.
This default strategy can be explicitly requested using the `.` modifier.
In addition to using the default strategy, the attribute checks which other strategies could be applied, and displays all of the resulting patterns.

syntaxDefault Pattern

```lean
grindMod ::= ...
    | .
```

```lean
grindMod ::= ...
    | ·
```

The `.` modifier instructs `[grind]](#manual-grind)` to select a multi-pattern by traversing the conclusion of the
theorem, and then the hypotheses from left to right. We say this is the default modifier.
Each time it encounters a subexpression which covers an argument which was not
previously covered, it adds that subexpression as a pattern, until all arguments have been covered.
If `[grind!]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Attr___grind___)` is used, then only minimal indexable subexpressions are considered.

syntaxEquality Rewrites

```lean
grindMod ::= ...
    | =
```

The `=` modifier instructs `[grind]](#manual-grind)` to check that the conclusion of the theorem is an equality,
and then uses the left-hand side of the equality as a pattern. This may fail if not all of the arguments appear
in the left-hand side.

syntaxBackward Equality Rewrites

```lean
grindMod ::= ...
    | =_
```

The `=_` modifier instructs `[grind]](#manual-grind)` to check that the conclusion of the theorem is an equality,
and then uses the right-hand side of the equality as a pattern. This may fail if not all of the arguments appear
in the right-hand side.

syntaxBidirectional Equality Rewrites

```lean
grindMod ::= ...
    | _=_
```

The `_=_` modifier acts like a macro which expands to `=` and `=_`. It adds two patterns,
allowing the equality theorem to trigger in either direction.

syntaxForward Reasoning

```lean
grindMod ::= ...
    | →
```

The `→` modifier instructs `[grind]](#manual-grind)` to select a multi-pattern from the hypotheses of the theorem.
In other words, `[grind]](#manual-grind)` will use the theorem for forwards reasoning.
To generate a pattern, it traverses the hypotheses of the theorem from left to right.
Each time it encounters a subexpression which covers an argument which was not
previously covered, it adds that subexpression as a pattern, until all arguments have been covered.
If `[grind!]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Attr___grind___)` is used, then only minimal indexable subexpressions are considered.

syntaxBackward Reasoning

```lean
grindMod ::= ...
    | ←
```

The `←` modifier instructs `[grind]](#manual-grind)` to select a multi-pattern from the conclusion of theorem.
In other words, `[grind]](#manual-grind)` will use the theorem for backwards reasoning.
This may fail if not all of the arguments to the theorem appear in the conclusion.
Each time it encounters a subexpression which covers an argument which was not
previously covered, it adds that subexpression as a pattern, until all arguments have been covered.
If `[grind!]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Attr___grind___)` is used, then only minimal indexable subexpressions are considered.

It is important to inspect the patterns generated by the `[@[]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)grind[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Attributes/#Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)` attribute to ensure that they match the correct parts of the lemma.
If the pattern is too strict, the lemma will not be applied in situations where it would be relevant, leading to less automation.
If it is too general, then performance will suffer as the lemma is tried in many situations where it is not helpful.

There are also three less commonly used modifiers for lemmas:

syntaxLeft-to-Right Traversal

```lean
grindMod ::= ...
    | =>
```

```lean
grindMod ::= ...
    | ⇒
```

The `⇒` modifier instructs `[grind]](#manual-grind)` to select a multi-pattern by traversing all the hypotheses from
left to right, followed by the conclusion.
Each time it encounters a subexpression which covers an argument which was not
previously covered, it adds that subexpression as a pattern, until all arguments have been covered.
If `[grind!]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Attr___grind___)` is used, then only minimal indexable subexpressions are considered.

syntaxRight-to-Left Traversal

```lean
grindMod ::= ...
    | <=
```

```lean
grindMod ::= ...
    | ⇐
```

The `⇐` modifier instructs `[grind]](#manual-grind)` to select a multi-pattern by traversing the conclusion, and then
all the hypotheses from right to left.
Each time it encounters a subexpression which covers an argument which was not
previously covered, it adds that subexpression as a pattern, until all arguments have been covered.
If `[grind!]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Attr___grind___)` is used, then only minimal indexable subexpressions are considered.

syntaxBackward Reasoning on Equality

```lean
grindMod ::= ...
    | ←=
```

The `←=` modifier is unlike the other `[grind]](#manual-grind)` modifiers, and it used specifically for
backwards reasoning on equality. When a theorem's conclusion is an equality proposition and it
is annotated with `@[grind ←=]`, grind `will` instantiate it whenever the corresponding disequality
is assumed—this is a consequence of the fact that grind performs all proofs by contradiction.
Ordinarily, the grind attribute does not consider the `=` symbol when generating patterns.

**Example: The @[grind ←=] Attribute**

When attempting to prove that `a⁻¹ = b`, `[grind]](#manual-grind)` uses `[inv_eq]](#manual-inv_eq-_LPAR_in-The--____LSQ_grind-_______RSQ_--Attribute_RPAR_)` due to the `[@[]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)grind ←=[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Attributes/#Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)` annotation.

```lean
@[grind ←=]
theorem inv_eq [One α] [[Mul]](#manual-Mul___mk) α] [Inv α] {a b : α}
(w : a * b = 1) : a⁻¹ = b :=
sorry
```

syntaxFunction-Valued Congruence Closure

```lean
grindMod ::= ...
    | funCC
```

The `funCC` modifier marks global functions that support **function-valued congruence closure**.
Given an application `f a₁ a₂ … aₙ`, when `funCC := true`,
`[grind]](#manual-grind)` generates and tracks equalities for all partial applications:

- `f a₁`
- `f a₁ a₂`
- `…`
- `f a₁ a₂ … aₙ`

Some additional modifiers can be used to add other kinds of lemmas to the index.
This includes extensionality theorems, injectivity theorems for functions, and a shortcut to add all constructors of an inductively defined predicate to the index.

syntaxExtensionality

```lean
grindMod ::= ...
    | ext
```

The `[ext]](#manual-ext)` modifier marks extensionality theorems for use by `[grind]](#manual-grind)`.
For example, the standard library marks `[funext]](#manual-funext)` with this attribute.

Whenever `[grind]](#manual-grind)` encounters a disequality `a ≠ b`, it attempts to apply any
available extensionality theorems whose matches the type of `a` and `b`.

In addition, adding `[@[]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)grind ext[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Attributes/#Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)` to a structure registers a its extensionality theorem.

**Example: The @[grind ext] Attribute**

`[Point]](#manual-Point-_LPAR_in-The--____LSQ_grind-ext_RSQ_--Attribute_RPAR_)` is a structure with two fields:

```lean
structure Point where
x : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)
y : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)
```

By default, `[grind]](#manual-grind)` can solve goals like this one, because definitional equality includes [η-equivalence]](#manual---tech-term-___-equivalence) for product types:

```lean
example (p : [Point]](#manual-Point-_LPAR_in-The--____LSQ_grind-ext_RSQ_--Attribute_RPAR_)) : p = ⟨p.[x]](#manual-Point___x-_LPAR_in-The--____LSQ_grind-ext_RSQ_--Attribute_RPAR_), p.[y]](#manual-Point___y-_LPAR_in-The--____LSQ_grind-ext_RSQ_--Attribute_RPAR_)⟩ := byp:[Point]](#manual-Point-_LPAR_in-The--____LSQ_grind-ext_RSQ_--Attribute_RPAR_)⊢ p [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) { [x]](#manual-Point___x-_LPAR_in-The--____LSQ_grind-ext_RSQ_--Attribute_RPAR_) := p.[x]](#manual-Point___x-_LPAR_in-The--____LSQ_grind-ext_RSQ_--Attribute_RPAR_), [y]](#manual-Point___y-_LPAR_in-The--____LSQ_grind-ext_RSQ_--Attribute_RPAR_) := p.[y]](#manual-Point___y-_LPAR_in-The--____LSQ_grind-ext_RSQ_--Attribute_RPAR_) } [grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

```lean

```

syntaxInjectivity

```lean
grindMod ::= ...
    | inj
```

The `inj` modifier marks injectivity theorems for use by `[grind]](#manual-grind)`.
The conclusion of the theorem must be of the form `[Function.Injective]](#manual-Function___Injective) f`
where the term `f` contains at least one constant symbol.

**Example: Injectivity Patterns**

This function `[double]](#manual-double-_LPAR_in-Injectivity-Patterns_RPAR_)` doubles its argument:

```lean
def double (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := x + x
```

By default, `[grind]](#manual-grind)` cannot prove the following theorem:

```lean
theorem A {n k : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)} :
[double]](#manual-double-_LPAR_in-Injectivity-Patterns_RPAR_) (n + 5) = [double]](#manual-double-_LPAR_in-Injectivity-Patterns_RPAR_) (k - 3) →
n + 8 = k := byn:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)k:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ [double]](#manual-double-_LPAR_in-Injectivity-Patterns_RPAR_) [(]](#manual-HAdd___mk)n [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 5[)]](#manual-HAdd___mk) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [double]](#manual-double-_LPAR_in-Injectivity-Patterns_RPAR_) [(]](#manual-HSub___mk)k [-]](#manual-HSub___mk) 3[)]](#manual-HSub___mk) → n [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 8 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) k
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

However, `[double]](#manual-double-_LPAR_in-Injectivity-Patterns_RPAR_)` is injective, and this fact can be registered for `[grind]](#manual-grind)` using the `grind inj` attribute:

```lean
@[grind inj]
theorem double_inj : [Function.Injective]](#manual-Function___Injective) [double]](#manual-double-_LPAR_in-Injectivity-Patterns_RPAR_) := by⊢ [Function.Injective]](#manual-Function___Injective) [double]](#manual-double-_LPAR_in-Injectivity-Patterns_RPAR_)
[simp]](#manual-simp) [only]](#manual-simp) [[double]](#manual-double-_LPAR_in-Injectivity-Patterns_RPAR_), [Function.Injective]](#manual-Function___Injective)]⊢ ∀ ⦃a₁ a₂ : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⦄, a₁ [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) a₁ [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) a₂ [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) a₂ → a₁ [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) a₂
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

This injectivity lemma suffices to prove the theorem:

```lean
theorem B {n k : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)} :
[double]](#manual-double-_LPAR_in-Injectivity-Patterns_RPAR_) (n + 5) = [double]](#manual-double-_LPAR_in-Injectivity-Patterns_RPAR_) (k - 3) →
n + 8 = k := byn:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)k:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ [double]](#manual-double-_LPAR_in-Injectivity-Patterns_RPAR_) [(]](#manual-HAdd___mk)n [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 5[)]](#manual-HAdd___mk) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [double]](#manual-double-_LPAR_in-Injectivity-Patterns_RPAR_) [(]](#manual-HSub___mk)k [-]](#manual-HSub___mk) 3[)]](#manual-HSub___mk) → n [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 8 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) k
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

syntaxConstructor Patterns

```lean
grindMod ::= ...
    | intro
```

The `[intro]](#manual-intro)` modifier instructs `[grind]](#manual-grind)` to use the constructors (introduction rules)
of an inductive predicate as E-matching theorems.Example:

```lean
inductive [Even]](#manual-Even___zero-next) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Prop where
| [zero]](#manual-Even___zero-next) : [Even]](#manual-Even___zero-next) 0
| add2 : [Even]](#manual-Even___zero-next) x → [Even]](#manual-Even___zero-next) (x + 2)
[attribute]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___attribute) [grind intro] [Even]](#manual-Even___zero-next)
example (h : [Even]](#manual-Even___zero-next) x) : [Even]](#manual-Even___zero-next) (x + 6) := byx:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h:[Even]](#manual-Even___zero-next) x⊢ [Even]](#manual-Even___zero-next) [(]](#manual-HAdd___mk)x [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 6[)]](#manual-HAdd___mk) [grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
example : [Even]](#manual-Even___zero-next) 0 := by⊢ [Even]](#manual-Even___zero-next) 0 [grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

Here `attribute [grind intro] Even` acts like a macro that expands to
`attribute [grind] Even.zero` and `attribute [grind] Even.add2`.
This is especially convenient for inductive predicates with many constructors.

**Example: Patterns for Constructors**

The predicate `[Decreasing]](#manual-Decreasing-_LPAR_in-Patterns-for-Constructors_RPAR_)` states that each of the values in a list of integers is less than the one before, and the function `[decreasing]](#manual-decreasing-_LPAR_in-Patterns-for-Constructors_RPAR_)` checks this property, returning a `[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`.

```lean
inductive Decreasing : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) → Prop
| nil : [Decreasing]](#manual-Decreasing-_LPAR_in-Patterns-for-Constructors_RPAR_) []
| singleton : [Decreasing]](#manual-Decreasing-_LPAR_in-Patterns-for-Constructors_RPAR_) [x]
| cons : [Decreasing]](#manual-Decreasing-_LPAR_in-Patterns-for-Constructors_RPAR_) (x :: xs) → y > x → [Decreasing]](#manual-Decreasing-_LPAR_in-Patterns-for-Constructors_RPAR_) (y :: x :: xs)
def decreasing : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| [] | [_] => [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| y :: x :: xs => y > x && [decreasing]](#manual-decreasing-_LPAR_in-Patterns-for-Constructors_RPAR_) (x :: xs)
```

The function is correct if it returns `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` exactly when `[Decreasing]](#manual-Decreasing-_LPAR_in-Patterns-for-Constructors_RPAR_)` holds for its argument.

syntaxUnfolding During Preprocessing

```lean
grindMod ::= ...
    | unfold
```

The `[unfold]](#manual-unfold)` modifier instructs `[grind]](#manual-grind)` to unfold the given definition during the preprocessing step.
Example:

```lean
@[grind unfold] def [h](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/releases/v4.28.0/#h) (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) := 2 * x
example : 6 ∣ 3*[h](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/releases/v4.28.0/#h) x := byx:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ 6 [∣]](#manual-Dvd___mk) 3 [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) [h](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/releases/v4.28.0/#h) x [grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

syntaxNormalization Rules

```lean
grindMod ::= ...
    | norm
```

The `norm` modifier instructs `[grind]](#manual-grind)` to use a theorem as a normalization rule. That is,
the theorem is applied during the preprocessing step.
This feature is meant for advanced users who understand how the preprocessor and `[grind]](#manual-grind)`'s search
procedure interact with each other.
New users can still benefit from this feature by restricting its use to theorems that completely
eliminate a symbol from the goal. Example:

```
theorem max_def : max n m = if n ≤ m then m else n
```

For a negative example, consider:

```
opaque f : Int → Int → Int → Int
theorem fax1 : f x 0 1 = 1 := sorry
theorem fax2 : f 1 x 1 = 1 := sorry
attribute [grind norm] fax1
attribute [grind =] fax2

example (h : c = 1) : f c 0 c = 1 := by
  grind -- fails
```

In this example, `fax1` is a normalization rule, but it is not applicable to the input goal since
`f c 0 c` is not an instance of `f x 0 1`. However, `f c 0 c` matches the pattern `f 1 x 1` modulo
the equality `c = 1`. Thus, `[grind]](#manual-grind)` instantiates `fax2` with `x := 0`, producing the equality
`f 1 0 1 = 1`, which the normalizer simplifies to `[True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro)`. As a result, nothing useful is learned.
In the future, we plan to include linters to automatically detect issues like these.
Example:

```lean
opaque [f](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/releases/v4.27.0/#f) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
opaque g : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
@[grind norm] [axiom]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___axiom-next) fax : [f](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/releases/v4.27.0/#f) x = x + 2
@[grind norm ←] [axiom]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___axiom-next) fg : [f](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/releases/v4.27.0/#f) x = g x
example : [f](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/releases/v4.27.0/#f) x ≥ 2 := byx:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ [f](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/releases/v4.27.0/#f) x ≥ 2 [grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
example : [f](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/releases/v4.27.0/#f) x ≥ g x := byx:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ [f](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/releases/v4.27.0/#f) x ≥ g x [grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
example : [f](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/releases/v4.27.0/#f) x + g x ≥ 4 := byx:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ [f](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/releases/v4.27.0/#f) x [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) g x ≥ 4 [grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

The `[grind]](#manual-grind)` tactic can work with a source algebra that doesn't have a great deal of solving infrastructure (e.g. bitvectors) by “̲injecting”̲ it into another algebra that has more solving infrastructure (like natural numbers or integers).
Homomorphism rules describe the injection from source to target, and how the injection commutes with other operations (like addition or multiplication in the case of bitvectors).
Homomorphism predicates present additional facts that `[grind]](#manual-grind)` can use about the injection (like that a bitvector of length `n` corresponds to a natural number less than `2^n`).

syntaxHomomorphism Rules

```lean
grindMod ::= ...
    | hom
```

The `hom` modifier marks a theorem as a homomorphism rule for `[grind]](#manual-grind)`.

Homomorphism rules translate terms from a source domain into a target domain that has a
dedicated solver. A collection of homomorphism rules encodes an algebra homomorphism
`h : A → B`: each rule states how `h` commutes with a source-domain operation, as in
`h (f x y) = g (h x) (h y)`. Example: injecting bitvector operations into integer
arithmetic using `[BitVec.toNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Bitvectors/#BitVec___toNat)`:

```
@[grind hom] theorem toNat_add (x y : BitVec w) :
    (x + y).toNat = (x.toNat + y.toNat) % 2^w
```

The rules must be unconditional equations (or `[Iff](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Iff___intro)`s). They are applied to fixpoint
outside the E-graph, and only the final result is internalized.

syntaxHomomorphism Predicates

```lean
grindMod ::= ...
    | hom_pred
```

The `hom_pred` modifier marks a theorem as a homomorphism predicate for `[grind]](#manual-grind)`.

Homomorphism predicates are facts that `[grind]](#manual-grind)` instantiates eagerly for the terms it
internalizes. The conclusion of the theorem must contain an application `f a₁ … aₙ`
whose trailing arguments are exactly the theorem's explicit parameters; the head
symbol `f` becomes the trigger. Whenever `[grind]](#manual-grind)` internalizes a term with head `f`,
the theorem is instantiated with the term's trailing arguments, and the resulting
fact is asserted. Typical uses are range facts for injection functions, and
translations of relations into a target domain. Examples:

```
@[grind hom_pred] theorem BitVec.toNat_range (x : BitVec w) : x.toNat < 2^w
@[grind hom_pred] theorem UInt8.le_iff (a b : UInt8) : a ≤ b ↔ a.toBitVec ≤ b.toBitVec
```

The first theorem is triggered by terms of the form `[BitVec.toNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Bitvectors/#BitVec___toNat) x`, and the second
one by `a ≤ b` applications. `[grind]](#manual-grind)` uses the types of `a` and `b` to discard
irrelevant instantiations.

### 16.6.2. Inspecting Patterns {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--The--grind--tactic--E___matching--Inspecting-Patterns}

The `grind?` attribute is a version of the `grind` attribute that additionally displays the generated pattern or [multi-pattern]](#manual---tech-term-multi-pattern).
Patterns and multi-patterns are displayed as lists of subexpressions, each of which is a pattern; ordinary patterns are displayed as singleton lists.
In these displayed patterns, the names of defined constants are printed as-is.
When the theorem's parameters occur in the pattern, they are displayed using numbers rather than names.
In particular, they are numbered from right to left, starting at 0; this representation is referred to as *de Bruijn indices*.

**Example: Inspecting Patterns**

In order to use this proof that divisibility is transitive with `[grind]](#manual-grind)`, it requires E-matching patterns:

```lean

```

The right attribute to use is `[@[]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)grind →[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Attributes/#Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)`, because there should be a pattern for each premise.
Using `[@[]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)grind? →[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Attributes/#Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)`, it is possible to see which patterns are generated:

```lean
[attribute]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___attribute) [[grind?]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Attr___grind___-next) →] [div_trans]](#manual-div_trans-_LPAR_in-Inspecting-Patterns_RPAR_)
```

There are two:

```lean
[div_trans]](#manual-div_trans-_LPAR_in-Inspecting-Patterns_RPAR_): [[@]](#manual-Dvd___mk)[Dvd.dvd]](#manual-Dvd___mk) `[[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)] `[Nat.instDvd] #4 #3, [@]](#manual-Dvd___mk)[Dvd.dvd]](#manual-Dvd___mk) `[[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)] `[Nat.instDvd] #3 #2]
```

Arguments are numbered from right to left, so `#0` is the assumption that `k ∣ j`, while `#4` is `n`.
Thus, these two patterns correspond to the terms `n ∣ k` and `k ∣ j`.

The rules for selecting patterns from subexpressions of the hypotheses and conclusion are subtle.

**Example: Forward Pattern Generation**

```lean
[axiom]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___axiom-next) p : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
[axiom]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___axiom-next) q : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean
@[[grind!?]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Attr___grind______) →] theorem h₁ (w : [p]](#manual-p-_LPAR_in-Forward-Pattern-Generation_RPAR_) ([q]](#manual-q-_LPAR_in-Forward-Pattern-Generation_RPAR_) x) = 7) : [p]](#manual-p-_LPAR_in-Forward-Pattern-Generation_RPAR_) (x + 1) = [q]](#manual-q-_LPAR_in-Forward-Pattern-Generation_RPAR_) x := sorry
```

```lean
[h₁]](#manual-h___-_LPAR_in-Forward-Pattern-Generation_RPAR_): [[q]](#manual-q-_LPAR_in-Forward-Pattern-Generation_RPAR_) #1]
```

The pattern is `q x`.
Counting from the right, parameter `#0` is the premise `w` and parameter `#1` is the implicit parameter `x`.

Why did `@[grind! →]`? select `q #1`?
The attribute `@[grind! →]` finds patterns by traversing the hypotheses (that is, parameters whose types are propositions) from left to right.
In this case, there's only a single hypothesis: `p (q x) = 7`.
The heuristic described above says that `grind!` will search for a minimal [indexable]](#manual---tech-term-indexable) subexpression which [covers]](#manual---tech-term-cover) a previously uncovered parameter.
There's just one uncovered parameter, namely `x`.
The whole hypothesis `p (q x) = 7` can't be used because `[grind]](#manual-grind)` will not index on equality.
The right-hand side `7` is not helpful, because it doesn't determine the value of `x`.
`p (q x)` is not suitable because it is not minimal: it has `q x` inside of it, which is indexable (its head is the constant `q`), and it determines the value of `x`.
The expression `q x` itself is minimal, because `x` is not indexable.
Thus, `q x` is selected as the pattern.

**Example: Backward Pattern Generation**

In this example, the `←` modifier indicates that the pattern should be found in the conclusion:

```lean
set_option trace.grind.debug.ematch.pattern true [in]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___in)
@[[grind?]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Attr___grind___-next) ←] theorem h₂ (w : 7 = p (q x)) : p (x + 1) = q x := sorry
```

The left side of the equality is used because `[Eq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl)` is not indexable and `[HAdd.hAdd]](#manual-HAdd___mk)` has lower priority than `p`.

```lean
[h₂]](#manual-h___-_LPAR_in-Backward-Pattern-Generation_RPAR_): [p (#1 + 1)]
```

**Example: Bidirectional Equality Pattern Generation**

In this example, two separate E-matching patterns are generated from the equality conclusion.
One matches the left-hand side, and the other matches the right-hand side.

```lean
@[[grind?]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Attr___grind___-next) _=_] theorem h₃ (w : 7 = p (q x)) : p (x + 1) = q x := sorry
```

```lean
[h₃]](#manual-h___-_LPAR_in-Bidirectional-Equality-Pattern-Generation_RPAR_): [q #1]
```

The entire left side of the equality is used instead of just `x + 1` because `[HAdd.hAdd]](#manual-HAdd___mk)` has lower priority than `p`.

```lean
[h₃]](#manual-h___-_LPAR_in-Bidirectional-Equality-Pattern-Generation_RPAR_): [p (#1 + 1)]
```

**Example: Patterns from Conclusion and Hypotheses**

Without any modifiers, `[@[]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)grind[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Attributes/#Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)` produces a multipattern by first checking the conclusion and then the premises:

```lean
@[[grind?]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Attr___grind___-next) .] theorem h₄ (w : p x = q y) : p (x + 2) = 7 := sorry
```

Here, argument `x` is `#2`, `y` is `#1`, and `w` is `#0`.
The resulting multipattern contains the left-hand side of the equality, which is the only [minimal]](#manual---tech-term-minimal) [indexable]](#manual---tech-term-indexable) subexpression of the conclusion that covers an argument (namely `x`).
It also contains `q y`, which is the only minimal indexable subexpression of the hypothesis `w` that covers an additional argument (namely `y`).

```lean
[h₄]](#manual-h___-_LPAR_in-Patterns-from-Conclusion-and-Hypotheses_RPAR_): [p (#2 + 2), q #1]
```

**Example: Failing Backward Pattern Generation**

In this example, pattern generation fails because the theorem's conclusion doesn't mention the argument `y`.

```lean
@[[grind?]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Attr___grind___-next) ←] theorem h₅ (w : p x = q y) : p (x + 2) = 7 := sorry
```

```lean
`@[grind ←] theorem [h₅]](#manual-h___-_LPAR_in-Failing-Backward-Pattern-Generation_RPAR_)` failed to find patterns in the theorem's conclusion, consider using different options or the `grind_pattern` command
```

**Example: Left-to-Right Generation**

In this example, the pattern is generated by traversing the premises from left to right, followed by the conclusion:

```lean
@[[grind?]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Attr___grind___-next) =>] theorem h₆
(_ : q (y + 2) = q y)
(_ : q (y + 1) = q y) :
p (x + 2) = 7 :=
sorry
```

In the patterns, `y` is argument `#3` and `x` is argument `#2`, because [automatic implicit parameters]](#manual---tech-term-automatic-implicit-parameters) are inserted from left to right and `y` occurs before `x` in the theorem statement.
The premises are arguments `#1` and `#0`.
In the resulting multipattern, `y` is covered by a subexpression of the first premise, and `z` is covered by a subexpression of the conclusion:

```lean
[h₆]](#manual-h___-_LPAR_in-Left-to-Right-Generation_RPAR_): [q (#3 + 2), p (#2 + 2)]
```

### 16.6.3. Resource Limits {#manual-grind-limits}

E-matching can generate an unbounded number of theorem [instances]](#manual---tech-term-instance).
For the sake of both efficiency and termination, `[grind]](#manual-grind)` limits the number of times that E-matching can run using two mechanisms:

Generations
:   Each term is assigned a *generation*, and terms produced by E-matching have a generation that is one greater than the maximal generation of all the terms used to instantiate the theorem.
    E-matching only considers terms whose generation is beneath a configurable threshold.
    The `gen` option to `[grind]](#manual-grind)` controls the generation threshold.

Round Limits
:   Each invocation of the E-matching engine is referred to as a *round*.
    Only a limited number of rounds of E-matching are performed.
    The `ematch` option to `[grind]](#manual-grind)` controls the round limit.

**Example: Too Many Instances**

E-matching can generate too many theorem [instances]](#manual---tech-term-instance).
Some patterns may even generate an unbounded number of instances.

In this example, `[s_eq]](#manual-s_eq-_LPAR_in-Too-Many-Instances_RPAR_)` is added to the index with the pattern `s x`:

```lean
def s (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) := 0
@[[grind?]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Attr___grind___-next) =] theorem s_eq (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [s]](#manual-s-_LPAR_in-Too-Many-Instances_RPAR_) x = [s]](#manual-s-_LPAR_in-Too-Many-Instances_RPAR_) (x + 1) :=
[rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)
```

```lean
[s_eq]](#manual-s_eq-_LPAR_in-Too-Many-Instances_RPAR_): [[s]](#manual-s-_LPAR_in-Too-Many-Instances_RPAR_) #0]
```

Attempting to use this theorem results in many facts about `[s]](#manual-s-_LPAR_in-Too-Many-Instances_RPAR_)` applied to concrete values being generated.
In particular, `[s_eq]](#manual-s_eq-_LPAR_in-Too-Many-Instances_RPAR_)` is instantiated with a new `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` in each of the five rounds.
First, `[grind]](#manual-grind)` instantiates `[s_eq]](#manual-s_eq-_LPAR_in-Too-Many-Instances_RPAR_)` with `x := 0`, which generates the term `[s]](#manual-s-_LPAR_in-Too-Many-Instances_RPAR_) 1`.
This matches the pattern `s x`, and is thus used to instantiate `[s_eq]](#manual-s_eq-_LPAR_in-Too-Many-Instances_RPAR_)` with `x := 1`, which generates the term `[s]](#manual-s-_LPAR_in-Too-Many-Instances_RPAR_) 2`,
and so on until the round limit is reached.

```lean
example : [s]](#manual-s-_LPAR_in-Too-Many-Instances_RPAR_) 0 > 0 := by⊢ [s]](#manual-s-_LPAR_in-Too-Many-Instances_RPAR_) 0 > 0
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

```lean
`grind` failed
grindh:[s]](#manual-s-_LPAR_in-Too-Many-Instances_RPAR_) 0 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0⊢ [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)
[grind] Goal diagnostics

- [facts] Asserted facts
  - [prop] [s]](#manual-s-_LPAR_in-Too-Many-Instances_RPAR_) 0 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0
  - [prop] [s]](#manual-s-_LPAR_in-Too-Many-Instances_RPAR_) 0 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [s]](#manual-s-_LPAR_in-Too-Many-Instances_RPAR_) 1
  - [prop] [s]](#manual-s-_LPAR_in-Too-Many-Instances_RPAR_) 1 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [s]](#manual-s-_LPAR_in-Too-Many-Instances_RPAR_) 2
  - [prop] [s]](#manual-s-_LPAR_in-Too-Many-Instances_RPAR_) 2 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [s]](#manual-s-_LPAR_in-Too-Many-Instances_RPAR_) 3
  - [prop] [s]](#manual-s-_LPAR_in-Too-Many-Instances_RPAR_) 3 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [s]](#manual-s-_LPAR_in-Too-Many-Instances_RPAR_) 4
  - [prop] [s]](#manual-s-_LPAR_in-Too-Many-Instances_RPAR_) 4 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [s]](#manual-s-_LPAR_in-Too-Many-Instances_RPAR_) 5
- [eqc] Equivalence classes
  - [eqc] {[s]](#manual-s-_LPAR_in-Too-Many-Instances_RPAR_) 0, 0, [s]](#manual-s-_LPAR_in-Too-Many-Instances_RPAR_) 1, [s]](#manual-s-_LPAR_in-Too-Many-Instances_RPAR_) 2, [s]](#manual-s-_LPAR_in-Too-Many-Instances_RPAR_) 3, [s]](#manual-s-_LPAR_in-Too-Many-Instances_RPAR_) 4, [s]](#manual-s-_LPAR_in-Too-Many-Instances_RPAR_) 5}
- [ematch] E-matching patterns
  - [thm] [s_eq]](#manual-s_eq-_LPAR_in-Too-Many-Instances_RPAR_): [[s]](#manual-s-_LPAR_in-Too-Many-Instances_RPAR_) #0]
- [cutsat] Assignment satisfying linear constraints
  - [assign] [s]](#manual-s-_LPAR_in-Too-Many-Instances_RPAR_) 0 := 0
  - [assign] [s]](#manual-s-_LPAR_in-Too-Many-Instances_RPAR_) 1 := 0
  - [assign] [s]](#manual-s-_LPAR_in-Too-Many-Instances_RPAR_) 2 := 0
  - [assign] [s]](#manual-s-_LPAR_in-Too-Many-Instances_RPAR_) 3 := 0
  - [assign] [s]](#manual-s-_LPAR_in-Too-Many-Instances_RPAR_) 4 := 0
  - [assign] [s]](#manual-s-_LPAR_in-Too-Many-Instances_RPAR_) 5 := 0
- [limits] Thresholds reached
  - [limit] maximum number of E-matching rounds has been reached, threshold: `(ematch := 5)`

[grind] Diagnostics

- [thm] E-Matching instances
  - [thm] [s_eq]](#manual-s_eq-_LPAR_in-Too-Many-Instances_RPAR_) ↦ 5
```

Increasing the round limit to 20 causes E-matching to terminate due to the default generation limit of 8:

```lean
example : [s]](#manual-s-_LPAR_in-Too-Many-Instances_RPAR_) 0 > 0 := by⊢ [s]](#manual-s-_LPAR_in-Too-Many-Instances_RPAR_) 0 > 0
[grind]](#manual-grind) (ematch := 20)All goals completed! 🐙
```

```lean
`grind` failed
grindh:[s]](#manual-s-_LPAR_in-Too-Many-Instances_RPAR_) 0 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0⊢ [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)
[grind] Goal diagnostics
```

**Example: Increasing E-matching Limits**

`[iota]](#manual-iota-_LPAR_in-Increasing-E-matching-Limits_RPAR_)` returns the list of all numbers strictly less than its argument, and the theorem `[iota_succ]](#manual-iota_succ-_LPAR_in-Increasing-E-matching-Limits_RPAR_)` describes its behavior on `[Nat.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`:

```lean
def iota : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| 0 => []
| n + 1 => n :: [iota]](#manual-iota-_LPAR_in-Increasing-E-matching-Limits_RPAR_) n
@[grind =] theorem iota_succ : [iota]](#manual-iota-_LPAR_in-Increasing-E-matching-Limits_RPAR_) (n + 1) = n :: [iota]](#manual-iota-_LPAR_in-Increasing-E-matching-Limits_RPAR_) n :=
[rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)
```

## The grind tactic — 16.7. Linear Integer Arithmetic {#manual-the-grind-tactic-167-linear-integer-arithmetic}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Linear-Integer-Arithmetic/

The linear integer arithmetic solver implements a model-based decision procedure for linear integer arithmetic.
The solver can process four categories of linear polynomial constraints (where `p` is a [linear polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Degree_of_a_polynomial)):

Equality
:   `p = 0`

Divisibility
:   `d ∣ p`

Inequality
:   `p ≤ 0`

Disequality
:   `p ≠ 0`

It is complete for linear integer arithmetic, and natural numbers are supported by converting them to integers with `[Int.ofNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)`.
Support for additional types that can be embedded into `[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)` can be added via instances of `[Lean.Grind.ToInt]](#manual-Lean___Grind___ToInt___mk)`.
Nonlinear terms (e.g. `x * x`) are allowed, and are represented as variables.
The solver is additionally capable of propagating information back to the metaphorical `[grind]](#manual-grind)` whiteboard, which can trigger further progress from the other subsystems.
By default, it is enabled; it can be disabled using the flag `-lia`

**Example: Examples of Linear Integer Arithmetic**

All of these statements can be proved using the linear integer arithmetic solver.
In the first example, the left-hand side must be a multiple of 2, and thus cannot be 5:

```lean
example {x y : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)} : 2 * x + 4 * y ≠ 5 := byx:[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)y:[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)⊢ 2 [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) x [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 4 [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) y ≠ 5
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

The solver supports mixing equalities and inequalities:

```lean
example {x y : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)} :
2 * x + 3 * y = 0 →
1 ≤ x →
y < 1 := byx:[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)y:[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)⊢ 2 [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) x [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 3 [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) y [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0 → 1 [≤]](#manual-LE___mk) x → y [<]](#manual-LT___mk) 1
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

It also supports linear divisibility constraints:

```lean
example (a b : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)) :
2 ∣ a + 1 →
2 ∣ b + a →
¬ 2 ∣ b + 2 * a := bya:[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)b:[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)⊢ 2 [∣]](#manual-Dvd___mk) a [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 1 → 2 [∣]](#manual-Dvd___mk) b [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) a → [¬](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)2 [∣]](#manual-Dvd___mk) b [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 2 [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) a
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

Without `lia`, `[grind]](#manual-grind)` cannot prove the statement:

```lean
example (a b : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)) :
2 ∣ a + 1 →
2 ∣ b + a →
¬ 2 ∣ b + 2 * a := bya:[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)b:[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)⊢ 2 [∣]](#manual-Dvd___mk) a [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 1 → 2 [∣]](#manual-Dvd___mk) b [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) a → [¬](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)2 [∣]](#manual-Dvd___mk) b [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 2 [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) a
[grind]](#manual-grind) -liaAll goals completed! 🐙
```

### 16.7.1. Rational Solutions {#manual-cutsat-qlia}

The solver is complete for linear integer arithmetic.
However, the search can become vast with very few constraints, but the solver was not designed to perform massive case-analysis.
The `qlia` option to `[grind]](#manual-grind)` reduces the search space by instructing the solver to accept rational solutions.
With this option, the solver is likely to be faster, but it is incomplete.

**Example: Rational Solutions**

The following example has a rational solution, but does not have integer solutions:

```lean
example {x y : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)} :
27 ≤ 13 * x + 11 * y →
13 * x + 11 * y ≤ 30 →
-10 ≤ 9 * x - 7 * y →
9 * x - 7 * y > 4 := byx:[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)y:[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)⊢ 27 [≤]](#manual-LE___mk) 13 [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) x [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 11 [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) y → 13 [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) x [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 11 [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) y [≤]](#manual-LE___mk) 30 → -10 [≤]](#manual-LE___mk) 9 [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) x [-]](#manual-HSub___mk) 7 [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) y → 9 [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) x [-]](#manual-HSub___mk) 7 [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) y > 4
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

Because it uses the rational solution, `[grind]](#manual-grind)` fails to refute the negation of the goal when `+qlia` is specified:

```lean
example {x y : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)} :
27 ≤ 13 * x + 11 * y →
13 * x + 11 * y ≤ 30 →
-10 ≤ 9 * x - 7 * y →
9 * x - 7 * y > 4 := byx:[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)y:[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)⊢ 27 [≤]](#manual-LE___mk) 13 [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) x [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 11 [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) y → 13 [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) x [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 11 [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) y [≤]](#manual-LE___mk) 30 → -10 [≤]](#manual-LE___mk) 9 [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) x [-]](#manual-HSub___mk) 7 [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) y → 9 [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) x [-]](#manual-HSub___mk) 7 [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) y > 4
[grind]](#manual-grind) +qliaAll goals completed! 🐙
```

### 16.7.2. Nonlinear Constraints {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--The--grind--tactic--Linear-Integer-Arithmetic--Nonlinear-Constraints}

The solver currently does support nonlinear constraints, and treats nonlinear terms such as `x * x` as variables.

**Example: Nonlinear Terms**

The linear integer arithmetic solver fails to prove this theorem:

```lean
example (x : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)) : x * x ≥ 0 := byx:[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)⊢ x [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) x ≥ 0
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

```lean
example (x : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)) : x*x ≥ 0 := byx:[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)⊢ x [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) x ≥ 0
```


The term `x ^ 2` is “quoted” in `「x ^ 2」 + 1 ≤ 0` to indicate that `x ^ 2` is treated as a variable.

### 16.7.3. Division and Modulus {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--The--grind--tactic--Linear-Integer-Arithmetic--Division-and-Modulus}

The solver supports linear division and modulo operations.

**Example: Linear Division and Modulo**

```lean
example (x y : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)) :
x = y / 2 →
y % 2 = 0 →
y - 2 * x = 0 := byx:[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)y:[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)⊢ x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) y [/]](#manual-HDiv___mk) 2 → y [%]](#manual-HMod___mk) 2 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0 → y [-]](#manual-HSub___mk) 2 [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

### 16.7.4. Algebraic Processing {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--The--grind--tactic--Linear-Integer-Arithmetic--Algebraic-Processing}

The solver normalizes commutative (semi)ring expressions.

**Example: Commutative (Semi)ring Normalization**

Commutative ring normalization allows this goal to be solved:

```lean
example (a b : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
(h₁ : a + 1 ≠ a * b * a)
(h₂ : a * a * b ≤ a + 1) :
b * a ^ 2 < a + 1 := bya:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)b:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h₁:a [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 1 ≠ a [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) b [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) ah₂:a [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) a [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) b [≤]](#manual-LE___mk) a [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 1⊢ b [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) a [^]](#manual-HPow___mk) 2 [<]](#manual-LT___mk) a [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 1
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

### 16.7.5. Propagating Information {#manual-cutsat-mbtc}

The solver also implements *model-based theory combination*, which is a mechanism for propagating equalities back to the metaphorical shared whiteboard.
These additional equalities may in turn trigger new congruences.
Model-based theory combination increases the size of the search space; it can be disabled using the option `grind -mbtc`.

**Example: Propagating Equalities**

In the example above, the linear inequalities and disequalities imply `y = 0`:

```lean
example (f : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) → [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)) (x y : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)) :
f x = 0 →
0 ≤ y → y ≤ 1 → y ≠ 1 →
f (x + y) = 0 := byf:[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) → [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)x:[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)y:[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)⊢ f x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0 → 0 [≤]](#manual-LE___mk) y → y [≤]](#manual-LE___mk) 1 → y ≠ 1 → f [(]](#manual-HAdd___mk)x [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) y[)]](#manual-HAdd___mk) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

Consequently `x = x + y`, so `f x = f (x + y)` by [congruence]](#manual---tech-term-Congruence-closure).
Without model-based theory combination, the proof gets stuck:

```lean
example (f : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) → [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)) (x y : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)) :
f x = 0 →
0 ≤ y → y ≤ 1 → y ≠ 1 →
f (x + y) = 0 := byf:[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) → [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)x:[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)y:[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)⊢ f x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0 → 0 [≤]](#manual-LE___mk) y → y [≤]](#manual-LE___mk) 1 → y ≠ 1 → f [(]](#manual-HAdd___mk)x [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) y[)]](#manual-HAdd___mk) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0
[grind]](#manual-grind) -mbtcAll goals completed! 🐙
```

### 16.7.6. Other Types {#manual-cutsat-ToInt}

The LIA solver can also process linear constraints that contain natural numbers.
It converts them into integer constraints using `Int.ofNat`.

**Example: Natural Numbers as Linear Integer Arithmetic**

```lean
example (x y z : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) :
x < y + z →
y + 1 < z →
z + x < 3 * z := byx:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)y:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)z:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ x [<]](#manual-LT___mk) y [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) z → y [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 1 [<]](#manual-LT___mk) z → z [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) x [<]](#manual-LT___mk) 3 [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) z
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

There is an extensible mechanism via the `[Lean.Grind.ToInt]](#manual-Lean___Grind___ToInt___mk)` type class to tell the solver that a type embeds in the integers.
Using this, we can solve goals such as:

```lean
example (a b c : [Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) 11) : a ≤ 2 → b ≤ 3 → c = a + b → c ≤ 5 := bya:[Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) 11b:[Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) 11c:[Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) 11⊢ a [≤]](#manual-LE___mk) 2 → b [≤]](#manual-LE___mk) 3 → c [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) a [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) b → c [≤]](#manual-LE___mk) 5
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
example (a : [Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) 2) : a ≠ 0 → a ≠ 1 → [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False) := bya:[Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) 2⊢ a ≠ 0 → a ≠ 1 → [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
example (a b c : [UInt64](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#UInt64___ofBitVec)) : a ≤ 2 → b ≤ 3 → c - a - b = 0 → c ≤ 5 := bya:[UInt64](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#UInt64___ofBitVec)b:[UInt64](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#UInt64___ofBitVec)c:[UInt64](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#UInt64___ofBitVec)⊢ a [≤]](#manual-LE___mk) 2 → b [≤]](#manual-LE___mk) 3 → c [-]](#manual-HSub___mk) a [-]](#manual-HSub___mk) b [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0 → c [≤]](#manual-LE___mk) 5
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```
