### 16.7.7. Implementation Notes {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--The--grind--tactic--Linear-Integer-Arithmetic--Implementation-Notes}

The implementation of the linear integer arithmetic solver is inspired by Section 4 of Jovanović and de Moura (2023)Dejan Jovanović and Leonardo de Moura, 2023. [“Cutting to the Chase: Solving Linear Integer Arithmetic”](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-642-22438-6_26). In *Automated Deduction: CADE '23.* (LNCS 6803).
Compared to the paper, it includes several enhancements and modifications such as:

- extended constraint support (equality and disequality),
- an optimized encoding of the `Cooper-Left` rule using a “big”-disjunction instead of fresh variables, and
- decision variable tracking for case splits (disequalities, `Cooper-Left`, `Cooper-Right`).

The solver procedure builds a model (that is, an assignment of the variables in the term) incrementally, resolving conflicts through constraint generation.
For example, given a partial model `{x := 1}` and constraint `3 ∣ 3 * y + x + 1`:

- The solver cannot extend the model to `y` because `3 ∣ 3 * y + 2` is unsatisfiable.
- Thus, it resolves the conflict by generating the implied constraint `3 ∣ x + 1`.
- The new constraint forces the solver to find a new assignment for `x`.

When assigning a variable `y`, the solver considers:

- The best upper and lower bounds (inequalities).
- A divisibility constraint.
- All disequality constraints where `y` is the maximal variable.

The `Cooper-Left` and `Cooper-Right` rules handle the combination of inequalities and divisibility.
For unsatisfiable disequalities `p ≠ 0`, the solver generates the case split: `p + 1 ≤ 0 ∨ -p + 1 ≤ 0`.

---



## The grind tactic — 16.8. Algebraic Solver (Commutative Rings, Fields) {#manual-the-grind-tactic-168-algebraic-solver-commutative-rings-fields}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Algebraic-Solver-_LPAR_Commutative-Rings___-Fields_RPAR_/

The `ring` solver in `[grind]](#manual-grind)` is inspired by Gröbner basis computation procedures and term rewriting completion.
It views multivariate polynomials as rewriting rules.
For example, the polynomial equality `x * y + x - 2 = 0` is treated as a rewriting rule `x * y ↦ -x + 2`.
It uses superposition to ensure the rewriting system is confluent.

The following examples demonstrate goals that can be decided by the `ring` solver.
In these examples, the `Lean` and `Lean.Grind` namespaces are open:

```lean
[open]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___open) Lean Grind
```

**Example: Commutative Rings**

```lean
example [[CommRing]](#manual-Lean___Grind___CommRing___mk) α] (x : α) : (x + 1) * (x - 1) = x ^ 2 - 1 := byα:Type u_1inst✝:[CommRing]](#manual-Lean___Grind___CommRing___mk) αx:α⊢ [(]](#manual-HAdd___mk)x [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 1[)]](#manual-HAdd___mk) [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) [(]](#manual-HSub___mk)x [-]](#manual-HSub___mk) 1[)]](#manual-HSub___mk) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) x [^]](#manual-HPow___mk) 2 [-]](#manual-HSub___mk) 1
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

**Example: Ring Characteristics**

The solver “knows” that `16*16 = 0` because the [ring characteristic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Characteristic_%28algebra%29) (that is, the minimum number of copies of the multiplicative identity that sum to the additive identity) is `256`, which is provided by the `[IsCharP]](#manual-Lean___Grind___IsCharP___mk)` instance.

```lean
example [[CommRing]](#manual-Lean___Grind___CommRing___mk) α] [[IsCharP]](#manual-Lean___Grind___IsCharP___mk) α 256] (x : α) :
(x + 16)*(x - 16) = x^2 := byα:Type u_1inst✝¹:[CommRing]](#manual-Lean___Grind___CommRing___mk) αinst✝:[IsCharP]](#manual-Lean___Grind___IsCharP___mk) α 256x:α⊢ [(]](#manual-HAdd___mk)x [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 16[)]](#manual-HAdd___mk) [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) [(]](#manual-HSub___mk)x [-]](#manual-HSub___mk) 16[)]](#manual-HSub___mk) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) x [^]](#manual-HPow___mk) 2
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

**Example: Standard Library Types**

Types in the standard library are supported by the solver out of the box.
`UInt8` is a commutative ring with characteristic `256`, and thus has instances of `[CommRing]](#manual-Lean___Grind___CommRing___mk) [UInt8](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#UInt8___ofBitVec)` and `[IsCharP]](#manual-Lean___Grind___IsCharP___mk) [UInt8](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#UInt8___ofBitVec) 256`.

```lean
example (x : [UInt8](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#UInt8___ofBitVec)) : (x + 16) * (x - 16) = x ^ 2 := byx:[UInt8](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Fixed-Precision-Integers/#UInt8___ofBitVec)⊢ [(]](#manual-HAdd___mk)x [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 16[)]](#manual-HAdd___mk) [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) [(]](#manual-HSub___mk)x [-]](#manual-HSub___mk) 16[)]](#manual-HSub___mk) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) x [^]](#manual-HPow___mk) 2
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

**Example: More Commutative Ring Proofs**

The axioms of a commutative ring are sufficient to prove these statements.

```lean

a + b + c = 3 →
a ^ 2 + b ^ 2 + c ^ 2 = 5 →
a ^ 3 + b ^ 3 + c ^ 3 = 7 →
a ^ 4 + b ^ 4 = 9 - c ^ 4 := byα:Type u_1inst✝:[CommRing]](#manual-Lean___Grind___CommRing___mk) αa:αb:αc:α⊢ a [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) b [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) c [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 3 → a [^]](#manual-HPow___mk) 2 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) b [^]](#manual-HPow___mk) 2 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) c [^]](#manual-HPow___mk) 2 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 5 → a [^]](#manual-HPow___mk) 3 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) b [^]](#manual-HPow___mk) 3 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) c [^]](#manual-HPow___mk) 3 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 7 → a [^]](#manual-HPow___mk) 4 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) b [^]](#manual-HPow___mk) 4 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 9 [-]](#manual-HSub___mk) c [^]](#manual-HPow___mk) 4

**Example: Characteristic Zero**

`ring` proves that `a + 1 = 2 + a` is unsatisfiable because the characteristic is known to be 0.

```lean
example [[CommRing]](#manual-Lean___Grind___CommRing___mk) α] [[IsCharP]](#manual-Lean___Grind___IsCharP___mk) α 0] (a : α) :
a + 1 = 2 + a → [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False) := byα:Type u_1inst✝¹:[CommRing]](#manual-Lean___Grind___CommRing___mk) αinst✝:[IsCharP]](#manual-Lean___Grind___IsCharP___mk) α 0a:α⊢ a [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 1 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 2 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) a → [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

**Example: Inferred Characteristic**

Even when the characteristic is not initially known, when `grind` discovers that `n = 0` for some numeral `n`, it makes inferences about the characteristic:

```lean

(h₁ : a + 6 = a) (h₂ : c = c + 9) (h : b + 3*c = 0) :
27*a + b = 0 := byα:Type u_1inst✝:[CommRing]](#manual-Lean___Grind___CommRing___mk) αa:αb:αc:αh₁:a [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 6 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) ah₂:c [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) c [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 9h:b [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 3 [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) c [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0⊢ 27 [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) a [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) b [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

### 16.8.1. Solver Type Classes {#manual-grind-ring-classes}

Users can enable the `ring` solver for their own types by providing instances of the following [type classes]](#manual---tech-term-type-class), all in the `Lean.Grind` namespace:

- `[Semiring]](#manual-Lean___Grind___Semiring___mk)`
- `[Ring]](#manual-Lean___Grind___Ring___mk)`
- `[CommSemiring]](#manual-Lean___Grind___CommSemiring___mk)`
- `[CommRing]](#manual-Lean___Grind___CommRing___mk)`
- `[IsCharP]](#manual-Lean___Grind___IsCharP___mk)`
- `[AddRightCancel]](#manual-Lean___Grind___AddRightCancel___mk)`
- `[NoNatZeroDivisors]](#manual-Lean___Grind___NoNatZeroDivisors___mk)`
- `[Field]](#manual-Lean___Grind___Field___mk)`

The algebraic solvers will self-configure depending on the availability of these instances, so not all need to be provided.
The capabilities of the algebraic solvers will, of course, degrade when some are not available.

The Lean standard library contains the applicable instances for the types defined in the standard library.
By providing these instances, other libraries can also enable `[grind]](#manual-grind)`'s `ring` solver.
For example, the Mathlib `CommRing` type class implements `Lean.Grind.CommRing` to ensure the `ring` solver works out-of-the-box.

#### 16.8.1.1. Algebraic Structures {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--The--grind--tactic--Algebraic-Solver-_LPAR_Commutative-Rings___-Fields_RPAR_--Solver-Type-Classes--Algebraic-Structures}

To enable the algebraic solver, a type should have an instance of the most specific possible algebraic structure that the solver supports.
In order of increasing specificity, that is `[Semiring]](#manual-Lean___Grind___Semiring___mk)`, `[Ring]](#manual-Lean___Grind___Ring___mk)`, `[CommSemiring]](#manual-Lean___Grind___CommSemiring___mk)`, `[CommRing]](#manual-Lean___Grind___CommRing___mk)`, and `[Field]](#manual-Lean___Grind___Field___mk)`.

type class

```lean

[Lean.Grind.Semiring.{u}]](#manual-Lean___Grind___Semiring___mk) (α : Type u) :
  Type u
```

A semiring, i.e. a type equipped with addition, multiplication, and a map from the natural numbers,
satisfying appropriate compatibilities.

Use `Ring` instead if the type also has negation,
`CommSemiring` if the multiplication is commutative,
or `CommRing` if the type has negation and multiplication is commutative.

In every ring there is a canonical map from the integers to the ring.

```lean

```

Scalar multiplication by integers.

```lean
neg_add_cancel : ∀ (a : α), [-]](#manual-Neg___mk)a [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0
```

Negation is the left inverse of addition.

```lean
sub_eq_add_neg : ∀ (a b : α), a [-]](#manual-HSub___mk) b [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) a [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) [-]](#manual-Neg___mk)b
```

Subtraction is addition of the negative.

```lean
neg_zsmul : ∀ (i : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)) (a : α), [-]](#manual-Neg___mk)i • a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [-]](#manual-Neg___mk)(i • a)
```

Scalar multiplication by the negation of an integer is the negation of scalar multiplication by that integer.

```lean
zsmul_natCast_eq_nsmul : ∀ (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (a : α), ↑n • a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) n • a
```

Scalar multiplication by natural numbers is consistent with scalar multiplication by integers.

```lean
intCast_ofNat : ∀ (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)), ↑([OfNat.ofNat]](#manual-OfNat___mk) n) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [OfNat.ofNat]](#manual-OfNat___mk) n
```

The canonical map from the integers is consistent with the canonical map from the natural numbers.

```lean
intCast_neg : ∀ (i : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)), ↑[(]](#manual-Neg___mk)[-]](#manual-Neg___mk)i[)]](#manual-Neg___mk) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [-]](#manual-Neg___mk)↑i
```

The canonical map from the integers is consistent with negation.

##### 16.8.1.1.1. Fields {#manual-grind-ring-field}

The `ring` solver also has support for `[Field]](#manual-Lean___Grind___Field___mk)`s.
If a `[Field]](#manual-Lean___Grind___Field___mk)` instance is available, the solver preprocesses the term `a / b` into `a * b⁻¹`.
It also rewrites every disequality `p ≠ 0` as the equality `p * p⁻¹ = 1`.

**Example: Fields and grind**

This example requires its `[Field]](#manual-Lean___Grind___Field___mk)` instance:

```lean
example [[Field]](#manual-Lean___Grind___Field___mk) α] (a : α) :
a ^ 2 = 0 →
a = 0 := byα:Type u_1inst✝:[Field]](#manual-Lean___Grind___Field___mk) αa:α⊢ a [^]](#manual-HPow___mk) 2 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0 → a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

type class

```lean
[Lean.Grind.Field.{u}]](#manual-Lean___Grind___Field___mk) (α : Type u) : Type u



[Lean.Grind.Field.{u}]](#manual-Lean___Grind___Field___mk) (α : Type u) : Type u
```

A field is a commutative ring with inverses for all non-zero elements.

Zero is not equal to one: fields are non trivial.

The inverse of zero is zero. This is a "junk value" convention.

```lean

```

The inverse of a non-zero element is a right inverse.

```lean
zpow_zero : ∀ (a : α), a [^]](#manual-HPow___mk) 0 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 1
```

The zeroth power of any element is one.

```lean
zpow_succ : ∀ (a : α) (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)), a [^]](#manual-HPow___mk) [(]](#manual-HAdd___mk)↑n [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 1[)]](#manual-HAdd___mk) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) a [^]](#manual-HPow___mk) ↑n [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) a
```

The (n+1)-st power of any element is the element multiplied by the n-th power.

```lean
zpow_neg : ∀ (a : α) (n : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)), a [^]](#manual-HPow___mk) [(]](#manual-Neg___mk)[-]](#manual-Neg___mk)n[)]](#manual-Neg___mk) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [(]](#manual-HPow___mk)a [^]](#manual-HPow___mk) n[)]](#manual-HPow___mk)⁻¹
```

Raising to a negative power is the inverse of raising to the positive power.

[Lean.Grind.IsCharP.{u}]](#manual-Lean___Grind___IsCharP___mk) (α : Type u)
  [[Lean.Grind.Semiring]](#manual-Lean___Grind___Semiring___mk) α]
  (p : [outParam]](#manual-outParam) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : Prop
```

A ring `α` has characteristic `p` if `[OfNat.ofNat]](#manual-OfNat___mk) x = 0` iff `x % p = 0`.

Note that for `p = 0`, we have `x % p = x`, so this says that `[OfNat.ofNat]](#manual-OfNat___mk)` is injective from `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` to `α`.

In the case of a semiring, we take the stronger condition that
`[OfNat.ofNat]](#manual-OfNat___mk) x = [OfNat.ofNat]](#manual-OfNat___mk) y` iff `x % p = y % p`.

```

```

Two numerals in a semiring are equal iff they are congruent module `p` in the natural numbers.

#### 16.8.1.3. Natural Number Zero Divisors {#manual-NoNatZeroDivisors}

The class `NoNatZeroDivisors` is used to control coefficient growth.
For example, the polynomial `2 * x * y + 4 * z = 0` is simplified to `x * y + 2 * z = 0`.
It also used when processing disequalities.

**Example: Using NoNatZeroDivisors**

In this example, `[grind]](#manual-grind)` relies on the `[NoNatZeroDivisors]](#manual-Lean___Grind___NoNatZeroDivisors___mk)` instance to simplify the goal:

```lean

2 * a + 2 * b = 0 →
b ≠ -a → [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False) := byα:Type u_1inst✝¹:[CommRing]](#manual-Lean___Grind___CommRing___mk) αinst✝:[NoNatZeroDivisors]](#manual-Lean___Grind___NoNatZeroDivisors___mk) αa:αb:α⊢ 2 [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) a [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 2 [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) b [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0 → b ≠ [-]](#manual-Neg___mk)a → [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)

  Prop
```

We say a module has no natural number zero divisors if
`k ≠ 0` and `k * a = k * b` implies `a = b` (here `k` is a natural number and `a` and `b` are element of the module).

For a module over the integers this is equivalent to
`k ≠ 0` and `k * a = 0` implies `a = 0`.
(See the alternative constructor `NoNatZeroDivisors.mk'`,
and the theorem `eq_zero_of_mul_eq_zero`.)

Instance Constructor

```lean
[Lean.Grind.NoNatZeroDivisors.mk]](#manual-Lean___Grind___NoNatZeroDivisors___mk).{u}
```

Methods

```lean
no_nat_zero_divisors : ∀ (k : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (a b : α), k ≠ 0 → k • a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) k • b → a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) b
```

If `k * a ≠ k * b` then `k ≠ 0` or `a ≠ b`.

The `ring` module also performs case-analysis for terms `a⁻¹` on whether `a` is zero or not.
In the following example, if `2*a` is zero, then `a` is also zero since
we have `NoNatZeroDivisors α`, and all terms are zero and the equality hold. Otherwise,
`ring` adds the equalities `a*a⁻¹ = 1` and `2*a*(2*a)⁻¹ = 1`, and closes the goal.

```lean
example [[Field]](#manual-Lean___Grind___Field___mk) α] [[NoNatZeroDivisors]](#manual-Lean___Grind___NoNatZeroDivisors___mk) α] (a : α) :
1 / a + 1 / (2 * a) = 3 / (2 * a) := byα:Type u_1inst✝¹:[Field]](#manual-Lean___Grind___Field___mk) αinst✝:[NoNatZeroDivisors]](#manual-Lean___Grind___NoNatZeroDivisors___mk) αa:α⊢ 1 [/]](#manual-HDiv___mk) a [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 1 [/]](#manual-HDiv___mk) [(]](#manual-HMul___mk)2 [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) a[)]](#manual-HMul___mk) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 3 [/]](#manual-HDiv___mk) [(]](#manual-HMul___mk)2 [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) a[)]](#manual-HMul___mk)
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

##### 16.8.1.3.1. Right-Cancellative Addition {#manual-AddRightCancel}

The `ring` solver automatically embeds `CommSemiring`s into a `CommRing` envelope (using the construction `Lean.Grind.Ring.OfSemiring.Q`).
However, the embedding is injective only when the `CommSemiring` implements the type class `AddRightCancel`.
`Nat` is an example of a commutative semiring that implements `AddRightCancel`.

```lean
example (x y : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) :
x ^ 2 * y = 1 →
x * y ^ 2 = y →
y * x = 1 := byx:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)y:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ x [^]](#manual-HPow___mk) 2 [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) y [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 1 → x [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) y [^]](#manual-HPow___mk) 2 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) y → y [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 1
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

### 16.8.2. Resource Limits {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--The--grind--tactic--Algebraic-Solver-_LPAR_Commutative-Rings___-Fields_RPAR_--Resource-Limits}

The `ring` solver propagates equalities back to the `grind` core by normalizing terms using the computed Gröbner basis.
In the following example, the equations `x ^ 2 * y = 1` and `x * y ^ 2 = y` imply the equalities `x = 1` and `y = 1`.
Thus, the terms `x * y` and `1` are equal, and consequently `some (x * y) = some 1` by congruence.

```lean
example (x y : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)) :
x ^ 2 * y = 1 →
x * y ^ 2 = y →
[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) (y * x) = [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) 1 := byx:[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)y:[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)⊢ x [^]](#manual-HPow___mk) 2 [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) y [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 1 → x [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) y [^]](#manual-HPow___mk) 2 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) y → [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [(]](#manual-HMul___mk)y [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) x[)]](#manual-HMul___mk) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) 1
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

## The grind tactic — 16.9. Linear Arithmetic Solver {#manual-the-grind-tactic-169-linear-arithmetic-solver}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Linear-Arithmetic-Solver/

The `[grind]](#manual-grind)` tactic includes a linear arithmetic solver for arbitrary types, called `linarith`, that is used for types not supported by [`cutsat`]](#manual-cutsat).
Like the [`ring`]](#manual-grind-ring) solver, it can be used with any type that has instances of certain type classes.
It self-configures depending on the availability of these type classes, so it is not necessary to provide all of them to use the solver; however, its capabilities are increased by the availability of more instances.
This solver is useful for reasoning about the real numbers, ordered vector spaces, and other types that can't be embedded into `[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)`.

The core functionality of `linarith` is a model-based solver for linear inequalities with integer coefficients.
It can be disabled using the option `grind -linarith`.

**Example: Goals Decided by linarith**

All of these examples rely on instances of the following ordering notation and `linarith` classes:

```lean
[variable]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___variable) [[LE]](#manual-LE___mk) α] [[LT]](#manual-LT___mk) α] [Std.LawfulOrderLT α] [Std.IsLinearOrder α]
[variable]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___variable) [[IntModule]](#manual-Lean___Grind___IntModule___mk) α] [[OrderedAdd]](#manual-Lean___Grind___OrderedAdd___mk) α]
```

Integer modules (`[IntModule]](#manual-Lean___Grind___IntModule___mk)`) are types with zero, addition, negation, subtraction, and scalar multiplication by integers that satisfy the expected properties of these operations.
Linear orders (`Std.IsLinearOrder`) are orders in which any pair of elements is ordered, and `[OrderedAdd]](#manual-Lean___Grind___OrderedAdd___mk)` states that adding a constant to both sides preserves orderings.

**Example: Commutative Ring Goals Decided by linarith**

For types that are commmutative rings (that is, types in which the multiplication operator is commutative) with `[CommRing]](#manual-Lean___Grind___CommRing___mk)` instances, `linarith` has more capabilities.

```lean
[variable]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___variable) [[LE]](#manual-LE___mk) R] [[LT]](#manual-LT___mk) R] [Std.IsLinearOrder R] [Std.LawfulOrderLT R]
[variable]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___variable) [[CommRing]](#manual-Lean___Grind___CommRing___mk) R] [[OrderedRing]](#manual-Lean___Grind___OrderedRing___mk) R]
```

The `[CommRing]](#manual-Lean___Grind___CommRing___mk) R` instance allows `linarith` to perform basic normalization, such as identifying linear atoms `a * b` and `b * a`, and to account for scalar multiplication on both sides.
The `[OrderedRing]](#manual-Lean___Grind___OrderedRing___mk) R` instance allows the solver to support constants, because it has access to the fact that `(0 : R) < 1`.

[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙

### 16.9.1. Supporting `linarith` {#manual-grind-linarith-classes}

To add support for a new type to `linarith`, the first step is to implement `[IntModule]](#manual-Lean___Grind___IntModule___mk)` if possible, or `[NatModule]](#manual-Lean___Grind___NatModule___mk)` otherwise.
Every `[Ring]](#manual-Lean___Grind___Ring___mk)` is already an `[IntModule]](#manual-Lean___Grind___IntModule___mk)`, and every `[Semiring]](#manual-Lean___Grind___Semiring___mk)` is already a `[NatModule]](#manual-Lean___Grind___NatModule___mk)`, so implementing one of those instances is also sufficient.
Next, one of the order classes (`Std.IsPreorder`, `Std.IsPartialOrder`, or `Std.IsLinearOrder`) should be implemented.
Typically an `IsPreorder` instance is enough when the context already includes a contradiction, but an `IsLinearOrder` instance is required in order to prove linear inequality goals.
Additional features are enabled by implementing `[OrderedAdd]](#manual-Lean___Grind___OrderedAdd___mk)`, which expresses that the additive structure in a module is compatible with the order, and `[OrderedRing]](#manual-Lean___Grind___OrderedRing___mk)`, which improves support for constants.

type class

```lean
[Lean.Grind.NatModule.{u}]](#manual-Lean___Grind___NatModule___mk) (M : Type u) : Type u



[Lean.Grind.NatModule.{u}]](#manual-Lean___Grind___NatModule___mk) (M : Type u) :
  Type u
```

A module over the natural numbers, i.e. a type with zero, addition, and scalar multiplication by natural numbers,
satisfying appropriate compatibilities.

Equivalently, an additive commutative monoid.

Use `[IntModule]](#manual-Lean___Grind___IntModule___mk)` if the type has negation.

[Lean.Grind.NatModule.mk]](#manual-Lean___Grind___NatModule___mk).{u}

## The grind tactic — 16.10. Annotating Libraries for `grind` {#manual-the-grind-tactic-1610-annotating-libraries-for}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Annotating-Libraries-for--grind/

To use `[grind]](#manual-grind)` effectively with a library, it must be annotated by applying the `grind` attribute to suitable lemmas or declaring `grind_pattern`s.
These annotations direct `[grind]](#manual-grind)`'s selection of theorems, which lead to further facts on the metaphorical whiteboard.
With too few annotations, `[grind]](#manual-grind)` will fail to use the lemmas; with too many, it may become slow or it fail due to exhausting resource limitations.
Annotations should generally be conservative: only add an annotation if you expect that `[grind]](#manual-grind)` should *always* instantiate the theorem once the patterns are matched.

### 16.10.1. Simp Lemmas {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--The--grind--tactic--Annotating-Libraries-for--grind--Simp-Lemmas}

Typically, many theorems that are annotated with `[@[]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)simp[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Attributes/#Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)` should also be annotated with `[@[]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)grind =[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Attributes/#Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)`.
One significant exception is that typically we avoid having `[@[]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)simp[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Attributes/#Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)` theorems that introduce an `if` on the right hand side, instead preferring a pair of theorems with the positive and negative conditions as hypotheses.
Because `[grind]](#manual-grind)` is designed to perform case splitting, it is generally better to instead annotate the single theorem introducing the `if` with `[@[]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)grind =[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Attributes/#Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)`.

Besides using `[@[]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)grind =[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Attributes/#Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)` to encourage `[grind]](#manual-grind)` to perform rewriting from left to right, you can also use `[@[]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)grind _=_[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Attributes/#Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)` to “saturate”, allowing bidirectional rewriting whenever either side is encountered.

### 16.10.2. Backwards and Forwards Reasoning {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--The--grind--tactic--Annotating-Libraries-for--grind--Backwards-and-Forwards-Reasoning}

Use `[@[]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)grind ←[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Attributes/#Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)` (which generates patterns from the conclusion of the theorem) for backwards reasoning theorems, i.e. theorems that should be tried when their conclusion matches a goal.
Some examples of theorems in the standard library that are annotated with `grind ←` are:

- ```lean
  Array.not_mem_empty (a : α) : ¬ a ∈ #[]
  ```
- ```lean
  Array.getElem_filter
  {xs : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) α} {p : α → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)} {i : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)}
  (h : i < (xs.[filter](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___filter) p).[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size)) :
  p (xs.[filter](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___filter) p)[i]
  ```
- ```lean
  List.Pairwise.tail
  {l : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α} (h : [Pairwise](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___Pairwise___nil) R l) :
  [Pairwise](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___Pairwise___nil) R l.[tail](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___tail)
  ```

In each case, the lemma is relevant when its conclusion matches a proof goal.

Use `[@[]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)grind →[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Attributes/#Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)` (which generates patterns from the hypotheses) for forwards reasoning theorems,
i.e. where facts should be propagated from existing facts on the whiteboard.
Some examples of theorems in the standard library that are annotated with `grind →` are:

- ```lean
  List.getElem_of_getElem? {l : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α} :
  l[i]? = [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) a →
  ∃ h : i < l.[length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length), l[i] = a
  ```
- ```lean
  Array.mem_of_mem_erase [[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk) α] {a b : α} {xs : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) α}
  (h : a ∈ xs.[erase](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___erase) b) :
  a ∈ xs
  ```
- ```lean
  List.forall_none_of_filterMap_eq_nil
  (h : [filterMap](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___filterMap) f xs = []) :
  ∀ x ∈ xs, f x = [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
  ```

In these cases, the theorems' assumptions determine when they are relevant.

There are many uses for custom patterns created with the `grind_pattern` command.
One common use is to introduce inequalities about terms, or membership propositions.

We might have

```lean
[variable]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___variable) [[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk) α]
theorem count_le_size {a : α} {xs : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) α} : count a xs ≤ xs.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size) :=
...
grind_pattern [count_le_size]](#manual-count_le_size) => count a xs
```

which will register this inequality as soon as a `count a xs` term is encountered (even if the problem has not previously involved inequalities).

We can also use multi-patterns to be more restrictive, e.g. only introducing an inequality about sizes if the whiteboard already contains facts about sizes:

```lean
theorem size_pos_of_mem {xs : [Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) α} (h : a ∈ xs) : 0 < xs.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size) :=
sorry
grind_pattern [size_pos_of_mem]](#manual-size_pos_of_mem) => a ∈ xs, xs.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size)
```

Unlike a `[@[]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)grind →[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Attributes/#Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)` attribute, which would cause this theorem to be instantiated whenever `a ∈ xs` is encountered, this pattern will only be used when `xs.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size)` is already on the whiteboard.
(Note that this grind pattern could also be produced using the `[@[]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)grind <=[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Attributes/#Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)` attribute, which looks at the conclusion first, then backwards through the hypotheses to select patterns.
On the other hand, `[@[]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)grind →[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Attributes/#Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)` would select only `a ∈ xs`.)

In Mathlib we might want to enable polynomial reasoning about the sine and cosine functions,
and so add a custom grind pattern

```lean
theorem sin_sq_add_cos_sq : [sin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Bigger-Examples/#sin) x ^ 2 + [cos](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Bigger-Examples/#cos) x ^ 2 = 1 := ...
grind_pattern [sin_sq_add_cos_sq]](#manual-sin_sq_add_cos_sq) => [sin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Bigger-Examples/#sin) x, [cos](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Bigger-Examples/#cos) x
```

which will instantiate the theorem as soon as **both** `[sin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Bigger-Examples/#sin) x` and `[cos](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Bigger-Examples/#cos) x` (with the same `x`) are encountered.
This theorem will then automatically enter the Gröbner basis module, and be used to reason about polynomial expressions involving both `[sin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Bigger-Examples/#sin) x` and `[cos](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Bigger-Examples/#cos) x`.
One both alternatively, more aggressively, write two separate grind patterns so that this theorem instantiated when either `[sin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Bigger-Examples/#sin) x` or `[cos](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Bigger-Examples/#cos) x` is encountered.

---



## The grind tactic — 16.11. Reducibility {#manual-the-grind-tactic-1611-reducibility}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Reducibility/

[Reducible]](#manual---tech-term-Reducible) definitions in terms are eagerly unfolded by `[grind]](#manual-grind)`.
This enables more efficient definitional equality comparisons and indexing.

**Example: Reducibility and Congruence Closure**

The definition of `[one]](#manual-one-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Congruence-Closure_RPAR_)` is not [reducible]](#manual---tech-term-Reducible):

```lean
def one := 1
```

This means that `[grind]](#manual-grind)` does not unfold it:

```lean
example : [one]](#manual-one-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Congruence-Closure_RPAR_) = 1 := by⊢ [one]](#manual-one-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Congruence-Closure_RPAR_) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 1 [grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

```lean
`grind` failed
grindh:[¬](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)[one]](#manual-one-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Congruence-Closure_RPAR_) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 1⊢ [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)
[grind] Goal diagnostics

- [facts] Asserted facts
  - [prop] [¬](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)[one]](#manual-one-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Congruence-Closure_RPAR_) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 1
- [eqc] False propositions
  - [prop] [one]](#manual-one-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Congruence-Closure_RPAR_) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 1
- [cutsat] Assignment satisfying linear constraints
  - [assign] [one]](#manual-one-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Congruence-Closure_RPAR_) := 2
```

`[two]](#manual-two-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Congruence-Closure_RPAR_)`, on the other hand, is an abbreviation and thus reducible:

```lean
abbrev two := 2
```

`[grind]](#manual-grind)` unfolds `[two]](#manual-two-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Congruence-Closure_RPAR_)` before adding it to the “whiteboard”, allowing the proof to be completed immediately:

```lean
example : [two]](#manual-two-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Congruence-Closure_RPAR_) = 2 := by⊢ [two]](#manual-two-_LPAR_in-Reducibility-and-Congruence-Closure_RPAR_) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 2 [grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

E-matching patterns also unfold reducible definitions.
The patterns generated for theorems about abbreviations are expressed in terms of the unfolded abbreviations.
Abbreviations should not generally be recursive; in particular, when using `[grind]](#manual-grind)`, recursive abbreviations can result in poor indexing performance and unpredictable patterns.

**Example: E-matching and Unfolding Abbreviations**

When adding `grind` annotations to theorems, E-matching patterns are generated based on the theorem statement.
These patterns determine when the theorem is instantiated.
The theorem `[one_eq_1]](#manual-one_eq_1-_LPAR_in-E-matching-and-Unfolding-Abbreviations_RPAR_)` mentions the [semireducible]](#manual---tech-term-Semireducible) definition `[one]](#manual-one-_LPAR_in-E-matching-and-Unfolding-Abbreviations_RPAR_)`, and the resulting pattern is also `[one]](#manual-one-_LPAR_in-E-matching-and-Unfolding-Abbreviations_RPAR_)`:

```lean
def one := 1
@[[grind?]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Attr___grind___-next) =]
theorem one_eq_1 : [one]](#manual-one-_LPAR_in-E-matching-and-Unfolding-Abbreviations_RPAR_) = 1 := by⊢ [one]](#manual-one-_LPAR_in-E-matching-and-Unfolding-Abbreviations_RPAR_) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 1 [rfl]](#manual-rfl)All goals completed! 🐙
```

```lean
[one_eq_1]](#manual-one_eq_1-_LPAR_in-E-matching-and-Unfolding-Abbreviations_RPAR_): [[one]](#manual-one-_LPAR_in-E-matching-and-Unfolding-Abbreviations_RPAR_)]
```

Applying the same annotation to a theorem about the [`reducible`]](#manual---tech-term-Reducible) abbreviation `[two]](#manual-two-_LPAR_in-E-matching-and-Unfolding-Abbreviations_RPAR_)` results in a pattern in which `[two]](#manual-two-_LPAR_in-E-matching-and-Unfolding-Abbreviations_RPAR_)` is unfolded:

```lean
abbrev two := 2
@[[grind?]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Attr___grind___-next) =]
theorem two_eq_2: [two]](#manual-two-_LPAR_in-E-matching-and-Unfolding-Abbreviations_RPAR_) = 2 := by⊢ [two]](#manual-two-_LPAR_in-E-matching-and-Unfolding-Abbreviations_RPAR_) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 2 [grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

```lean
[two_eq_2]](#manual-two_eq_2-_LPAR_in-E-matching-and-Unfolding-Abbreviations_RPAR_): [[@]](#manual-OfNat___mk)[OfNat.ofNat]](#manual-OfNat___mk) `[[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)] `[2] `[instOfNatNat 2]]
```

**Example: Recursive Abbreviations and grind**

Using the `grind` attribute to add E-matching patterns for a recursive abbreviation's [equational lemmas]](#manual---tech-term-equational-lemmas) does not result in useful patterns for recursive abbreviations.
The `[@[]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)grind?[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Attributes/#Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)` attribute on this definition of the Fibonacci function results in three patterns, each corresponding to one of the three possibilities:

```lean
@[[grind?]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Attr___grind___-next)]
def fib : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| 0 => 0
| 1 => 1
| n + 2 => fib n + fib (n + 1)
```

```lean
fib.eq_1: [fib `[0]]
```

```lean
fib.eq_2: [fib `[1]]
```

```lean
fib.eq_3: [fib (#0 + 2)]
```

Replacing the definition with an abbreviation results in patterns in which occurrences of the function are unfolded.
These patterns are not particularly useful:

```lean
@[[grind?]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Attr___grind___-next)]
abbrev fib : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| 0 => 0
| 1 => 1
| n + 2 => fib n + fib (n + 1)
```

```lean
fib.eq_1: [[@]](#manual-OfNat___mk)[OfNat.ofNat]](#manual-OfNat___mk) `[[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)] `[0] `[instOfNatNat 0]]
```

```lean
fib.eq_2: [[@]](#manual-OfNat___mk)[OfNat.ofNat]](#manual-OfNat___mk) `[[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)] `[1] `[instOfNatNat 1]]
```

```lean
fib.eq_3: [[@]](#manual-HAdd___mk)[HAdd.hAdd]](#manual-HAdd___mk) `[[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)] `[[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)] `[[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)] `[instHAdd] (fib #0) (fib (#0 + 1))]
```

---



## The grind tactic — 16.12. Bigger Examples {#manual-the-grind-tactic-1612-bigger-examples}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--grind--tactic/Bigger-Examples/

### 16.12.1. Integrating `grind`'s Features {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--The--grind--tactic--Bigger-Examples--Integrating--grind-___s-Features}

This example demonstrates how the various submodules of `[grind]](#manual-grind)` are seamlessly integrated.
In particular we can:

- instantiate theorems from the library, using custom patterns,
- perform case splitting,
- do linear integer arithmetic reasoning, including modularity conditions, and
- do Gröbner basis reasoning
  all without providing explicit instructions to drive the interactions between these modes of reasoning.

For this example we'll begin with a “mocked up” version of the real numbers, and the `sin` and `cos` functions.
Of course, this example works [without any changes](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/master/MathlibTest/grind/trig.lean) using Mathlib's versions of these!

```lean
[axiom]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___axiom-next) R : Type
@[[instance]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Attr___instance)] [axiom]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___axiom-next) instCommRingR : [Lean.Grind.CommRing]](#manual-Lean___Grind___CommRing___mk) [R]](#manual-R)
[axiom]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___axiom-next) sin : [R]](#manual-R) → [R]](#manual-R)
[axiom]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___axiom-next) cos : [R]](#manual-R) → [R]](#manual-R)
[axiom]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___axiom-next) trig_identity : ∀ x, ([cos]](#manual-cos) x)^2 + ([sin]](#manual-sin) x)^2 = 1
```

Our first step is to tell grind to “put the trig identity on the whiteboard” whenever it sees a goal involving `[sin]](#manual-sin)` or `[cos]](#manual-cos)`:

```lean
grind_pattern [trig_identity]](#manual-trig_identity) => [cos]](#manual-cos) x
grind_pattern [trig_identity]](#manual-trig_identity) => [sin]](#manual-sin) x
```

Note here we use **two** different patterns for the same theorem, so the theorem is instantiated even if `[grind]](#manual-grind)` sees just one of these functions.
If we preferred to more conservatively instantiate the theorem only when both `[sin]](#manual-sin)` and `[cos]](#manual-cos)` are present, we could have used a multi-pattern:

```lean
grind_pattern [trig_identity]](#manual-trig_identity) => [cos]](#manual-cos) x, [sin]](#manual-sin) x
```

For this example, either approach will work.

Because `grind` immediately notices the trig identity, we can prove goals like this:

```lean
example : ([cos]](#manual-cos) x + [sin]](#manual-sin) x)^2 = 2 * [cos]](#manual-cos) x * [sin]](#manual-sin) x + 1 := byx:[R]](#manual-R)⊢ [(]](#manual-HAdd___mk)[cos]](#manual-cos) x [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) [sin]](#manual-sin) x[)]](#manual-HAdd___mk) [^]](#manual-HPow___mk) 2 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 2 [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) [cos]](#manual-cos) x [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) [sin]](#manual-sin) x [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 1
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

Here `[grind]](#manual-grind)` does the following:

1. It notices `[cos]](#manual-cos) x` and `[sin]](#manual-sin) x`, so instantiates the trig identity.
2. It notices that this is a polynomial in `[CommRing]](#manual-Lean___Grind___CommRing___mk) [R]](#manual-R)`, and sends it to the Gröbner basis module.
   No calculation happens at this point: it's the first polynomial relation in this ring, so the Gröbner basis is updated to `[([cos]](#manual-cos) x)^2 + ([sin]](#manual-sin) x)^2 - 1]`.
3. It notices that the left and right hand sides of the goal are polynomials in `[CommRing]](#manual-Lean___Grind___CommRing___mk) [R]](#manual-R)`, and sends them to the Gröbner basis module for normalization.

Since their normal forms modulo `([cos]](#manual-cos) x)^2 + ([sin]](#manual-sin) x)^2 = 1` are equal, their equivalence classes are merged, and the goal is solved.

We can also do this sort of argument when [congruence closure]](#manual---tech-term-Congruence-closure) is needed:

```lean
example (f : [R]](#manual-R) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) :
f (([cos]](#manual-cos) x + [sin]](#manual-sin) x)^2) = f (2 * [cos]](#manual-cos) x * [sin]](#manual-sin) x + 1) := byx:[R]](#manual-R)f:[R]](#manual-R) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ f [(]](#manual-HPow___mk)[(]](#manual-HAdd___mk)[cos]](#manual-cos) x [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) [sin]](#manual-sin) x[)]](#manual-HAdd___mk) [^]](#manual-HPow___mk) 2[)]](#manual-HPow___mk) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) f [(]](#manual-HAdd___mk)2 [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) [cos]](#manual-cos) x [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) [sin]](#manual-sin) x [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 1[)]](#manual-HAdd___mk)
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

As before, `[grind]](#manual-grind)` instantiates the trig identity, notices that `([cos]](#manual-cos) x + [sin]](#manual-sin) x)^2` and `2 * [cos]](#manual-cos) x * [sin]](#manual-sin) x + 1` are equal modulo `([cos]](#manual-cos) x)^2 + ([sin]](#manual-sin) x)^2 = 1`,
puts those algebraic expressions in the same equivalence class, and then puts the function applications `f (([cos]](#manual-cos) x + [sin]](#manual-sin) x)^2)` and `f (2 * [cos]](#manual-cos) x * [sin]](#manual-sin) x + 1)` in the same equivalence class,
and closes the goal.

Notice that we've used an arbitrary function `f : [R]](#manual-R) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` here; let's check that `grind` can use some linear integer arithmetic reasoning after the Gröbner basis steps:

```lean
example (f : [R]](#manual-R) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) :
4 * f (([cos]](#manual-cos) x + [sin]](#manual-sin) x)^2) ≠ 2 + f (2 * [cos]](#manual-cos) x * [sin]](#manual-sin) x + 1) := byx:[R]](#manual-R)f✝:[R]](#manual-R) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)n:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)f:[R]](#manual-R) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ 4 [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) f [(]](#manual-HPow___mk)[(]](#manual-HAdd___mk)[cos]](#manual-cos) x [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) [sin]](#manual-sin) x[)]](#manual-HAdd___mk) [^]](#manual-HPow___mk) 2[)]](#manual-HPow___mk) ≠ 2 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) f [(]](#manual-HAdd___mk)2 [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) [cos]](#manual-cos) x [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) [sin]](#manual-sin) x [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 1[)]](#manual-HAdd___mk)
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

Here `[grind]](#manual-grind)` first works out that this goal reduces to `4 * n ≠ 2 + n` for some `n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` (i.e. by identifying the two function applications as described above), and then uses modularity to derive a contradiction.

Finally, we can also mix in some case splitting:

```lean
example (f : [R]](#manual-R) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) :
[max]](#manual-Max___mk) 3 (4 * f (([cos]](#manual-cos) x + [sin]](#manual-sin) x)^2)) ≠
2 + f (2 * [cos]](#manual-cos) x * [sin]](#manual-sin) x + 1) := byx:[R]](#manual-R)f✝:[R]](#manual-R) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)n:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)f:[R]](#manual-R) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ [max]](#manual-Max___mk) 3 [(]](#manual-HMul___mk)4 [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) f [(]](#manual-HPow___mk)[(]](#manual-HAdd___mk)[cos]](#manual-cos) x [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) [sin]](#manual-sin) x[)]](#manual-HAdd___mk) [^]](#manual-HPow___mk) 2[)]](#manual-HPow___mk)[)]](#manual-HMul___mk) ≠ 2 [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) f [(]](#manual-HAdd___mk)2 [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) [cos]](#manual-cos) x [*]](#manual-HMul___mk) [sin]](#manual-sin) x [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 1[)]](#manual-HAdd___mk)
[grind]](#manual-grind)All goals completed! 🐙
```

As before, `[grind]](#manual-grind)` first does the instantiation and Gröbner basis calculations required to identify the two function applications.
However the `cutsat` algorithm by itself can't do anything with `[max]](#manual-Max___mk) 3 (4 * n) ≠ 2 + n`.
Next, after instantiating `Nat.max_def` (automatically, because of an annotation in the standard library) which states `∀ {n m : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)}, [max]](#manual-Max___mk) n m = [if]](#manual-termIfThenElse) n ≤ m [then]](#manual-termIfThenElse) m [else]](#manual-termIfThenElse) n`, `[grind]](#manual-grind)` can then case split on the inequality.
In the branch `3 ≤ 4 * n`, `cutsat` again uses modularity to prove `4 * n ≠ 2 + n`.
In the branch `4 * n < 3`, `cutsat` quickly determines `n = 0`, and then notices that `4 * 0 ≠ 2 + 0`.

This has been, of course, a quite artificial example!
In practice, this sort of automatic integration of different reasoning modes is very powerful: the central “whiteboard” which tracks instantiated theorems and equivalence classes can hand off relevant terms and equalities to the appropriate modules (here, `cutsat` and Gröbner bases), which can then return new facts to the whiteboard.

### 16.12.2. `if`-`then`-`else` Normalization {#manual-grind-if-then-else-norm}

This example is a showcase for the “out of the box” power of `[grind]](#manual-grind)`.
Later examples will explore adding `[@[]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)grind[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Attributes/#Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)` annotations as part of the development process, to make `[grind]](#manual-grind)` more effective in a new domain.
This example does not rely on any of the algebra extensions to `[grind]](#manual-grind)`, we're just using:

- instantiation of annotated theorems from the library,
- [congruence closure]](#manual---tech-term-Congruence-closure), and
- case splitting.

The solution here builds on an earlier formalization by Chris Hughes, but with some notable improvements:

- the verification is separate from the code,
- the proof is now a one-liner combining `[fun_induction]](#manual-fun_induction)` and `[grind]](#manual-grind)`,
- the proof is robust to changes in the code (e.g. swapping out `[HashMap](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Maps-and-Sets/#Std___HashMap)` for `[TreeMap](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Maps-and-Sets/#Std___TreeMap)`) as well as changes to the precise verification conditions.

#### 16.12.2.1. The problem {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--The--grind--tactic--Bigger-Examples--if---then---else--Normalization--The-problem}

Here is Rustan Leino's original description of the problem, as [posted by Leonardo de Moura](https://leanprover.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/113488-general/topic/Rustan's.20challenge) on the Lean Zulip:

> The data structure is an expression with Boolean literals, variables, and if-then-else expressions.
>
> The goal is to normalize such expressions into a form where:
> a) No nested ifs: the condition part of an if-expression is not itself an if-expression
> b) No constant tests: the condition part of an if-expression is not a constant
> c) No redundant ifs: the then and else branches of an if are not the same
> d) Each variable is evaluated at most once: the free variables of the condition are disjoint from those in the then branch, and also disjoint from those in the else branch.
>
> One should show that a normalization function produces an expression satisfying these four conditions, and one should also prove that the normalization function preserves the meaning of the given expression.

#### 16.12.2.2. The Formal Statement {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--The--grind--tactic--Bigger-Examples--if---then---else--Normalization--The-Formal-Statement}

To formalize the statement in Lean, we use an inductive type `[IfExpr]](#manual-IfExpr)`:

```lean
/--
An if-expression is either boolean literal, a
numbered variable, or an if-then-else expression
where each subexpression is an if-expression.
-/
inductive IfExpr
| lit : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) → [IfExpr]](#manual-IfExpr)
| var : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [IfExpr]](#manual-IfExpr)
| ite : [IfExpr]](#manual-IfExpr) → [IfExpr]](#manual-IfExpr) → [IfExpr]](#manual-IfExpr) → [IfExpr]](#manual-IfExpr)
[deriving]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___optDeriving-next) [DecidableEq]](#manual-DecidableEq)
```

and define some inductive predicates and an `[eval]](#manual-IfExpr___eval)` function, so we can state the four desired properties:

```lean
[namespace]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) IfExpr
/--
An if-expression has a "nested if" if it contains
an if-then-else where the "if" is itself an if-then-else.
-/
def hasNestedIf : [IfExpr]](#manual-IfExpr) → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| [lit]](#manual-IfExpr___lit) _ => [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| [var]](#manual-IfExpr___var) _ => [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| [ite]](#manual-IfExpr___ite) ([ite]](#manual-IfExpr___ite) _ _ _) _ _ => [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| [ite]](#manual-IfExpr___ite) _ t e => t.[hasNestedIf]](#manual-IfExpr___hasNestedIf) || e.[hasNestedIf]](#manual-IfExpr___hasNestedIf)
/--
An if-expression has a "constant if" if it contains
an if-then-else where the "if" is itself a literal.
-/
def hasConstantIf : [IfExpr]](#manual-IfExpr) → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| [lit]](#manual-IfExpr___lit) _ => [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| [var]](#manual-IfExpr___var) _ => [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| [ite]](#manual-IfExpr___ite) ([lit]](#manual-IfExpr___lit) _) _ _ => [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| [ite]](#manual-IfExpr___ite) i t e =>
i.[hasConstantIf]](#manual-IfExpr___hasConstantIf) || t.[hasConstantIf]](#manual-IfExpr___hasConstantIf) || e.[hasConstantIf]](#manual-IfExpr___hasConstantIf)
/--
An if-expression has a "redundant if" if
it contains an if-then-else where
the "then" and "else" clauses are identical.
-/
def hasRedundantIf : [IfExpr]](#manual-IfExpr) → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| [lit]](#manual-IfExpr___lit) _ => [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| [var]](#manual-IfExpr___var) _ => [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| [ite]](#manual-IfExpr___ite) i t e => t == e || i.[hasRedundantIf]](#manual-IfExpr___hasRedundantIf) ||
t.[hasRedundantIf]](#manual-IfExpr___hasRedundantIf) || e.[hasRedundantIf]](#manual-IfExpr___hasRedundantIf)
/--
All the variables appearing in an if-expressions,
read left to right, without removing duplicates.
-/
def vars : [IfExpr]](#manual-IfExpr) → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| [lit]](#manual-IfExpr___lit) _ => []
| [var]](#manual-IfExpr___var) i => [i]
| [ite]](#manual-IfExpr___ite) i t e => i.[vars]](#manual-IfExpr___vars) ++ t.[vars]](#manual-IfExpr___vars) ++ e.[vars]](#manual-IfExpr___vars)
/--
A helper function to specify that two lists are disjoint.
-/
def _root_.List.disjoint {α} [[DecidableEq]](#manual-DecidableEq) α] :
[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| [], _ => [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| x::xs, ys => x ∉ ys && xs.[disjoint]](#manual-List___disjoint) ys
/--
An if expression evaluates each variable at most once if
for each if-then-else the variables in the "if" clause
are disjoint from the variables in the "then" clause
and the variables in the "if" clause
are disjoint from the variables in the "else" clause.
-/
def disjoint : [IfExpr]](#manual-IfExpr) → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| [lit]](#manual-IfExpr___lit) _ => [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| [var]](#manual-IfExpr___var) _ => [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| [ite]](#manual-IfExpr___ite) i t e =>
i.[vars]](#manual-IfExpr___vars).[disjoint]](#manual-List___disjoint) t.[vars]](#manual-IfExpr___vars) && i.[vars]](#manual-IfExpr___vars).[disjoint]](#manual-List___disjoint) e.[vars]](#manual-IfExpr___vars) &&
i.[disjoint]](#manual-IfExpr___disjoint) && t.[disjoint]](#manual-IfExpr___disjoint) && e.[disjoint]](#manual-IfExpr___disjoint)
/--
An if expression is "normalized" if it has
no nested, constant, or redundant ifs,
and it evaluates each variable at most once.
-/
def normalized (e : [IfExpr]](#manual-IfExpr)) : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) :=
!e.[hasNestedIf]](#manual-IfExpr___hasNestedIf) && !e.[hasConstantIf]](#manual-IfExpr___hasConstantIf) &&
!e.[hasRedundantIf]](#manual-IfExpr___hasRedundantIf) && e.[disjoint]](#manual-IfExpr___disjoint)
/--
The evaluation of an if expression
at some assignment of variables.
-/
def eval (f : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) : [IfExpr]](#manual-IfExpr) → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| [lit]](#manual-IfExpr___lit) b => b
| [var]](#manual-IfExpr___var) i => f i
| [ite]](#manual-IfExpr___ite) i t e => [bif]](#manual-boolIfThenElse) i.[eval]](#manual-IfExpr___eval) f [then]](#manual-boolIfThenElse) t.[eval]](#manual-IfExpr___eval) f [else]](#manual-boolIfThenElse) e.[eval]](#manual-IfExpr___eval) f
end IfExpr
```

Using these we can state the problem. The challenge is to inhabit the following type (and to do so nicely!):

```lean
def IfNormalization : Type :=
{ Z : [IfExpr]](#manual-IfExpr) → [IfExpr]](#manual-IfExpr) // ∀ e, (Z e).[normalized]](#manual-IfExpr___normalized) ∧ (Z e).[eval]](#manual-IfExpr___eval) = e.[eval]](#manual-IfExpr___eval) }
```

#### 16.12.2.3. Other solutions {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--The--grind--tactic--Bigger-Examples--if---then---else--Normalization--Other-solutions}

At this point, it's worth pausing and doing at least one of the following:

- Try to prove this yourself! It's quite challenging for a beginner!
  You can [have a go](https://live.lean-lang.org/#project=lean-nightly&url=https%3A%2F%2Fgist.githubusercontent.com%2Fkim-em%2Ff416b31fe29de8a3f1b2b3a84e0f1793%2Fraw%2F75ca61230b50c126f8658bacd933ecf7bfcaa4b8%2Fgrind_ite.lean)
  in the Live Lean editor without any installation.
- Read Chris Hughes's [solution](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/master/Archive/Examples/IfNormalization/Result.lean),
  which is included in the Mathlib Archive.
  This solution makes good use of Aesop, but is not ideal because

  1. It defines the solution using a subtype, simultaneously giving the construction and proving properties about it.
     We think it's better stylistically to keep these separate.
  2. Even with Aesop automation, there's still about 15 lines of manual proof work before we can hand off to Aesop.
- Read Wojciech Nawrocki's [solution](https://leanprover.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/113488-general/topic/Rustan's.20challenge/near/398824748).
  This one uses less automation, at about 300 lines of proof work.

#### 16.12.2.4. The solution using `[grind]](#manual-grind)` {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--The--grind--tactic--Bigger-Examples--if---then---else--Normalization--The-solution-using--grind}

Actually solving the problem is not that hard:
we just need a recursive function that carries along a record of “already assigned variables”,
and then, whenever performing a branch on a variable, adding a new assignment in each of the branches.
It also needs to flatten nested if-then-else expressions which have another if-then-else in the “condition” position.
(This is extracted from Chris Hughes's solution, but without the subtyping.)

Let's work inside the `IfExpr` namespace.

```lean
[namespace]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) IfExpr
```

```lean

This is pretty straightforward, but it immediately runs into a problem:

```lean
fail to show termination for
  IfExpr.normalize
with errors
failed to infer structural recursion:
Cannot use parameter assign:
  the type [HashMap](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Maps-and-Sets/#Std___HashMap) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) does not have a `.brecOn` recursor
Cannot use parameter #2:
  failed to eliminate recursive application
    normalize assign (a.[ite]](#manual-IfExpr___ite) (b.[ite]](#manual-IfExpr___ite) t e) (c.[ite]](#manual-IfExpr___ite) t e))


Could not find a decreasing measure.
```

Lean here is telling us that it can't see that the function is terminating.
Often Lean is pretty good at working this out for itself, but for sufficiently complicated functions
we need to step in to give it a hint.

In this case we can see that it's the recursive call
`ite (ite a b c) t e` which is calling `normalize` on `(ite a (ite b t e) (ite c t e))`
where Lean is having difficulty. Lean has made a guess at a plausible termination measure,
based on using automatically generated `[sizeOf]](#manual-SizeOf___mk)` function, but can't prove the resulting goal,
essentially because `t` and `e` appear multiple times in the recursive call.

To address problems like this, we nearly always want to stop using the automatically generated `sizeOf` function,
and construct our own termination measure. We'll use

```lean
@[simp] def normSize : [IfExpr]](#manual-IfExpr) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| [lit]](#manual-IfExpr___lit) _ => 0
| [var]](#manual-IfExpr___var) _ => 1
| [.ite]](#manual-IfExpr___ite) i t e => 2 * [normSize]](#manual-IfExpr___normSize) i + [max]](#manual-Max___mk) ([normSize]](#manual-IfExpr___normSize) t) ([normSize]](#manual-IfExpr___normSize) e) + 1
```

Many different functions would work here. The basic idea is to increase the “weight” of the “condition” branch
(this is the multiplicative factor in the `2 * normSize i` ),
so that as long the “condition” part shrinks a bit, the whole expression counts as shrinking even if the “then” and “else” branches have grown.
We've annotated the definition with `[@[]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)simp[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Attributes/#Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)` so Lean's automated termination checker is allowed to unfold the definition.

With this in place, the definition goes through using the `termination_by` clause:

```lean

| [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) b => [lit]](#manual-IfExpr___lit) b

Now it's time to prove some properties of this function.
We're just going to package together all the properties we want:

```lean
theorem normalize_spec
(assign : [Std.HashMap](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Maps-and-Sets/#Std___HashMap) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) (e : [IfExpr]](#manual-IfExpr)) :
(normalize assign e).[normalized]](#manual-IfExpr___normalized)
∧ (∀ f, (normalize assign e).[eval]](#manual-IfExpr___eval) f =
e.[eval]](#manual-IfExpr___eval) fun w => assign[w]?.[getD](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___getD) (f w))
∧ ∀ (v : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)),
v ∈ [vars]](#manual-IfExpr___vars) (normalize assign e) → ¬ v ∈ assign :=
sorry
```

That is:

- the result of `normalize` is actually normalized according to the initial definitions,
- if we normalize an “if-then-else” expression using some assignments, and then evaluate the remaining variables,
  we get the same result as evaluating the original “if-then-else” using the composite of the two assignments,
- and any variable appearing in the assignments no longer appears in the normalized expression.

You might think that we should state these three properties as separate lemmas,
but it turns out that proving them all at once is really convenient, because we can use the `[fun_induction]](#manual-fun_induction)`
tactic to assume that all these properties hold for `normalize` in the recursive calls, and then
`[grind]](#manual-grind)` will just put all the facts together for the result:

```lean

[disjoint]](#manual-IfExpr___disjoint) [vars]](#manual-IfExpr___vars) [eval]](#manual-IfExpr___eval) [List.disjoint]](#manual-List___disjoint)

The fact that the `[fun_induction]](#manual-fun_induction)` plus `[grind]](#manual-grind)` combination just works here is sort of astonishing.
We're really excited about this, and we're hoping to see a lot more proofs in this style!

A lovely consequence of highly automated proofs is that often you have some flexibility to change the statements,
without changing the proof at all! As examples, the particular way that we asserted above that
“any variable appearing in the assignments no longer appears in the normalized expression”
could be stated in many different ways (although not omitted!). The variations really don't matter,
and `[grind]](#manual-grind)` can both prove, and use, any of them:

Here we use `assign.contains v = false`:

## The mvcgen tactic {#manual-the-mvcgen-tactic}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--mvcgen--tactic/

## 17. The `mvcgen` tactic

## Tutorials

- [Verifying Imperative Programs Using `mvcgen`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/tutorials/4.34.0-rc1//#mvcgen-tactic-tutorial)

The `[mvcgen]](#manual-mvcgen)` tactic implements a *monadic verification condition generator*:
It breaks down a goal involving a program written using Lean's imperative [`do`](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Term___do) notation into a number of smaller [*verification conditions*](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--mvcgen--tactic/Overview/#--tech-term-verification-conditions) (VCs) that are sufficient to prove the goal.
In addition to a reference that describes the use of `[mvcgen]](#manual-mvcgen)`, this chapter includes a [tutorial](https://lean-lang.org/doc/tutorials/4.34.0-rc1//#mvcgen-tactic-tutorial) that can be read independently of the reference.

In order to use the `[mvcgen]](#manual-mvcgen)` tactic, `Std.Tactic.Do` must be imported and the namespace `Std.Do` must be opened.

1. [17.1. Overview](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--mvcgen--tactic/Overview/#The-Lean-Language-Reference--The--mvcgen--tactic--Overview)
2. [17.2. Predicate Transformers](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--mvcgen--tactic/Predicate-Transformers/#The-Lean-Language-Reference--The--mvcgen--tactic--Predicate-Transformers)
3. [17.3. Verification Conditions](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--mvcgen--tactic/Verification-Conditions/#The-Lean-Language-Reference--The--mvcgen--tactic--Verification-Conditions)
4. [17.4. Enabling `mvcgen` For Monads](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--mvcgen--tactic/Enabling--mvcgen--For-Monads/#The-Lean-Language-Reference--The--mvcgen--tactic--Enabling--mvcgen--For-Monads)
5. [17.5. Proof Mode](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The--mvcgen--tactic/Proof-Mode/#mvcgen-proof-mode)
